Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and, outside it, an outer membrane whose outer leaflet is made largely of lipopolysaccharide. This extra membrane keeps many compounds out and makes gram-negative bacteria harder to treat.

Antimicrobial peptides are part of innate immunity in many animals. Most are short, carry a positive charge and fold so that nonpolar and charged residues sit on opposite faces. The positive charge draws the peptide to the negatively charged surfaces of bacterial membranes, and the nonpolar face lets it insert into the lipid interior, forming pores. Mammalian plasma membranes have mostly neutral outer leaflets and contain cholesterol, which makes them less attractive targets.

Researchers tested peptide P, a 22-residue peptide with six lysines, against two bacteria and against human red blood cells. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) is the lowest concentration that stops visible growth. Hemolysis was measured as the release of hemoglobin from red blood cells, and membrane permeability was measured with a dye that enters only cells with damaged membranes (Table 1).

The MIC was read after 18 hours of growth in broth, and each measurement was repeated three times on separate days. Wells with no peptide grew to full density every time, and wells with no bacteria stayed clear, confirming that the medium was not contaminated.

Killing was rapid: at four times the MIC, more than 99% of S. aureus cells were killed within 20 minutes, before the cells could divide. In a serial-passage experiment, S. aureus was grown for 25 days in gradually rising concentrations of peptide P or of ciprofloxacin, an antibiotic that inhibits DNA gyrase. The MIC of ciprofloxacin rose 64-fold over this period, while the MIC of peptide P rose twofold. Adding 150 mM NaCl raised peptide P's MIC against S. aureus from 4 to 32 µg/mL.

qs.q: Why is peptide P less active against E. coli than against S. aureus?
o: E. coli divides too quickly to be killed
E. coli has a thicker peptidoglycan layer
Correct: a second barrier must be crossed.
E. coli membranes carry a positive charge
qs.x: Correct: Gram-negative bacteria have an outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharide that excludes many compounds. Loosening it lowered the MIC from 16 to 2 µg/mL, which identifies that barrier as the obstacle. Why the others are wrong: The thick peptidoglycan belongs to gram-positive cells; bacterial surfaces are negatively charged, which attracts the peptide; killing was faster than division. Trap: Assuming the thicker wall is always the greater barrier.

qs.q: Why does peptide P damage bacterial membranes but spare red blood cells?
o: Bacterial surfaces are more negatively charged
Red blood cells have no mitochondria to damage
Red blood cells have no plasma membrane
qs.x: Correct: The peptide's lysines give it a positive charge, and electrostatic attraction concentrates it on the negatively charged bacterial surface. Mammalian outer leaflets are largely neutral and contain cholesterol, which stiffens the bilayer, so only 3% hemolysis occurred at a concentration that permeabilized most bacteria. Why the others are wrong: Red blood cells have a plasma membrane; the mechanism does not involve mitochondria; cholesterol is found in animal rather than bacterial membranes. Trap: Looking for a target inside the cell when the mechanism acts at the surface.

qs.q: What does the salt result suggest about how the peptide works?
o: Correct: binding weakens, so more peptide is needed.
Salt destroys the peptide's amino acids
Salt does not break peptide bonds.
MIC measures growth inhibition, not nutrition.
qs.x: Correct: Dissolved ions surround charged groups and weaken the electrostatic attraction between the positively charged peptide and the negatively charged bacterial surface. More peptide is then needed, so the MIC rose from 4 to 32 µg/mL. This is a known obstacle to using such peptides in blood, which contains about 150 mM salt. Why the others are wrong: Salt does not hydrolyze the peptide; no membrane change is described; the assay measures inhibition of growth. Trap: Treating a change in MIC as proof that the drug was destroyed.

qs.q: Why did resistance develop so much more slowly to peptide P than to ciprofloxacin?
o: Peptide P was used at a lower concentration
Peptide P does not kill the bacteria
The membrane target has no single mutation
qs.x: Correct: Ciprofloxacin acts on one enzyme, so a single point mutation in DNA gyrase can reduce binding. Peptide P acts on the membrane itself, and a cell would need to remodel the charge of its entire surface, which is costly and requires many changes. Why the others are wrong: Both were tested the same way; killing speed does not by itself set the rate of resistance; the peptide killed effectively. Trap: Assuming resistance arises at the same rate for any effective drug.

qs.q: Why does rapid killing argue against a mechanism that blocks cell wall synthesis?
o: Killing speed is the same for every mechanism
Wall synthesis occurs only in gram-negative cells
Wall-synthesis inhibitors need cells to grow
Peptidoglycan is not part of the cell wall
qs.x: Correct: A drug that blocks wall synthesis kills as the growing cell fails to maintain its wall, which takes at least a division cycle. Peptide P killed more than 99% of cells in 20 minutes, before division, which fits immediate membrane damage. Why the others are wrong: Both gram types synthesize peptidoglycan; peptidoglycan is the wall's main polymer; killing speed varies by mechanism. Trap: Overlooking timing as evidence about mechanism.

r: E. coli plus a compound that loosens the outer membrane

passages.title: Individual influences on behavior · passage
text: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is defined by inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity that begin in childhood, exceed what is expected for the child's developmental level, and cause impairment. A central requirement is that the symptoms appear in more than one setting, which is why evaluations collect ratings from parents and from teachers rather than from either source alone.

The reason for that requirement is diagnostic rather than statistical. Difficulty confined to one setting usually has a cause located in that setting: a mismatch between a child and a particular classroom, an unmanageable schedule at home, or a teacher whose tolerance for movement is low. A disorder of attentional control, by contrast, should follow the child across settings, so cross-setting agreement is evidence that the problem is in the child rather than in the environment.

The treatments act on catecholamine signaling. Stimulants block reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, raising their availability in prefrontal circuits that support working memory and inhibitory control. Atomoxetine, a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, is an alternative that is not a stimulant.

A specialty clinic evaluated 200 children referred for attention problems, collecting standardized rating scales from one parent and one teacher for each child, and recorded whether the child ultimately met full diagnostic criteria after a full evaluation (Table 1).

The gradient is steep. Agreement between informants is almost diagnostic on its own, at 96%, while a single elevated informant leaves roughly nine in ten children not meeting criteria, which is what the cross-setting requirement is designed to accomplish.

Two cautions follow. These are referred children, so the proportions in each row describe a clinic population and not the general population, where the share of children with elevated ratings anywhere is much lower. More importantly, the rating pattern was part of the information available when the diagnosis was made, so the association between agreement and diagnosis is partly circular; an independent diagnostic procedure blind to the ratings would be needed to estimate how well informant agreement actually predicts the disorder.

qs.q: Why does the diagnosis require symptoms in more than one setting?
o: Difficulty in only one setting usually has a cause in that setting
Teachers rate children far more accurately than their parents do at home
The symptoms of this disorder appear only at school
Two settings provide twice as many symptoms to count
The count is not what changes.
qs.x: Correct: A disorder of attentional control should travel with the child, so problems confined to one setting point instead to something about that setting, and requiring both informants screens those cases out. Why the others are wrong: Neither informant is treated as the more accurate, the requirement is about generality rather than symptom count, and school-only presentation is exactly what the criterion excludes. Trap: Reading a criterion meant to locate the cause as a way of gathering more evidence.

qs.q: What is the strongest reason to doubt that informant agreement predicts the diagnosis as well as Table 1 suggests?
o: All of the children had been referred for attention problems
Only 200 children were evaluated at the clinic
The rating scales informed the diagnosis itself
Correct: the predictor entered the outcome.
One parent and one teacher rated each of the children
qs.x: Correct: Clinicians who made the diagnosis could see the rating scales, so children with agreement across settings were more likely to be diagnosed partly because the agreement counted as evidence, which inflates the association beyond what an independent diagnosis would show. Why the others are wrong: Sample size affects the precision of the estimates, referral status limits how far the proportions generalize, and the two-informant design is appropriate. Trap: Choosing a generalization limit when the flaw is that predictor and outcome are not independent.

qs.q: Which neurotransmitter systems do stimulant medications mainly act on?
qs.x: Correct: Stimulants block the transporters that clear dopamine and norepinephrine from the synapse, raising signaling in prefrontal circuits that support working memory and inhibition. Why the others are wrong: Serotonin and γ-aminobutyric acid are targets of antidepressants and anxiolytics, while acetylcholine, glycine, histamine and glutamate are not what these medications act on. Trap: Naming the best-known transmitter rather than the one the drug class targets.

qs.q: Stimulants also improve sustained attention in children without the disorder. Why does that matter for diagnosis?
o: It implies every child meets the criteria for the disorder
It means that medication is unnecessary for diagnosed children
It shows that stimulant medications do not actually work
Response to the drug cannot serve as a diagnostic test
qs.x: Correct: If a drug improves the measured function in people with and without the condition, then improving on the drug says nothing about whether the condition is present, so a trial of medication cannot be used to confirm a diagnosis. Why the others are wrong: The finding shows the drug works broadly rather than not at all, broad effectiveness is not evidence that everyone is affected, and nothing here bears on whether treatment helps those diagnosed. Trap: Converting a point about specificity into a claim about efficacy.

qs.q: Why do 12% of the children rated elevated at school only still meet full criteria?
o: Ratings from schools are sufficient on their own
The 88% who did not qualify show otherwise.
A parent may underreport symptoms seen at home
Correct: one informant can miss them.
The criteria require elevation in only a single setting
Those children in fact have no symptoms at all
qs.x: Correct: A rating scale is one informant's report, and a parent who sees the child mainly in unstructured time, or who is reluctant to report problems, can produce a low score in a child whose home difficulties emerge on fuller evaluation. Why the others are wrong: The criteria do demand cross-setting symptoms, school ratings alone leave most children not qualifying, and these children did meet criteria. Trap: Treating a rating scale as a direct measurement of symptoms rather than as a report.

r: Elevated at home and at school

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: When people explain behavior, they weigh dispositional causes, which lie in the person, against situational causes, which lie in the circumstances. The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to favor dispositional explanations for other people's behavior even when the situation is obvious. The actor-observer asymmetry adds that people explain their own behavior more situationally than they explain the same behavior in someone else. One proposed reason is a difference in perspective: an actor looks outward and sees the situation, while an observer looks at the actor.

Researchers tested 240 undergraduates. Each read a short scenario in which a student arrived 20 minutes late to a study group, with no explanation given. In the self condition, participants imagined that they themselves had arrived late. In the other condition, they read about a classmate. Half of the participants in each condition were also told that the campus shuttle had broken down that morning. Participants then rated, from 1 to 7, how much the lateness was caused by the person's character and how much by the circumstances (Table 1).

The researchers noted that imagining oneself in a scenario is not the same as actually being late, and that a participant who imagines being late may picture a reason without meaning to. To check this, they asked a separate group of 40 participants to describe what they had pictured; 32 reported imagining a specific cause, most often traffic or oversleeping. The researchers argued that this is itself part of the asymmetry: an actor supplies reasons that an observer never sees.

In a second study, participants in the other condition watched a 30-second video filmed from the late student's point of view, showing the empty shuttle stop and the walk to campus. Their character rating fell to 3.2. A third group watched the same scene filmed from across the street, showing the student walking; their character rating was 4.9.

qs.q: Which comparison best demonstrates the actor-observer asymmetry?
o: Other with and without shuttle information
Self versus other, no shuttle news
Self with and without shuttle information
qs.x: Correct: The asymmetry is the difference between explaining one's own behavior and the same behavior in another person. With the same information, participants rated character as the cause at 2.6 for themselves and 5.1 for a classmate. Why the others are wrong: The other comparisons vary information or camera angle within one perspective rather than comparing self with other. Trap: Choosing a comparison that varies something else while holding perspective constant.

qs.q: What do the camera angle results suggest?
o: The actor-observer effect disappears with video
qs.x: Correct: Both groups saw the same event; only the camera position differed. Seeing what the actor saw lowered character attributions to 3.2, while watching the actor from outside left them at 4.9. This supports the perspective explanation for the asymmetry. Why the others are wrong: One video did not reduce blame; ratings did respond to the videos; the effect remained in the outside-view group. Trap: Treating all video evidence as equally informative.

qs.q: Why does giving the shuttle information reduce character ratings more in the other condition?
o: Observers care more about accuracy than actors
Observers lacked what actors already knew
qs.x: Correct: Someone imagining their own lateness already has reasons in mind, so added information changes little (2.6 to 2.1). An observer starts without those reasons, so supplying one produces a larger change (5.1 to 4.0). Why the others are wrong: No measure of motivation is given; actor ratings shifted too; the information was presented as true. Trap: Explaining a group difference by a difference in motives rather than in information.

qs.q: Even when told about the shuttle, observers rated character at 4.0, above the actors' 2.1. Which conclusion does this best support?
o: The information reduces but keeps the bias
Situational information has no effect on observers
Actors ignore their own character entirely
Observers are unable to consider situations
qs.x: Correct: The observers' character ratings dropped when they learned about the shuttle, yet they remained well above the actors'. Knowing the situation helps, but the tendency to explain another person's behavior by their character is not erased. Why the others are wrong: The information clearly had an effect; observers did adjust; actors did not rate character at the minimum. Trap: Reading a partial change as no change or as a complete one.

qs.q: Which situation would most likely reduce the fundamental attribution error in everyday life?
o: Watching the person for a longer time
More observation keeps the observer's view.
Being told the person is usually reliable
Judging someone from a different culture
Unfamiliarity tends to increase the error.
Having been in the same situation
Correct: it supplies the actor's view.
qs.x: Correct: The error comes largely from not seeing the constraints the other person faces. Having faced the same constraints supplies that missing information, much as the actor-perspective video did. Why the others are wrong: Reputation is still information about the person; longer observation does not change the vantage point; unfamiliarity makes situational constraints harder to recognize. Trap: Assuming more observation automatically corrects a bias in perspective.

passages.title: Separation and purification methods · passage
text: Distillation separates liquids by exploiting differences in boiling point. Heating a mixture produces a vapor richer in the more volatile component, and condensing that vapor gives a distillate enriched in it. The enrichment achieved in one such cycle is set by the ratio of the components' vapor pressures at the boiling temperature.

One cycle is often not enough. Simple distillation, which condenses the vapor directly, works when the boiling points differ by roughly 25 degrees or more. When they are closer, the vapor is only slightly enriched and the distillate remains a mixture.

Fractional distillation addresses this by inserting a packed column between the flask and the condenser. Vapor rising through the packing repeatedly condenses and re-evaporates, and each cycle enriches it further, so a column of sufficient length can separate components differing by only a few degrees. The number of effective cycles is described as the column's theoretical plates.
A mixture of two liquids was distilled by both methods, and the composition of the first fraction collected was measured (Table 1).

The two methods diverge as the boiling points converge. Simple distillation gives a usable separation at a 44-degree difference and fails at 12 degrees, where the first fraction is only slightly enriched over the starting mixture, while fractional distillation exceeds 90% purity in every case.

The hexane and cyclohexane pair shows why the column matters. A single vaporization enriches the vapor from 50% to 58%, so about eight percentage points per cycle, and reaching 91% requires several such cycles, which the packing supplies within one apparatus.

Two limits should be kept in mind. These purities are for the first fraction, and later fractions are progressively poorer as the flask is depleted of the volatile component, so the yield at a stated purity is lower than the purity alone suggests. And a pair that forms an azeotrope cannot be separated beyond the azeotropic composition by either method, however many plates the column has.

qs.q: Why does fractional distillation succeed where simple distillation fails?
o: The mixture is heated more slowly in a column
Rate is not what creates the separation.
The column raises the boiling point of the mixture
Boiling point is set by the liquids.
The packing provides repeated vaporization cycles
The vapor is condensed at a lower temperature there
Condenser temperature is not the mechanism.
qs.x: Correct: Each condensation and re-evaporation within the packing enriches the vapor by the same factor as the first vaporization, so a column multiplies a small single-cycle enrichment into a large overall one. Why the others are wrong: Boiling point is a property of the liquids, condenser temperature only liquefies the vapor, and heating rate does not change the enrichment per cycle. Trap: Attributing the improvement to the temperature rather than to the number of cycles.

qs.q: What does the 58% figure for hexane indicate?
o: Hexane and cyclohexane cannot be separated
Cyclohexane is the more volatile component
Hexane boils lower and is enriched.
The simple apparatus was assembled wrongly
It performed as expected for one cycle.
qs.x: Correct: Starting from an equal mixture, a single vaporization produces a vapor that is 58% hexane, an enrichment of eight points, which is why many cycles are needed to approach purity. Why the others are wrong: The pair was separated by column, the simple apparatus worked correctly, and hexane is the more volatile of the two. Trap: Reading a poor result as a failure of the method rather than as the size of one cycle's effect.

qs.q: What determines the enrichment achieved in a single cycle?
o: The volume of the distillation flask being used
The length of the condenser attached
The ratio of the components' vapor pressures
The total mass of the mixture distilled
qs.x: Correct: The vapor above a mixture is richer in the component with the higher vapor pressure, and the ratio of those pressures fixes how much richer, which is the enrichment of one cycle. Why the others are wrong: Flask volume, condenser length and total mass affect the scale and rate of the operation rather than the composition of the vapor. Trap: Looking to the apparatus for a quantity set by the liquids themselves.

qs.q: By how many percentage points does the column improve the benzene fraction?
o: That is the improvement for acetone.
That is the improvement for methanol.
That is the improvement for hexane.
qs.x: Correct: Benzene reaches 71% by simple distillation and 96% with a column, an improvement of 25 points. Why the others are wrong: 5, 10 and 33 points are the improvements for the other three pairs. Trap: Taking the pair with the largest improvement rather than the one asked about.

qs.q: Why does an azeotrope defeat both methods?
o: Its vapor has the same composition as the liquid
Columns cannot be made long enough
Length would not help at all.
The components decompose on heating then
Azeotropes have no measurable boiling point at all
They boil at a fixed temperature.
qs.x: Correct: At the azeotropic composition the vapor and the liquid have the same proportions, so a vaporization cycle produces no enrichment and adding plates achieves nothing. Why the others are wrong: An azeotrope boils at a definite temperature, decomposition is unrelated, and the problem is not one of insufficient column length. Trap: Treating a thermodynamic limit as an engineering one.

passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Sociologists distinguish material culture, the physical objects a group makes and uses, from nonmaterial culture, its beliefs, norms and values. Culture changes unevenly: William Ogburn argued that material culture often changes faster than the norms that govern its use, leaving a culture lag during which a technology is in wide use before shared rules for it exist. Norms themselves vary in strength. Folkways are everyday customs whose violation brings mild disapproval; mores carry moral weight and their violation brings serious sanction; taboos are prohibitions so strong that the act is almost unthinkable.

A society's dominant culture coexists with subcultures, which differ from it without rejecting it, and countercultures, which oppose it. Judging another culture by the standards of one's own is ethnocentrism; understanding practices on their own terms is cultural relativism.

Researchers surveyed 4,000 adults in one country about the use of personal recording devices in public, a technology adopted rapidly over the previous decade. Respondents rated how wrong each act is on a 1 to 7 scale and reported whether they would say something to the person (Table 1).

The researchers noted two limits of the survey. First, what people say they would do is not what they do: self-reported willingness to speak up is usually higher than observed behavior, so the figures in the last two columns should be read as attitudes rather than as predictions. Second, the sample was drawn from an online panel, which underrepresents adults without regular internet access, a group that is older and less urban on average.

Respondents aged 18 to 29 rated recording a stranger's conversation at 3.4, while those over 60 rated it at 4.9. In follow-up interviews, many respondents of all ages said they were unsure what the rules were and that no clear etiquette had developed. Researchers in a second country, where recording in public has been regulated for 20 years, found far less disagreement across age groups on the same items.

qs.q: Which act is best described as violating a taboo?
o: Recording a friend without telling them
It is rated 1.4 and rarely challenged.
Recording a conversation on a train
qs.x: Correct: The locker room item drew a wrongness rating of 6.8, with 61% willing to confront the person and 92% supporting a legal prohibition. Near-unanimous condemnation and legal backing mark the strongest category of norm. Why the others are wrong: The street performance is barely disapproved, and the other two items draw mixed, moderate reactions typical of contested norms. Trap: Ranking acts by how unpleasant they sound rather than by the strength of the social reaction.

qs.q: Which finding best illustrates culture lag?
o: A low rating for recording a street performance
Widespread use with no agreed etiquette
Correct: the technology outpaced the norms.
qs.x: Correct: Culture lag is the gap between a change in material culture and the norms that follow it. Rapid adoption of recording devices, combined with respondents of every age saying they did not know the rules, is exactly that gap. Why the others are wrong: Items with near-unanimous agreement show norms that have already settled, which is the opposite of lag. Trap: Choosing the item with the strongest opinion when lag is marked by the absence of agreement.

qs.q: What does the age difference on the train item most likely reflect?
o: Older adults cannot operate recording devices
Younger adults are less moral in general
They agreed on the locker room item.
The question was unclear to older adults
qs.x: Correct: People are socialized in the era they grow up in. Those who came of age with recording devices in constant use absorbed more permissive expectations, giving 3.4 against 4.9. The gap is largest on precisely the item where no settled rule exists. Why the others are wrong: Device skill was not measured; both groups condemned the locker-room item strongly; both groups answered the same question. Trap: Reading a difference in norms as a difference in character.

qs.q: What does the comparison with the second country suggest?
o: Age has no effect on attitudes anywhere
Age mattered in the first country.
Correct: less variation where regulation is long-standing.
Here the law preceded the consensus.
qs.x: Correct: Where recording in public has been regulated for two decades, age groups agreed far more closely. A clear formal rule gives everyone the same reference point, which narrows the gap that culture lag opens. Why the others are wrong: Nothing is reported about how often people record there; age mattered in the surveyed country; this example shows regulation preceding agreement rather than following it. Trap: Assuming law always codifies an existing consensus.

qs.q: A traveler calls the second country's rules "an overreaction" without learning why they were adopted. Which concept does this illustrate?
o: That means understanding practices on their own terms.
That is a group opposing the dominant culture.
Correct: judging by one's own standards.
qs.x: Correct: Evaluating another society's practice by the standards of one's own, without examining its context, is ethnocentrism. Cultural relativism would involve asking what problem those rules were meant to solve. Why the others are wrong: Relativism is the opposite stance, culture lag concerns the pace of normative change, and a counterculture is a group rather than a judgment. Trap: Choosing a term that names the situation instead of the attitude described.

h: Respondents who said a law should prohibit it (%)
r: Recording a stranger's conversation on a train
Recording a friend without telling them

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Enzymes from organisms that live at different temperatures often catalyze the same reaction with the same active-site residues, yet they differ in speed and in heat tolerance. One explanation is that a protein must be flexible enough to move through the conformational changes of its catalytic cycle but rigid enough to stay folded. A protein from a heat-loving organism may be well suited to high temperatures yet sluggish at room temperature, because the same interactions that hold it together also restrict its motion.

To test this idea, researchers purified adenylate kinase, which catalyzes 2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP, from a bacterium that grows best at 37 °C (Enzyme M) and from a related species isolated from a hot spring that grows best at 70 °C (Enzyme T). The two proteins share 74% sequence identity, and every residue that contacts the substrates is conserved. Turnover number (kcat) was measured at several temperatures with saturating substrate (Table 1). Each value is the mean of three runs that differed by less than 5%.

The researchers also measured the melting temperature (Tm), the temperature at which half of the protein is unfolded, using circular dichroism. Enzyme M had a Tm of 47 °C and Enzyme T had a Tm of 82 °C. Inspection of the Enzyme T crystal structure showed that Glu142, a surface residue far from the active site, forms an ion pair with Arg87. A mutant of Enzyme T in which Glu142 was replaced by glutamine (E142Q) had a Tm of 71 °C. At 40 °C, the kcat of E142Q was 5.8 s⁻¹.

Heat tolerance has practical uses. Enzymes from heat-loving organisms are used in laboratory methods that cycle between high temperatures, such as the polymerase chain reaction, and in industrial processes that run hot to keep reactants dissolved and to limit microbial growth. Engineers who want an enzyme that is both stable and fast at moderate temperatures often start by adding or removing surface ion pairs and then testing how the changes affect Tm and kcat separately.

In a final experiment, Enzyme M was held at 60 °C for 10 minutes in the presence of substrate. Its activity was then measured after the solution was cooled to 30 °C. The rate was 4% of the rate of an unheated sample. When fresh, unheated Enzyme M was added to the heated solution, the rate returned to the expected value.

qs.q: Which explanation of the kcat values of the two enzymes at 20–30 °C is most consistent with the passage?
o: Enzyme T is too rigid to cycle quickly at low temperature
Correct: the stabilizing interactions that resist unfolding also slow conformational change.
Enzyme T makes the reaction less favorable overall
An enzyme cannot change ΔG of the reaction.
Enzyme T is partly unfolded when the temperature is low
Its Tm is 82 °C, so it is folded at 20–30 °C.
Enzyme T is missing some of the residues that bind substrate
qs.x: Correct: Enzyme T is folded and has the same active site, yet it turns over about eight times more slowly than Enzyme M at 20–30 °C. The passage proposes that the interactions that keep a heat-tolerant protein folded also restrict the motions needed for catalysis, so it is sluggish at low temperature. Why the others are wrong: A Tm of 82 °C means Enzyme T is folded well below that temperature; the substrate-contacting residues are conserved; a catalyst changes the rate, not the free energy change. Trap: Assuming a slow enzyme must be damaged or missing part of its active site.

qs.q: To estimate the activation energy of Enzyme T from Table 1, which plot should the researchers make?
o: kcat against T, which has a slope of Eₐ/R
kcat is not linear in T.
1/kcat against 1/T, which has a slope equal to Eₐ/R
This is not the Arrhenius form.
ln kcat against T in kelvin, which has a slope of −Eₐ/R
ln kcat against 1/T, which has a slope of −Eₐ/R
Correct: the linear form of the Arrhenius equation.
qs.x: Correct: Taking the natural log of k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT) gives ln k = ln A − (Eₐ/R)(1/T), so a plot of ln k against 1/T (in kelvin) is a straight line with slope −Eₐ/R. Only the points below the Tm should be used. Why the others are wrong: The rate constant rises exponentially, not linearly, with temperature; ln k is linear in 1/T, not in T; a double-reciprocal plot belongs to Michaelis–Menten analysis, not to the Arrhenius equation. Trap: Mixing up the Arrhenius plot with a Lineweaver–Burk plot.

qs.q: What do the results for the E142Q mutant most strongly suggest?
o: The mutation shifts the equilibrium toward ATP and AMP
Enzymes and mutations do not change Keq.
The Glu142–Arg87 ion pair stabilizes the folded enzyme
Correct: Tm fell by 11 °C while kcat stayed the same.
Glu142 is required for the chemical step of catalysis
Glutamine side chains cannot form hydrogen bonds
Glutamine's amide is a good hydrogen bond donor and acceptor.
qs.x: Correct: Replacing the charged Glu with the neutral Gln removes the salt bridge to Arg87. The Tm dropped from 82 °C to 71 °C, but kcat at 40 °C (5.8 s⁻¹) was essentially the same as the wild type (5.9 s⁻¹). The residue therefore contributes to stability, not to catalysis. Why the others are wrong: An unchanged kcat rules out a catalytic role, and Glu142 is far from the active site; glutamine hydrogen bonds well but carries no charge; no enzyme or mutation alters the equilibrium constant. Trap: Assuming any residue whose mutation matters must be in the active site.

qs.q: Which observation shows that the loss of Enzyme M activity at 60 °C is due to the enzyme rather than the substrate?
o: Raising substrate levels after heating restored the rate
This would point to substrate loss, and it was not observed.
Enzyme M activity at 50 °C is lower than at 40 °C
This does not separate enzyme loss from substrate loss.
Fresh enzyme added after heating restored the rate
Correct: the substrate was still usable.
Enzyme M is faster than Enzyme T at 30 °C
This compares enzymes, not substrate stability.
qs.x: Correct: If heat had destroyed the substrate, adding new enzyme would not help. Because fresh enzyme restored the expected rate in the same heated solution, the substrate survived and the original enzyme had been inactivated, consistent with unfolding above its Tm of 47 °C. Why the others are wrong: Comparing the two enzymes at 30 °C says nothing about heat damage; a lower rate at 50 °C is the finding being explained, not evidence for a cause; restoring activity by adding substrate would implicate the substrate. Trap: Choosing a result that restates the observation instead of one that tests the explanation.

qs.q: If kcat were measured at 75 °C, how would E142Q most likely compare with wild-type Enzyme T?
o: Higher, because glutamine is less charged than glutamate
The same, because the active site is unchanged
A folded active site is needed for activity.
Higher, because kcat rises with temperature for both
This holds only while the protein stays folded.
Lower, because most E142Q molecules would be unfolded
Correct: 75 °C is above its Tm of 71 °C.
qs.x: Correct: At 75 °C, more than half of E142Q is unfolded because its Tm is 71 °C, while wild-type Enzyme T, whose Tm is 82 °C, is mostly folded and still speeding up, as its rise from 20 to 35 s⁻¹ between 60 and 70 °C shows. The mutant should therefore be slower. Why the others are wrong: The Arrhenius trend holds only for folded enzyme; an identical active site is useless once the protein unfolds; removing the charge lowered stability rather than raising activity. Trap: Applying the Arrhenius trend past the melting temperature.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: A cross between two carriers of a recessive allele is expected to produce affected offspring in a quarter of cases, but an observed proportion in a real family rarely matches that figure. The expectation describes the probability for each conception independently, and a small number of conceptions is a small sample from it.

Two further effects move the observed proportion. Incomplete penetrance means some individuals carrying the genotype do not show the phenotype, which lowers the observed proportion of affected offspring without changing the genotype ratio; and ascertainment through an affected child guarantees at least one affected offspring in every family studied, which raises it.
The two biases therefore act in opposite directions, and a study must correct for both before an observed proportion can be compared with the expected quarter.
Offspring were counted in several sets of families (Table 1).

The prospective sample gave 0.248, close to the expected quarter. Ascertaining families through an affected child raised the proportion to 0.341, and excluding the index child from the count overcorrected it to 0.091 because the siblings of an affected child are no more likely to be affected than any other offspring of the same couple.
The penetrance sample gave 0.176, which is close to 0.25 multiplied by 0.70, so a reduced penetrance scales the observed proportion rather than changing the shape of the expectation.

Two qualifications apply. The prospective sample counts conceptions that reached birth, and if the genotype causes early pregnancy loss the affected offspring are undercounted in every sample including the prospective one, which would bias all four proportions downward. And the penetrance figure of 70 percent was itself estimated from a separate family study, so the agreement between 0.176 and the predicted 0.175 is partly circular and does not independently confirm the penetrance. An independent estimate would have to come from a different design, such as genotyping a population sample and counting how many carriers of the genotype are unaffected, which does not depend on families having been noticed in the first place.

qs.q: Why does ascertainment through an affected child raise the proportion?
o: Affected children have more affected siblings than expected
Correct: families with none are missed.
The genotype changes with the sampling
qs.x: Correct: Selecting families because they contain an affected child excludes all the carrier couples who happened to have none, so the sampled families are enriched for affected offspring. Why the others are wrong: Siblings of an affected child carry the ordinary risk, genotypes do not depend on how families were found, and the proportion rose to 0.341. Trap: Treating a selected sample as a random one.

qs.q: Why does excluding the index child overcorrect?
o: Correct: removing one removes too much.
The index child was not actually affected
qs.x: Correct: The index child is one guaranteed affected offspring, but removing it from a family that was only sampled because of it leaves a set of siblings whose expected proportion is a quarter, and dividing by the remaining offspring of all 240 families gives 0.091 rather than 0.25. Why the others are wrong: The index child is affected by definition, exclusion removes rather than adds, and the result is below the expectation. Trap: Correcting a selection bias by subtraction without reconsidering the denominator.

qs.q: Why does reduced penetrance scale rather than reshape the expectation?
o: Correct: the genotype ratio is unchanged.
It alters the proportion of carriers among the offspring
It changes the ratio to 1 in 3
qs.x: Correct: Penetrance is the probability that a given genotype produces the phenotype, so it multiplies the quarter rather than altering how the genotypes are distributed. Why the others are wrong: The carrier proportion is unaffected, no new ratio is produced, and the effect is multiplicative. Trap: Confusing a change in expression with a change in transmission.

qs.q: How many affected offspring would be expected in the prospective sample at full penetrance?
o: That is the reduced penetrance sample.
qs.x: Correct: A quarter of 892 offspring is 223, against the 221 observed. Why the others are wrong: The others are the observed count and the counts from the other two samples. Trap: Giving an observed value where an expectation was asked for.

qs.q: Why is the penetrance agreement partly circular?
o: Penetrance cannot be estimated at all
The figure came from family data
qs.x: Correct: The 70 percent penetrance was derived from family studies of the same kind, so finding that it predicts this sample's proportion is partly a restatement of where the figure came from. Why the others are wrong: Penetrance is routinely estimated, the agreement is close rather than exact, and the circularity is real. Trap: Taking a prediction as confirmation when the parameter was fitted to similar data.

r: Families found through an affected child

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: Stereotype threat is the performance decrement that appears when a person is at risk of confirming a negative stereotype about a group they belong to. The proposed mechanism is not reduced ability or effort but competition for working memory: monitoring one's own performance, suppressing anxious thoughts and worrying about what a poor score would mean all consume the same limited resource the task requires.

The mechanism generates a testable prediction. If threat acts through working memory, then a measure of load taken during the task should rise under threatening conditions and should move inversely with performance, and interventions that reduce threat should lower load as well as raising scores. If load stayed constant while scores moved, the account would be in trouble.

Two interventions are commonly used. Self-affirmation has the person write briefly about a value that matters to them before the task, which is held to reduce the stake the task carries for the self. Explicitly describing the stereotype as unfounded removes the inference a poor score would license.

Students completed the same difficult quantitative test under one of four randomly assigned framings. A concurrent secondary task indexed working memory load, scored so that higher values mean more load (Table 1).

The two columns move inversely across all four conditions, from 62 and 7.8 in the threatening condition to 74 and 5.1 in the puzzle framing, with the two interventions landing in between on both measures. That is the pattern the working memory account predicts.

The correspondence is suggestive but not decisive. Load and score are both outcomes measured at the same time, so a third factor, such as how engaging each framing felt, could move them together, and a mediation claim requires showing that the load change accounts for the score change statistically. The secondary task also competes with the test for resources, so the measurement may itself alter what it measures, and the test was difficult by design, which is the condition under which threat effects are largest and therefore not a general estimate.

qs.q: Which result supports the working memory account?
o: Self-affirmation raised the measured load index
Scores exceeded 60 points in all of the four conditions
Four different framings were tested in the study
The number of conditions is not a result.
Load moved inversely with score across the conditions
qs.x: Correct: The account predicts that threat consumes working memory, so load should rise as scores fall, and the table shows exactly that from 7.8 and 62 under threat to 5.1 and 74 under the puzzle framing. Why the others are wrong: Affirmation reduced load, the common floor above 60 bears on nothing, and the number of conditions is a design feature. Trap: Selecting a true statement about the table that does not test the hypothesis.

qs.q: Why does the puzzle framing help?
o: The time limit for the test has been removed
Anxiety is unaffected by how a task is framed
No judgment of ability is implied by the task
Correct: nothing is at stake for the stereotype.
The questions themselves have been made easier
qs.x: Correct: Threat arises from the possibility of confirming a stereotype, and a task presented as a puzzle rather than as a measure of ability provides no inference about ability to be confirmed, so the monitoring that consumes working memory does not begin. Why the others are wrong: The items and the timing were constant, and framing clearly moved the load index. Trap: Attributing a framing effect to a change in task difficulty.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the account?
o: Load was highest in the diagnostic framing
That is what the account predicts.
Scores rose after the self-affirmation task
Students were already aware of the stereotype in question
Load fell under the interventions while scores stayed low
Correct: the mediator moved without the outcome.
qs.x: Correct: If relieving load left performance unchanged, then load could not be the route by which threat lowers scores, which is the central claim, so that dissociation is the damaging result. Why the others are wrong: High load under threat and improved scores after affirmation are both predicted, and awareness of the stereotype is assumed by the account. Trap: Choosing the result that is most striking rather than the one that breaks the proposed link.

qs.q: What was randomly assigned in this experiment?
o: The working memory load measure used
The group membership of the students
The items that appeared on the test
The test was the same for all.
qs.x: Correct: Students were randomly assigned to one of four framings, which is what licenses a causal claim about framing, while the test, the group memberships and the load measure were held constant. Why the others are wrong: Test content and the load measure did not vary, and group membership is a characteristic rather than a manipulation. Trap: Treating the variable the study is about as the variable that was assigned.

qs.q: Which practical implication follows most directly?
o: Present assessments as tools for learning
Correct: it removes the ability inference.
Separate students by group for testing
Reduce the difficulty of all assessments
qs.x: Correct: The effective manipulation here was describing the task as a puzzle rather than as a measure of ability, which maps onto presenting assessment as feedback for learning rather than as a verdict. Why the others are wrong: Separating by group heightens the salience that drives threat, and neither difficulty nor timing was the operative variable. Trap: Drawing an implication from a feature of the task that the experiment held constant.

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: Solomon Asch studied conformity by asking participants to judge which of three comparison lines matched a standard line. The task was easy: people working alone were correct almost every time. In the group version, several confederates answered aloud before the participant and gave the same wrong answer on certain trials. About a third of participants' responses matched the wrong majority, and about three-quarters of participants conformed at least once.

Psychologists distinguish two reasons for conformity. Normative influence is the wish to be accepted, which produces public agreement without private belief. Informational influence is the belief that others know better, which changes private judgment as well. Ambiguous tasks favor informational influence, while clear tasks with a visible audience favor normative influence.

Researchers ran a modern replication with 160 participants in four conditions. In every condition, five confederates answered before the participant on 12 of 18 trials, giving a wrong answer on each of those 12. In the private condition, the participant wrote answers on a card that the others could not see. In the unanimous condition, all five confederates gave the same wrong answer. In the dissenter condition, the fourth confederate gave the correct answer. In the hard condition, the comparison lines differed by only 1 mm, making the judgment genuinely difficult (Table 1).

The researchers also recorded how long each participant took to answer on the critical trials. In the unanimous spoken condition, participants who went along with the majority took about 1.8 seconds longer than those who gave the correct answer, which the researchers read as a sign of conflict between what they saw and what they said.

In interviews afterward, most participants in the unanimous spoken condition said they had seen the correct answer but had not wanted to appear foolish. In the hard condition, most said they had not been sure and had assumed the others saw better.

qs.q: Which comparison best isolates normative influence?
o: Hard versus easy judgment, both spoken
qs.x: Correct: Normative influence depends on being seen by the group. Holding everything else constant and removing the audience cut conformity from 31% to 8%, which measures the part driven by the wish to be accepted. Why the others are wrong: Comparing unanimity with a dissenter changes the group's agreement; changing difficulty changes how much people rely on others for information; the last comparison varies both. Trap: Picking a comparison in which more than one factor changes.

qs.q: Why is conformity highest in the hard condition?
o: The task had no correct answer
The audience was the same as in the unanimous condition.
The group was larger in that condition
qs.x: Correct: When the lines differ by 1 mm, participants cannot be confident, so they treat the majority's answer as evidence. Their interviews confirm this: they assumed the others saw better. Why the others are wrong: Group size and audience were held constant; a correct answer existed. Trap: Explaining every rise in conformity by social pressure.

qs.q: Why does a single dissenter reduce conformity so sharply?
o: The dissenter makes the task ambiguous
The dissenter makes the group smaller
Unanimity is what creates the pressure
The dissenter gives the participant new information about the lines
The lines were easy to judge.
qs.x: Correct: Asch found that breaking unanimity matters more than how many people agree. One ally shows that disagreeing is possible, and the fear of standing alone drops. Why the others are wrong: There were still five confederates; the easy task needed no extra information; the task remained unambiguous. Trap: Assuming conformity depends simply on how many people hold the majority view.

qs.q: What do the interview responses add to the numerical results?
o: They prove that participants were lying
They replace the need for the written condition
They show the task was impossible
They suggest which kind of influence operated
Correct: public agreement versus private belief.
qs.x: Correct: Participants in the easy spoken condition said they had seen the right answer but did not want to look foolish, which fits normative influence, while those in the hard condition said they assumed the others saw better, which fits informational influence. The behavioral conditions test the same distinction more directly. Why the others are wrong: Self-reports are evidence, not proof of lying; the written condition provides stronger evidence than self-report; most answers were correct, so the task was manageable. Trap: Treating self-report as either worthless or decisive.

qs.q: A student concludes from the 31% figure that most people conform. What is the best correction?
o: Only one person conformed in that condition
The figure counts trials, not people
Conformity never occurs on easy tasks
It occurred on 31% of critical trials.
qs.x: Correct: The 31% is the proportion of critical responses that matched the wrong majority, averaged across participants. A separate figure shows that 27% of participants never conformed, so the statistic does not mean that most people conform on most trials. Why the others are wrong: 46% belongs to the hard condition; conformity did occur; many participants conformed at least once. Trap: Reading a per-trial percentage as a per-person one.

h: Participants' wrong answers on the 12 critical trials (%)

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Le Châtelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium responds to a change by shifting in the direction that partly opposes it. Ammonia is made industrially by the Haber process: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. The equilibrium constant Kp depends only on temperature; pressure and catalysts do not change it. Because the reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants and lowers Kp.

The reaction also has four moles of gas on the left and two on the right, so compressing the mixture shifts it toward ammonia. The reaction is slow at low temperature, however, because breaking the triple bond of N₂ has a high activation energy. An iron catalyst lowers that barrier and speeds both the forward and the reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but its position does not change.
An engineering team measured the percentage of ammonia present at equilibrium under several conditions (Table 1). In each run the starting mixture was one part N₂ to three parts H₂ by moles.

The team also considered what sets the starting ratio. Using one part N₂ to three parts H₂ matches the stoichiometry of the reaction, which gives the highest conversion of both gases; an excess of either one would raise the conversion of the other but leave the excess gas unreacted and circulating through the plant. Hydrogen for the process is usually obtained from methane and steam, a step that is itself energy-intensive, so plants are designed around the cost of hydrogen as much as around the equilibrium yield. Roughly 1% of the world's energy use goes into this one reaction, which supplies the nitrogen in most agricultural fertilizer.

Industrial plants typically run at about 400 °C and 200 atm. The team also noted that ammonia is removed continuously by cooling it to a liquid while the unreacted gases are recycled through the reactor.

qs.q: Why does the ammonia percentage fall as temperature rises?
o: Correct: added heat shifts it back toward reactants.
The catalyst stops working when hot
It reverts to N₂ and H₂.
Pressure was held constant in each row.
qs.x: Correct: In an exothermic reaction, heat behaves like a product. Adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants, so Kp and the equilibrium percentage of ammonia both fall, from 81% at 200 °C to 5% at 600 °C. Why the others are wrong: The equilibrium position does not depend on the catalyst; each comparison holds pressure fixed; the reverse reaction gives back the original reactants. Trap: Expecting more ammonia at higher temperature because the reaction goes faster.

qs.q: Why does raising the pressure increase the yield?
o: Pressure converts the gases into liquids
The reaction occurs in the gas phase.
The product side has fewer gas moles
Pressure raises the value of Kp
qs.x: Correct: Compressing the mixture raises the partial pressures of all species. The system shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules, which is the ammonia side, so the percentage rises from 25% to 47% as pressure goes from 100 to 400 atm. Why the others are wrong: Kp is fixed at a given temperature; catalysts lower activation energy; the gases are not liquefied in the reactor. Trap: Assuming a greater yield means a larger equilibrium constant.

qs.q: Why does industry use 400 °C rather than 200 °C, where the yield is far higher?
o: The catalyst does not work at 200 °C
It cut the time to four hours there.
The equilibrium percentage is highest there.
Correct: yield without speed is useless.
qs.x: Correct: Thermodynamics favors low temperature, but kinetics does not. Even with a catalyst, reaching equilibrium takes four hours at 200 °C and only 20 minutes at 400 °C. The higher temperature trades some yield for a rate the plant can use. Why the others are wrong: Kp is larger at the lower temperature; the catalyst works there; ammonia's equilibrium share is highest at 200 °C. Trap: Choosing conditions from the equilibrium table alone.

qs.q: Why does removing ammonia as a liquid increase the total amount produced?
o: It has left the gas phase.
Kp is unchanged at fixed temperature.
The system shifts to replace it
Cooling is used to liquefy it.
qs.x: Correct: Taking a product out lowers its partial pressure, so the reaction quotient falls below Kp and the forward reaction proceeds until equilibrium is restored. Repeating this converts far more of the starting gases than a single equilibrium would allow. Why the others are wrong: Kp is a constant at a given temperature; the liquid is removed from the reaction; the gas is cooled, not heated. Trap: Treating a one-time equilibrium percentage as the maximum obtainable yield.

qs.q: How would the catalyst change the time to equilibrium and the yield at 400 °C and 200 atm?
o: Less time and a lower yield
The equilibrium position does not move.
Less time and a higher yield
Yield is set by the equilibrium constant.
Correct: it speeds both directions equally.
The same time and a higher yield
A catalyst's role is to speed the approach.
qs.x: Correct: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so it speeds both. Equilibrium arrives sooner but its position, and therefore the percentage of ammonia, is unchanged. Why the others are wrong: Any change in yield would require a change in Kp, which depends only on temperature. Trap: Assuming a catalyst produces more product rather than producing it sooner.

h: Time to reach equilibrium, no catalyst
Time to reach equilibrium, with catalyst

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination are distinct. A stereotype is a belief about the attributes of a group, prejudice is an evaluative attitude toward the group, and discrimination is behavior that treats people differently on the basis of group membership. A person can hold a stereotype without endorsing it, and can behave in a discriminatory way without reporting a hostile attitude.

That last possibility motivated implicit measures. A reaction-time association task infers the strength of a learned association from how quickly a person pairs group labels with evaluative words, on the premise that such associations operate without deliberate control and so escape both self-presentation and introspective limits. Explicit measures, by contrast, ask directly, and are subject to both.

The principle of correspondence predicts how each should behave. Deliberate, considered actions should be predicted better by explicit attitudes, because the person has time to apply what they endorse. Spontaneous, hard-to-monitor behaviors should be predicted better by implicit associations.

Researchers measured explicit attitudes with a questionnaire, implicit associations with a reaction-time task, and four outcomes in 800 adults, then computed the correlation of each outcome with each measure (Table 1).

The pattern is a crossover rather than a contest. The two deliberate, verbal outcomes correlate with the explicit measure at 0.61 and 0.52 and with the implicit score near 0.15, while the two spontaneous nonverbal outcomes reverse that, which is what correspondence predicts and which neither measure would produce on its own.

Several things the table does not settle matter. All of these are correlations in a single cross-sectional sample, so nothing here shows that changing an association would change a behavior; only manipulating the association could. The table also gives no information about the test-retest reliability of the implicit measure, a standing criticism of it, and a measure that is unstable over weeks cannot support claims about enduring individual differences even when it predicts behavior on the day of testing.

qs.q: What pattern do the correlations in Table 1 show?
o: Explicit self-report measures are without predictive value
The implicit score predicts every outcome better than the explicit measure
It predicts the verbal outcomes worse.
The two measures are interchangeable indices of the same attitude
Each measure predicts the kind of behavior that matches it
Correct: deliberate with explicit, spontaneous with implicit.
qs.x: Correct: Deliberate verbal outcomes correlate with the explicit measure near 0.5 to 0.6 and with the implicit score near 0.15, while spontaneous nonverbal outcomes reverse the pattern, a crossover that matches the correspondence principle. Why the others are wrong: The implicit score is the weaker predictor for the verbal outcomes, the divergence rules out interchangeability, and the explicit measure is the stronger predictor twice. Trap: Treating the question as asking which measure is better overall.

qs.q: Which of the outcomes measured is best described as discrimination?
o: Agreement with an item describing a group's attributes
The score on the reaction-time association task
That is a measure, not behavior.
The chosen seating distance in a waiting room
Correct: it is behavior toward a person.
qs.x: Correct: Discrimination is differential behavior toward people on the basis of group membership, and physically placing oneself further away is such a behavior, whereas the other three are self-reports or a laboratory index. Why the others are wrong: Reported willingness is an attitude, the association score is a measure of a presumed association, and endorsing attributes is stereotyping. Trap: Classifying by how negative the content sounds rather than by whether it is behavior.

qs.q: Which standing criticism of implicit measures do these data leave untouched?
o: Whether the measure is stable when a person is retested
Correct: no repeated testing was done.
Whether the measure predicts any kind of behavior at all
Whether it relates to nonverbal behavior specifically
Seating and eye contact address this.
Whether it diverges from what people report explicitly
qs.x: Correct: Test-retest reliability requires measuring the same people twice, and this study measured each participant once, so the criticism that implicit scores fluctuate from session to session is neither supported nor answered here. Why the others are wrong: Predictive validity, divergence from explicit measures and relevance to nonverbal behavior are each addressed by at least one column of the table. Trap: Picking a criticism the data in fact speak to because it is the most familiar one.

qs.q: Which correlation in Table 1 is the largest in absolute value?
o: Correct: explicit attitude with willingness to befriend.
qs.x: Correct: The largest value in the table is 0.61, the correlation between the explicit measure and self-reported willingness to befriend, which is unsurprising because both are verbal self-reports made in the same session. Why the others are wrong: 0.52 is the next largest, 0.43 is the strongest implicit correlation, and 0.19 is one of the weakest. Trap: Choosing the largest implicit correlation because the implicit measure is the novel one.

qs.q: Which change to the design would permit a causal claim?
o: Add a third and a fourth nonverbal behavioral outcome
Measure explicit attitudes twice rather than once
Experimentally alter the associations and then measure behavior
Increase the sample from the 800 adults tested to 2,000 or more
qs.x: Correct: Every number in the table is a correlation within one sample, so a causal claim requires manipulating the proposed cause, for instance by training a counterstereotypical association and then observing whether the behavior shifts. Why the others are wrong: A larger sample narrows confidence intervals, additional outcomes remain observational, and repeated measurement addresses reliability rather than causation. Trap: Mistaking a more precise correlation for evidence of cause.

r: Hiring recommendation on a rated form
Seating distance chosen in a waiting room
Duration of eye contact during conversation

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: A cell more than a few hundred micrometres from a blood vessel cannot obtain enough oxygen by diffusion alone, so any mass of tissue larger than that must acquire a blood supply or stop growing. A mass that has not acquired one reaches a size at which cells at the centre die as fast as cells at the edge divide, and the mass stops enlarging while remaining alive.

Acquiring a supply involves releasing a factor that causes nearby vessels to grow towards the mass. Release of that factor is itself triggered by low oxygen, so the mass that most needs a supply is the one that signals most strongly for it, and the signal stops when the supply arrives.
Tumour masses were implanted into tissue either with or without an inhibitor of the growth factor, and size, vessel density and the fraction of dying cells were measured over six weeks (Table 1).

Without the inhibitor the masses reached eleven millimetres with a dense vessel network and only four percent of cells dying. The high dose of inhibitor held them to under two millimetres with almost no vessels and a quarter of cells dying, while the fraction of dividing cells was essentially unchanged across every condition at around twenty one percent.

That the dividing fraction did not change is the central result. The inhibitor did not slow division; it limited the size that could be supported, and the mass stopped enlarging because cells were dying at the centre at the same rate as cells were being produced at the edge.

Raising the oxygen available to the tissue in the presence of the high dose allowed the masses to reach four millimetres with the vessel count still at three. Oxygen reached the interior by diffusion from a richer source rather than through new vessels, which separates the supply of oxygen from the growth of vessels as the thing that actually limits size.

Two qualifications apply. Vessels per field counts vessel cross sections in a stained section, and a field at the edge of a mass contains vessels of the surrounding tissue as well as vessels that grew into the mass, so the count at low vessel density is the least reliable. And the dying cell fraction is measured at one moment and depends on how long a dying cell remains recognisable, so a change in that interval would change the fraction without any change in the rate of death.

qs.q: Why does a mass without a blood supply stop enlarging while remaining alive?
o: The whole mass dies at that size
Division ceases entirely in such a mass
Death at the centre matches division
Correct: the net change is zero.
qs.x: Correct: Cells beyond the diffusion distance die while cells at the surface continue dividing, and when the two rates match the mass holds a constant size without being dead. Why the others are wrong: Division continues at a normal fraction, the surface cells survive, and the diffusion distance does impose a limit. Trap: Assuming that a mass which stops growing must have stopped dividing.

qs.q: Why is the unchanged dividing fraction the central result?
o: It shows oxygen does not affect division
It shows division was not slowed
It shows the inhibitor failed to act at all
qs.x: Correct: Because the proportion of dividing cells was the same in every condition, the reduction in size cannot be attributed to slower division and must follow from the loss of a supportable volume. Why the others are wrong: The inhibitor clearly acted on vessels and size, the oxygen comparison is a separate point, and the unchanged fraction is what identifies the mechanism. Trap: Overlooking the variable that did not change when it is the one that excludes an explanation.

qs.q: What does the oxygen condition separate?
o: Both were measured in every condition.
The inhibitor's effect from the implantation procedure
qs.x: Correct: Masses grew from two to four millimetres while the vessel count remained at three, so the recovery came from oxygen reaching the interior rather than from new vessels, which shows that oxygen and not vessels is the limiting quantity. Why the others are wrong: The procedure was constant across conditions, division and death were measured everywhere, and the size increase without vessels is the informative comparison. Trap: Treating a means and the thing it supplies as interchangeable.

qs.q: Why is the vessel count least reliable at low density?
o: Correct: a few count for much.
The stain fails when vessels are sparse
Low counts cannot be measured at all
qs.x: Correct: A field at the edge of a mass contains vessels belonging to the surrounding tissue, and when the mass itself has very few vessels those neighbouring ones make up a large share of the count. Why the others are wrong: The stain does not depend on density, a count of three was obtained, and the contamination is proportionally worst at low counts. Trap: Assuming that a counting error affects all values equally when it is additive.

qs.q: How many times larger in diameter is the untreated mass than the high dose mass?
qs.x: Correct: Eleven point four divided by one point nine is six, so the untreated masses were six times the diameter of the most heavily treated ones. Why the others are wrong: The others are the two diameters and their difference rather than their ratio. Trap: Subtracting when the question asks how many times larger.

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: Obedience research asks what makes an ordinary person carry out instructions that harm someone else. In the standard paradigm a participant is told to deliver increasing electric shocks to another person who is in fact a confederate and receives none, and the measure is the fraction who continue to the maximum level on the generator.

Two accounts compete. A dispositional account locates obedience in the person, so the people who continue would be unusually callous. A situational account locates it in the features of the setting: the physical presence of a legitimate authority, the distance of the victim, the absence of visible dissent, and a graded sequence of requests in which each step is barely worse than the one before. The experimental strategy is therefore to hold the task constant and vary one situational feature at a time.
Participants were drawn from the same community sample and randomly assigned across five variations, each identical to the baseline procedure except in the feature named (Table 1).

Every manipulation moved the rate, and the largest single drop, to 10%, came from watching two other apparently ordinary participants refuse. Making the victim visible cut obedience by 25 points, and removing either the authority's presence or the authority's legitimacy produced similar rates near 20%, which suggests that presence and legitimacy contribute in comparable measure.

What the design can and cannot show is worth separating. Random assignment across variations licenses causal claims about the situational features. The design says nothing, however, about which individuals obey, because personality was not measured; the finding is that the rate is movable, not that dispositions are irrelevant. The procedure also depends on participants believing the shocks were real, and it deliberately imposed severe distress, which is why review boards would not approve it today and why replications use milder analogues.

qs.q: Which variation produced the largest reduction in obedience?
o: Instructions come from an ordinary person rather than an authority
The authority gives instructions by telephone
The victim is seated in the same room as the participant
qs.x: Correct: The dissenting-confederates condition yields 10%, the lowest in the table, a 55-point drop from baseline, indicating that visible refusal by peers is the most powerful of the features varied. Why the others are wrong: Victim proximity leaves 40%, and the two conditions that remove the authority's presence or legitimacy both leave about 20%. Trap: Choosing the condition that sounds most dramatic rather than reading the column.

qs.q: What do the five variations taken together support?
o: Obedience to authority cannot be studied experimentally
Situational features substantially determine the rate
The people who continue are unusually cruel individuals
Obedience is fixed by stable features of personality
qs.x: Correct: Holding the task constant and varying one feature at a time moved obedience from 65% to as low as 10%, which establishes that the rate depends heavily on the circumstances rather than on who happened to be recruited. Why the others are wrong: Personality was neither manipulated nor measured, so claims about cruel individuals are unsupported, and the table is itself the product of experiments. Trap: Concluding that dispositions do not matter when the study simply did not measure them.

qs.q: Why is the condition with an ordinary person giving instructions informative?
o: It proves that the authority's presence is entirely irrelevant
Removing presence also lowered the rate.
It provides a measure of how distressed the victim appeared
The victim's behavior was held constant.
It demonstrates that no one obeys instructions from anybody
It separates legitimacy from the instruction itself
Correct: the orders are the same.
qs.x: Correct: The same instructions are given by someone with no claim to authority, so the 20% rate shows that it is the authority's legitimacy, rather than the content of the orders, that carries most of the baseline obedience. Why the others are wrong: A fifth of participants still complied, the telephone condition shows presence matters too, and the victim's scripted behavior did not change. Trap: Reading a reduction as abolition.

qs.q: Which concept best explains why a present, legitimate authority raises obedience?
o: Responsibility is shifted to the authority
Correct: the participant becomes an instrument.
Participants find delivering shocks intrinsically rewarding
Participants had not understood the task instructions
The authority is physically compelling compliance
No force was used in the procedure.
qs.x: Correct: In the presence of an authority who accepts responsibility for the outcome, participants come to see themselves as carrying out another person's plan rather than as the agent of the harm, which lowers the felt cost of continuing. Why the others are wrong: Participants were visibly distressed rather than gratified, no physical coercion occurred, and the instructions were understood. Trap: Looking for a motive to harm when the mechanism is a reassignment of responsibility.

qs.q: What would these data not establish?
o: Which individuals are most likely to comply
Correct: no person-level variable was measured.
That the legitimacy of the authority affects compliance
That victim proximity reduces the rate of obedience
That visible dissent by peers reduces obedience sharply
qs.x: Correct: Every variation manipulated the situation, and no characteristic of the participants was measured, so the study cannot say which kinds of people obey even though it establishes a great deal about which circumstances produce obedience. Why the others are wrong: Proximity, dissent and legitimacy were each manipulated with random assignment and each moved the rate. Trap: Assuming a well-designed experiment answers every question one might ask of its topic.

h: Share continuing to the maximum shock
r: Baseline, authority present, victim in another room
Victim seated in the same room
Instructions given by an ordinary person, no authority

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: The presence of others changes performance, and the direction depends on the task. Social facilitation is the improvement seen on simple or well-learned tasks when others are present; impairment appears on complex or novel tasks. Zajonc's account is that the presence of others raises arousal, and arousal strengthens whatever response is dominant. On a well-practiced task the dominant response is the correct one, so performance improves; on a novel task the dominant responses are errors, so performance worsens.

Social loafing is a different phenomenon that is easily confused with it. Loafing is the reduction in individual effort that occurs when contributions are pooled and no one's output can be identified, and its remedy is making individual contributions visible, which is close to the opposite of removing an audience.

Participants completed two tasks either alone in a cubicle or at a desk observed by two silent confederates, with task and audience condition crossed so that each cell had a separate group of participants. Scores are percent correct (Table 1).

The crossover is the result. An audience adds 9 points to typing and removes 15 points from the logic puzzle, so the effect of being watched reverses with the nature of the task, which no account positing a single direction of effect can produce.

Arousal was not measured, and that is the gap. The arousal account predicts the crossover, but so does an account in which an audience consumes attention that complex tasks require and simple ones do not, and these data cannot distinguish them. Recording heart rate or skin conductance would show whether arousal rose, and manipulating how much attention the audience demanded, for instance by having observers face away, would separate the two. The between-groups design also means that differences between the people assigned to each cell contribute to the variance, and a within-subject design would be more sensitive if practice effects could be controlled.

qs.q: Why does an audience help typing and hurt the logic puzzle?
o: Arousal strengthens whichever response is dominant
Correct: dominant responses differ by task.
Arousal improves performance on any task at all
The puzzle score fell by 15 points.
Logic puzzles require no attention to solve
An audience distracts only while people are typing
qs.x: Correct: Raised arousal favors the dominant response, which is correct typing for a practiced skill and an error for an unfamiliar puzzle, so the same increase in arousal moves the two scores in opposite directions. Why the others are wrong: Puzzles are attention-demanding, arousal did not help in both cases, and the typing score rose rather than fell. Trap: Looking for a single direction of effect when the account predicts a reversal.

qs.q: How does social loafing differ from social facilitation?
o: It occurs only when a task is simple
Loafing is not task-specific in that way.
It concerns pooled effort that cannot be identified
It describes an improvement in the group's performance
It requires an audience to be watching closely
qs.x: Correct: Loafing arises when individual contributions are merged and unidentifiable, so effort falls; the remedy is making each person's output visible, which is nearly the opposite of removing observers.
