Why the others are wrong: Loafing is not confined to simple tasks, it involves reduced rather than improved output, and close observation reduces it. Trap: Grouping the two phenomena because both involve other people.

qs.q: Which measurement would best distinguish the arousal account from an attention account?
o: The number of observers present in the room
Participants' ratings of how much they liked the task
The time each participant spent on the task
Physiological arousal recorded during each task
Correct: it tests the proposed mediator.
qs.x: Correct: The arousal account specifies an intervening physiological state, so recording heart rate or skin conductance tests whether that state actually rose, while an attention account predicts the same behavioral crossover without it. Why the others are wrong: Adding observers strengthens the manipulation without identifying the mechanism, and time on task and task liking are not the mediator either account proposes. Trap: Strengthening the manipulation instead of measuring the mediator.

qs.q: How could the puzzle result be reduced in a workplace?
o: Increase the time pressure on the task as well
Require that the task be done in public first
Allow practice before anyone is observed
Correct: practice makes the correct response dominant.
Add more observers to the room during the task
qs.x: Correct: Impairment occurs because errors are dominant on an unfamiliar task, so practicing until the correct response is dominant converts the audience effect from a cost into a benefit. Why the others are wrong: Public performance of a novel task, added time pressure and additional observers all intensify the impairment. Trap: Treating the effect as something to be endured rather than as something practice removes.

qs.q: Why does it matter that the logic puzzle was novel?
o: Novelty removes arousal from the situation
Novel tasks cannot be scored for their accuracy at all
Novel tasks are easier than practiced tasks
Novelty makes incorrect responses the dominant ones
Correct: that is what arousal amplifies.
qs.x: Correct: The account turns on which response is dominant, and on an unfamiliar task the most readily available responses are wrong, which is why raised arousal lowers the score. Why the others are wrong: The puzzle was scored, novel tasks are harder rather than easier, and novelty does not eliminate arousal. Trap: Treating novelty as a feature of the measure rather than of the response hierarchy.

passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: Researchers investigated the cytotoxic effects of a novel chemotherapeutic agent on a human breast cancer cell line. Cells were exposed to varying concentrations of the drug (0, 10, 20, 40, and 80 µM) for 48 hours, after which cell viability was assessed using an MTT assay. The results, expressed as a percentage of the untreated control, are summarized in Table 1. The standard deviation for each concentration reflects the variability observed across three independent experiments. The data suggest a dose‑dependent decrease in viability, with the highest concentration (80 µM) reducing viability to 20 % of the control. These findings support further investigation of the drug’s therapeutic potential and warrant additional studies to elucidate its mechanism of action.

qs.q: What is the cell viability at a drug concentration of 20 µM?
qs.x: The table shows that at 20 µM the viability is 70 % of the untreated control. Trap: Option A (45 %) corresponds to the 40 µM concentration, which could mislead readers who overlook the concentration‑viability pairing.

qs.q: Which control would best distinguish an effect of the drug from an effect of the solvent used to dissolve it?
o: A vehicle control containing the solvent used to dissolve the drug.
A positive control using a known cytotoxic agent.
A negative control with no cells.
A time‑zero control measuring viability immediately after drug addition.
qs.x: Correct: A) A vehicle control receives the solvent alone, so any change in viability beyond it is due to the drug. Why the others are wrong: B) A positive control checks that the assay can detect cytotoxicity but does not separate drug from solvent. C) A no-cell blank corrects background absorbance. D) A time-zero control sets the starting viability, not the solvent effect. Trap: Choosing a positive control because it validates the assay, even though only a vehicle-only control isolates the solvent effect.

qs.q: What is the percent decrease in viability from the control to the 80 µM concentration?
qs.x: The control is 100 %. At 80 µM viability is 20 %, so the decrease is 100 % – 20 % = 80 %. Trap: Option B (50 %) might be chosen by students who mistakenly calculate the difference between 70 % (20 µM) and 20 % (80 µM) instead of comparing to the control.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is FALSE?
o: The viability decreases as drug concentration increases.
The standard deviation increases with higher drug concentrations.
The 10 µM concentration shows a lower viability than the 20 µM concentration.
The 0 µM concentration serves as the control and is set to 100 % viability.
qs.x: Viability falls with dose (100, 85, 70, 45, 20 %) and the SD rises monotonically (2, 3, 4, 5, 6), so A, B and D are true. C is false because 10 µM (85 %) has higher, not lower, viability than 20 µM (70 %). Trap: Option B looks suspicious because of the word 'increases', but the SD does increase at every step (2 to 6).

qs.q: Assuming viability falls linearly between the 20 µM and 40 µM points, at about what concentration would viability be 50% of control?
qs.x: Correct: C) Between 20 and 40 µM viability falls from 70% to 45%, or 1.25 percentage points per µM; dropping from 70% to 50% needs 16 µM, so about 36 µM. Why the others are wrong: A) 25 µM would give about 64%. B) 30 µM would give about 58%. D) 40 µM gives 45%, which is below 50%. Trap: Picking 40 µM because 45% is the closest tabulated value, without interpolating between the 20 and 40 µM points.

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Midvale investigated the effects of a new dietary supplement on the gut microbiome of adult mice. Over a 12‑week period, 48 mice were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control diet, a diet supplemented with 0.5% of the compound, 1.0%, or 2.0%. Fecal samples were collected at baseline, week 6, and week 12. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, the relative abundance of major bacterial phyla (Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria) was quantified. Table 1 summarizes the average relative abundances (in %) for each group at week 12. The researchers hypothesized that higher supplement concentrations would shift the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio toward a healthier profile. They also monitored body weight and glucose tolerance as secondary outcomes. The study aimed to determine whether the supplement could modulate gut microbiota composition and improve metabolic markers without adverse effects.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which of the following statements best describes the trend in the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio across the supplement groups?
o: The ratio increases with higher supplement concentration.
The ratio decreases with higher supplement concentration.
The ratio remains unchanged across all groups.
The ratio first increases then decreases as concentration rises.
qs.x: The Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio is calculated by dividing the Firmicutes percentage by the Bacteroidetes percentage. For Control: 55.2/35.1 ≈ 1.57. For 0.5%: 52.8/37.6 ≈ 1.41. For 1.0%: 49.5/40.2 ≈ 1.23. For 2.0%: 46.0/42.5 ≈ 1.08. The ratio steadily decreases as supplement concentration increases. Trap: Option A incorrectly assumes a direct proportionality between supplement dose and the ratio.

qs.q: In a parallel-group study like this one, which design element would best control for potential confounding by baseline microbiome composition?
o: Using a crossover design where each mouse receives all supplement levels sequentially.
Randomly assigning mice to groups and stratifying by initial Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio.
Increasing the sample size to 100 mice per group.
Administering the supplement only to mice that already have a high Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio.
qs.x: Correct: Stratifying the random assignment by initial Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio gives every group a comparable distribution of baseline microbiomes. Why the others are wrong: A) giving every mouse all supplement levels in sequence is a crossover, not a parallel-group design, and carry-over of microbiome changes would confound later periods. C) a larger sample improves precision but does not by itself balance baseline composition. D) giving the supplement only to mice with a high initial ratio builds a baseline difference between groups into the comparison. Trap: Choosing the crossover because each animal is its own control, although the supplement's lasting effect on the microbiome carries over between periods.

qs.q: If the researchers report that the 2.0% supplement group had a 12% reduction in fasting glucose compared to the control, what is the absolute change in glucose (mg/dL) if the control group's fasting glucose was 140 mg/dL?
qs.x: Correct: A 12% reduction of a 140 mg/dL control value is 0.12 × 140 = 16.8 mg/dL (the 2.0% group would be at 123.2 mg/dL). Why the others are wrong: A) 12.8 mg/dL does not follow from 12% of 140. C) 18.4 mg/dL does not follow from 12% of 140. D) 20.0 mg/dL would be a 14.3% reduction. Trap: Reporting the final glucose value (123.2 mg/dL) or the percent itself (12) instead of the absolute change, 16.8 mg/dL.

qs.q: Which of the following interpretations of Table 1 is a misreading of the data?
o: The 2.0% group had lower Firmicutes than the control group
Bacteroidetes abundance rose with each increase in supplement concentration
Proteobacteria abundance stayed within about 5.0-5.4% in all groups
Because the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio fell, the supplement improved glucose tolerance
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 reports only phylum abundances at week 12; it contains no glucose tolerance data, so a change in the ratio cannot be taken as proof of improved metabolic function. Why the others are wrong: A) Firmicutes were 46.0% versus 55.2%, so this is supported. B) Bacteroidetes were 35.1, 37.6, 40.2 and 42.5%, a steady rise, so this is supported. C) Proteobacteria ranged from 5.0 to 5.4%, so this is supported. Trap: Treating a shift in the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio (1.57 to 1.08) as direct proof of better metabolic health.

qs.q: Why is the 16S rRNA gene used to profile the relative abundance of bacterial phyla in fecal samples?
o: Conserved regions bind universal primers; hypervariable regions differ by taxon
It encodes a protein that is identical in every bacterial species
It is present only in Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes
It is a eukaryotic gene that marks host contamination
qs.x: The bacterial 16S rRNA gene contains conserved sequences, which allow universal PCR primers, flanking hypervariable regions, which differ among taxa and permit classification into phyla and genera. Trap: Option B confuses a rRNA gene with a protein-coding gene.

passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Social capital refers to the resources a person can draw on through social relationships. The distinction that matters for outcomes is between two kinds. Bonding capital links people who are alike, typically within a family, a congregation or a block, and supplies trust, mutual aid and informal insurance. Bridging capital links people across groups and supplies what a closed circle cannot: information from outside, contacts in other institutions, and routes into labor markets a neighborhood is not already connected to.

The two kinds are not substitutes, and a neighborhood can be high on one and low on the other. A tight community with no outside links is rich in support and poor in access, which predicts resilience without mobility; a neighborhood whose residents have many outside contacts but little internal cohesion may have access without the trust needed to act collectively.

Investigators followed 90 neighborhoods in one metropolitan area for five years. Bonding and bridging indices were built from resident surveys at baseline, neighborhoods were grouped by whether each index fell above or below the metropolitan median, and the change in the employment rate over the five years was recorded from administrative data (Table 1).

Bridging is what moves employment: the two high-bridging groups gain 2.9 and 4.1 points while the high-bonding, low-bridging group is flat at 0.4. Bonding is not useless, though, because adding it to high bridging raises the gain from 2.9 to 4.1, which is consistent with internal trust helping a neighborhood act on outside information.

Nothing was assigned here. Neighborhoods were classified on characteristics they already had, and the kind of place that develops outside ties is also likely to differ in transit access, in the age and education of its residents, and in how far it sits from areas where employment was growing anyway. A measure of the pathway would help: if bridging capital works through information, then counting job referrals received by residents would show the mechanism directly rather than leaving it to be inferred from the employment column.

qs.q: Which kind of capital best predicts employment gains in Table 1?
o: Neither index showed any relationship to employment
Bridging capital, the ties that link across groups
Correct: both high-bridging groups gained most.
Both indices contributed in equal measure here
Bridging accounts for most of it.
Bonding capital on its own, without outside ties
qs.x: Correct: The two high-bridging groups gained 2.9 and 4.1 points while the high-bonding, low-bridging group gained only 0.4, so bridging is doing most of the work, with bonding adding to it when bridging is already present. Why the others are wrong: Bonding alone was nearly flat, the groups differ widely, and the two indices are not equal contributors. Trap: Splitting the difference when the table clearly favors one index.

qs.q: What does bonding capital typically supply?
o: Support and mutual aid within a group
Correct: trust among people who are alike.
Access to institutions outside the neighborhood
qs.x: Correct: Bonding ties connect similar people and provide trust, informal help and a kind of mutual insurance, which is why high-bonding neighborhoods are resilient even when their employment is not improving. Why the others are wrong: Outside access is what bridging ties supply, formal authority is a feature of institutions, and personal assets are not a form of social capital at all. Trap: Equating any beneficial resource with social capital.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects a causal reading of these results?
o: Employment change was taken from administrative tax records
The follow-up period extended over five years
Ninety neighborhoods were followed for the study
Neighborhoods were classified, not assigned, by type
qs.x: Correct: A neighborhood's position on the two indices reflects everything about its history and location, so places with high bridging capital may differ in transit, education and proximity to growing employment, any of which could produce the gradient. Why the others are wrong: Administrative records are a strength, and the sample size and follow-up period are adequate for the comparison. Trap: Looking for a flaw in the measurement when the problem is in the assignment.

qs.q: Which type of neighborhood lost employment over the five years?
o: The neighborhoods low on both indices
High bonding with low bridging capital
High on both of the two indices
Low bonding with high bridging capital
qs.x: Correct: Only the neighborhoods low on both indices declined, by 1.1 points, which fits an account in which neither internal trust nor outside access was available to buffer a labor-market shock. Why the others are wrong: Each of the other three types gained, by 0.4, 2.9 and 4.1 points respectively. Trap: Reading the smallest gain as a loss.

qs.q: Which additional measure would best show the pathway by which bridging capital acts?
o: The number of job referrals residents received
Correct: it measures the information flow.
The median housing price within each neighborhood
The average number of years residents had lived there
The total number of residents in each neighborhood
qs.x: Correct: The proposed mechanism is access to information and contacts from outside, so counting referrals received puts the intervening step on the table instead of inferring it from the employment outcome it is meant to explain. Why the others are wrong: Residential tenure, housing price and population size are neighborhood characteristics rather than measures of information reaching residents. Trap: Adding a reasonable control variable instead of measuring the mechanism.

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Environmental justice research examines whether environmental hazards and benefits are distributed unevenly across groups. Two explanations are debated. In the siting explanation, polluting facilities are built in neighborhoods with less political power. In the move-in explanation, housing near existing facilities is cheaper, so lower-income households move there afterward. The two can be separated only by data that record the order of events.

Researchers linked the locations of 1,100 industrial facilities that report toxic releases to census data for the surrounding tracts across three decades. For each facility, they recorded the characteristics of its tract in the decade before it opened and in the two decades after. They also measured ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and, from a state health registry, the rate of childhood asthma emergency visits (Table 1).

To check that the comparison tracts were reasonable, the researchers matched each facility tract to a tract in the same metropolitan area with similar population density and distance from the city center, since both affect land cost and the kinds of businesses that locate there. They also repeated the analysis using only facilities that opened in the middle decade, so that a full decade of data was available on each side of the opening, and the pattern was unchanged. Facilities that had closed during the study period were analyzed separately; disparities in those tracts persisted after closure, although PM2.5 in them fell toward the level of the comparison tracts within a few years of closure.

The researchers noted that income and demographic composition in these tracts were already different from comparison tracts before siting and changed only modestly afterward. They also noted that tracts were not assigned at random, that asthma has other causes including indoor allergens and secondhand smoke, and that people who live in a tract today may have moved there recently.

qs.q: What do the before-siting figures most directly address?
o: Whether the facilities comply with regulations
Whether disparities came before the facilities
Correct: they test the move-in explanation.
qs.x: Correct: If disparities appeared only after siting, the move-in explanation would be supported. The data show that tracts chosen for facilities already had lower income, lower homeownership and a higher share of residents of color a decade before, which points to siting rather than later in-migration. Why the others are wrong: Causation of asthma, resident opinion and regulatory compliance are different questions. Trap: Treating any disparity as evidence for a particular explanation without the timing data.

qs.q: Why is the modest change after siting important?
o: It shows the facilities later closed
It proves the facilities cause poverty
Income was already low before siting.
qs.x: Correct: The move-in explanation predicts that a tract's composition changes substantially after a facility opens. Income went from 71% to 68% of the state median and the share of residents of color from 46% to 52%, changes too small to account for the gap, which existed beforehand. Why the others are wrong: The income gap preceded siting; exposure and health measures do differ; nothing is said about closures. Trap: Reading a small change as no effect on residents.

qs.q: What most limits the conclusion that facility emissions cause the higher asthma rate?
o: Tracts differ in other asthma risks
Correct: confounding by housing and smoke exposure.
PM2.5 was measured in both groups
Asthma visits came from a health registry
qs.x: Correct: Neighborhoods differ in housing quality, indoor allergens, secondhand smoke exposure and access to care, all of which affect asthma. Without accounting for these, the difference between 34 and 19 visits per 1,000 cannot be attributed to emissions alone. Why the others are wrong: Measuring exposure in both groups, using registry data and following three decades all improve the study. Trap: Choosing a design feature that strengthens the study when asked for a limitation.

qs.q: Which concept best describes the pattern the siting explanation proposes?
o: Correct: routine decisions produce unequal outcomes.
The sick role in affected families
That describes expectations for people who are ill.
That concerns performance under a negative stereotype.
qs.x: Correct: Institutional discrimination refers to unequal outcomes produced by the ordinary policies and procedures of organizations, such as siting decisions that follow land cost and local political capacity, without requiring individual prejudice. Why the others are wrong: Stereotype threat concerns test performance; residential mobility is what the move-in explanation describes; the sick role concerns the social expectations of illness. Trap: Assuming unequal outcomes require someone's intent.

qs.q: Which additional measurement would best strengthen the link between emissions and asthma?
o: Total number of facilities in the state
A count does not link exposure to health.
Average income in the state as a whole
A statewide figure adds no comparison.
The number of workers each facility employs
Asthma rates before and after opening
qs.x: Correct: Comparing asthma rates in the same tracts before and after a facility opened holds constant the many fixed features of each neighborhood, so a rise that follows openings is much harder to explain by pre-existing differences. Why the others are wrong: Facility counts, statewide income and employment figures do not connect exposure to health within the same population. Trap: Adding data that describe the setting instead of testing the relationship.

h: Tracts that later received a facility, decade before siting
Tracts with a facility, two decades after
r: Median household income (% of state median)
Residents who are people of color (%)

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: The demographic transition describes a shift from high birth and death rates to low ones. In stage 1, both are high and population grows slowly. In stage 2, death rates fall first, usually because of clean water, sanitation and vaccination, while birth rates stay high, so population grows rapidly. In stage 3, birth rates fall as child survival improves, women gain education and employment, and families move to cities where children cost more to raise. In stage 4, both rates are low and growth is slow. Some countries have entered a stage in which births fall below deaths and the population shrinks without immigration.

The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman would have at current age-specific rates. A TFR of about 2.1 is replacement level in countries with low child mortality. Even when fertility falls to replacement, a population keeps growing for decades because a large share of it is young and entering childbearing years, an effect called population momentum.

These measures have limits. The crude birth and death rates depend on a population's age structure, so a country with many older residents can show a high death rate even when people there live long lives: Country D's rate of 12 per 1,000 reflects its age structure rather than poor health. Comparing countries fairly often requires age-adjusted rates or measures such as life expectancy at birth. The TFR has its own limitation, because it describes the rates of one year rather than the completed families of any real group of women. If fertility is falling, the TFR of a given year underestimates how many children women who are young that year will eventually have.

Country A built its first national vaccination program 15 years ago, and its death rate has fallen from 20 per 1,000 over that period. Country D's population declined by 0.3% last year despite net immigration of 2 per 1,000.

qs.q: What is the rate of natural increase in Country A, per 1,000?
qs.x: Correct: Natural increase is the crude birth rate minus the crude death rate, here 38 − 12 = 26 per 1,000, or 2.6% per year, excluding migration. Why the others are wrong: The rates are not added or divided, and 12 is the death rate alone. Trap: Confusing natural increase with total population change, which also includes migration.

qs.q: Which country best fits stage 2 of the transition?
o: Its birth rate has already fallen substantially.
Correct: falling deaths with still-high births.
qs.x: Correct: Country A's death rate has dropped from 20 to 12 per 1,000 since vaccination began, while its birth rate remains at 38. That gap produces rapid growth and a very young population, 44% under 15. Why the others are wrong: Country B is mid-transition, Country C has completed it, and Country D is beyond it. Trap: Classifying a country by its growth rate alone rather than by which rate is changing.

qs.q: Why would Country B keep growing for decades even if its TFR fell to 2.1 next year?
o: Its young cohort has yet to have children
It leads to a stable size eventually.
Fertility rates cannot fall that quickly
Its death rate would rise immediately
qs.x: Correct: Thirty percent of Country B's population is under 15. As that cohort enters childbearing age, the number of births stays high even at replacement fertility, so the population continues to grow until the age structure evens out. Why the others are wrong: Replacement fertility eventually stabilizes a population; death rates respond slowly; rapid fertility declines have occurred. Trap: Assuming replacement fertility means an immediate end to growth.

qs.q: What is the most likely consequence of Country D's age structure?
o: A growing labor force over the next decade
Few young people are entering it.
qs.x: Correct: With more than twice as many people over 64 as under 15, the number of workers supporting each retiree falls, which strains pension and health systems. This is why some countries in this position encourage immigration or later retirement. Why the others are wrong: The small young cohort limits labor force growth; the TFR is well below replacement; the median age rises as the population ages. Trap: Expecting low fertility to correct itself quickly.

qs.q: Why can Country D's population shrink despite net immigration?
o: Its death rate is the highest shown
Emigration is not counted in net immigration
Deaths exceed births by more than 2
qs.x: Correct: Natural change is 9 − 12 = −3 per 1,000. Adding net immigration of 2 per 1,000 leaves about −1 per 1,000, or roughly the 0.3% decline reported once rounding is considered. Why the others are wrong: Immigration tends to add people of childbearing age; Country A has the same death rate; a net figure already accounts for departures. Trap: Assuming any immigration is enough to prevent decline.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: Dissolving a nonvolatile solute in a liquid lowers its vapor pressure, raises its boiling point and lowers its freezing point. These are colligative properties: they depend on the number of dissolved particles, not on what the particles are. The changes are ΔTb = iKb·m and ΔTf = iKf·m, where m is molality, Kb and Kf are constants of the solvent, and i is the van 't Hoff factor, the number of particles each formula unit produces in solution. For water, Kb = 0.512 °C·kg/mol and Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol.
Osmotic pressure follows Π = iMRT, where M is molarity. Because it can be large even for dilute solutions, it is the colligative property used to measure the molar mass of proteins.
Students measured freezing points of aqueous solutions, each prepared at 0.100 mol of solute per kilogram of water (Table 1).

Colligative properties are at work in several familiar situations. Salt spread on an icy road lowers the freezing point of the water film, so ice melts at temperatures below 0 °C. Antifreeze in a car both lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point of the coolant. In the body, the osmotic pressure set by plasma proteins pulls fluid back into capillaries at their venous end, and a low plasma protein level allows fluid to accumulate in the tissues as edema. Each of these depends on the number of dissolved particles rather than on their chemical identity, which is why the van 't Hoff factor matters so much for ionic solutes.

The students noted that the apparent values of i for the salts fall short of the whole numbers predicted from their formulas. In concentrated solutions, oppositely charged ions spend part of their time close together as ion pairs and behave as fewer particles. At 0.0010 mol/kg, the apparent i for NaCl rose to 1.97.

qs.q: Why does 0.100 mol/kg NaCl lower the freezing point more than the same amount of glucose?
o: Each formula unit gives two particles
Ionic solutes bind water more tightly
Binding strength is not what the law describes.
Sodium chloride has a larger molar mass
Molar mass does not enter the equation.
qs.x: Correct: NaCl dissociates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so a 0.100 molal solution contains close to 0.200 mol of particles per kilogram. Glucose stays as one particle, so its freezing point depression is roughly half as large. Why the others are wrong: Colligative properties do not depend on the identity or mass of the particles; the equations count particles rather than interactions; glucose does not evaporate. Trap: Comparing masses when the law counts particles.

qs.q: What freezing point would 0.100 mol/kg of a solute with i = 3.00 produce?
qs.x: Correct: ΔTf = iKf·m = 3.00 × 1.86 × 0.100 = 0.558 °C, and because the freezing point is lowered, the solution freezes at −0.558 °C. Why the others are wrong: Using i = 1 ignores dissociation; 5.58 uses a tenfold higher concentration; the freezing point goes down, not up. Trap: Reporting the size of the change as if it were the temperature.

qs.q: Why is the apparent i for MgCl₂ 2.70 rather than 3.00?
o: The measurement was taken too early
The same pattern appears for NaCl.
The formula produces only two ions
It gives Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻.
Some ions remain paired in solution
Correct: paired ions act as one particle.
qs.x: Correct: In solution, Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ attract each other, and some spend part of the time associated. A paired cation and anion lower the freezing point as a single particle, so the effective number of particles is below three. The effect is stronger for Mg²⁺ because of its higher charge. Why the others are wrong: MgCl₂ is soluble; the formula gives three ions; the deviation is systematic across the salts. Trap: Assuming complete dissociation always means the full whole-number value.

qs.q: What does the rise of NaCl's apparent i to 1.97 at 0.0010 mol/kg show?
o: Ion pairing weakens as the solution is diluted
Dilution increases the number of ions
The constant Kf changes with concentration
It is a property of the solvent.
Sodium chloride dissociates more at low temperature
qs.x: Correct: In a dilute solution, ions are farther apart and spend less time paired, so the measured behavior approaches the ideal value of 2. Colligative equations describe ideal solutions, which real solutions approach as they are diluted. Why the others are wrong: Dilution lowers the number of particles per kilogram; Kf depends on the solvent; the comparison varies concentration. Trap: Reading a higher apparent i as more solute dissolving.

qs.q: Why is osmotic pressure the preferred colligative property for finding a protein's molar mass?
o: Osmotic pressure does not depend on particle number
Dilute protein still gives usable pressure
Correct: the other changes are too small.
Proteins lower the freezing point most of all
Their molar mass makes molality tiny.
Proteins cannot be dissolved in water
qs.x: Correct: A protein's large molar mass means even a few grams per liter give a very low molality, so the freezing point change would be thousandths of a degree and hard to measure. Osmotic pressure for the same solution is large enough to read on a simple column of liquid. Why the others are wrong: Proteins dissolve; osmotic pressure depends on particle concentration; a tiny molality produces a tiny freezing point change. Trap: Assuming a large molecule produces a large colligative effect.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: Two genes on the same chromosome are inherited together unless a crossover separates them. The frequency with which they are separated increases with the distance between them, so recombination frequency is used as a measure of distance, with one percent recombination defined as one map unit.

The relationship breaks down over long distances. Two genes far apart are separated by a crossover in so many meioses that the observed recombination frequency approaches fifty percent, the same value expected for genes on different chromosomes, so a large distance cannot be measured directly.

The solution is to measure in short steps and add them. Three-point crosses give the distances between adjacent pairs, and summing the intervals gives a total that exceeds the directly measured frequency between the outer genes, because double crossovers between them restore the original arrangement.
Recombination was measured between four genes in order (Table 1).

The three adjacent intervals summed to 35.6 map units while the directly measured A to D frequency was 29.4 percent, a shortfall of 6.2 that corresponds to the double crossovers that returned the outer markers to their parental combination. Those were detected by scoring the middle markers.
The interference column records that fewer double crossovers were seen than the product of the single frequencies would predict, so a crossover in one interval reduces the chance of another nearby.

Two qualifications apply. Map distances built by addition assume the gene order is known, and an incorrect order produces a map that is internally consistent and wrong, so the order must be established from the double crossover classes rather than assumed. And recombination frequency is not uniform along a chromosome, with regions near the centromere recombining far less than their physical length would suggest, so a map in these units is a map of recombination rather than of DNA.

qs.q: Why does a long distance underestimate itself?
o: Recombination is less frequent when far apart
Long distances cannot be measured at all
qs.x: Correct: Two crossovers between the outer markers put them back in their original combination, so those meioses are scored as non-recombinant and the frequency is too low. Why the others are wrong: Long distances are measurable, recombination between distant genes is more frequent, and the bias is downward. Trap: Assuming an observed frequency counts every crossover that occurred.

qs.q: Why must the gene order be established rather than assumed?
o: A wrong order still adds up
Addition fails with the wrong order
Order cannot be determined from crosses
qs.x: Correct: Summing intervals produces a self-consistent map for whatever order is assumed, so the order has to be determined independently from the rarest recombinant classes. Why the others are wrong: Order is determined from the double crossover classes, addition still works arithmetically, and the order determines the map. Trap: Mistaking internal consistency for evidence of correctness.

qs.q: Why is this a map of recombination rather than of DNA?
o: DNA length cannot be measured by any method
It is a map of DNA
qs.x: Correct: Regions differ several fold in how often they recombine per unit of physical length, so equal map distances do not correspond to equal amounts of DNA. Why the others are wrong: Physical distance is measurable by sequencing, recombination is markedly non-uniform, and the units are recombinational. Trap: Reading a genetic map as a physical one.

qs.q: By how many map units did the sum exceed the direct measurement?
qs.x: Correct: The summed distance of 35.6 exceeds the directly measured 29.4 by 6.2 map units. Why the others are wrong: The others are the two totals and one interval. Trap: Reporting a total where a difference was asked for.

qs.q: Why does the interference column matter?
qs.x: Correct: Fewer double crossovers were observed than the product of the single interval frequencies predicts, which means a crossover in one interval suppresses one nearby and the intervals cannot be treated as independent. Why the others are wrong: 214 doubles were counted, interference reduces the count, and the non-independence affects map construction. Trap: Multiplying interval frequencies as though crossovers were independent events.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: Many organisms defend themselves with short peptides that kill bacteria by disrupting their membranes rather than by inhibiting an enzyme. Such a peptide is typically cationic and amphipathic: it carries a net positive charge that draws it to the negatively charged bacterial surface, and it folds so that its hydrophobic residues lie on one face and its charged residues on the other.

Once bound, the peptide inserts its hydrophobic face into the lipid interior and disrupts the barrier, and the cell loses its ion gradients and dies. Because the target is the membrane's physical integrity rather than a specific protein, resistance is harder to acquire than it is against a conventional antibiotic.

Selectivity for bacteria over host cells comes from the difference in surface charge. Bacterial membranes carry anionic phospholipids on their outer face, while animal cell membranes present mostly neutral phosphatidylcholine and carry cholesterol, which stiffens the bilayer and resists insertion.
A synthetic peptide was tested against bacteria and red cells under varying salt (Table 1).

The peptide is sixteen times less active at physiological salt than in salt-free medium, while its effect on red cells barely changes, so the selectivity ratio collapses from 32 to 2. Lowering the pH at physiological salt restores much of the activity.

The salt sensitivity is what the electrostatic mechanism predicts: added ions screen the attraction between the cationic peptide and the anionic bacterial surface, and the initial binding step is weakened.

Two qualifications apply. The minimum inhibitory concentration is measured in a defined medium, and serum proteins bind such peptides and reduce the free concentration substantially, so activity in blood is lower than these figures suggest. And a peptide that disrupts membranes is not without a target in the host: the modest haemolysis seen here sets a ceiling on the dose that can be given, which is why selectivity rather than potency is the limiting property.

qs.q: Why does added salt reduce the peptide's activity?
o: The peptide's hydrophobic face is neutralized by the dissolved ions
Growth rate is not the variable.
qs.x: Correct: The peptide reaches the bacterial surface because its positive charge is attracted to the anionic membrane, and dissolved ions shorten the range of that attraction. Why the others are wrong: The peptide is chemically stable in salt, bacterial growth rate is not what was varied, and the ions affect the charged face rather than the hydrophobic one. Trap: Looking for a chemical effect on the peptide when the effect is on an electrostatic interaction.

qs.q: Why does the peptide spare animal cells?
o: Repair is not the stated reason.
Animal cells lack a membrane for the peptide to disrupt
qs.x: Correct: Host membranes present largely neutral headgroups, so the electrostatic attraction is weak, and cholesterol stiffens the bilayer against insertion. Why the others are wrong: Cell size is not the discriminator, membrane repair is not what was described, and animal cells certainly have membranes. Trap: Attributing selectivity to a host response rather than to membrane composition.

qs.q: Why is resistance harder to acquire?
o: The target is physical, not a protein
The peptide kills bacteria too quickly for resistance to develop at all
qs.x: Correct: Escaping the peptide would require remodelling the membrane's lipid composition and charge rather than altering one protein, so no single mutation confers resistance. Why the others are wrong: Being a natural product is irrelevant, bacterial proteases exist and do degrade such peptides, and the speed of killing is not what prevents resistance. Trap: Assuming a fast-acting agent cannot be resisted.

qs.q: How many times less active is the peptide at physiological salt?
o: That is the value at 50 millimolar.
qs.x: Correct: Dividing 32 by 2.0 micrograms per millilitre gives a sixteenfold loss of potency. Why the others are wrong: The other values are the individual concentrations at three salt conditions. Trap: Quoting a concentration where the ratio of two was asked for.

qs.q: Why is selectivity the limiting property rather than potency?
o: The peptide also damages host cells
Ease of measurement is not the reason.
A more potent peptide would be degraded faster in the bloodstream
qs.x: Correct: Raising the dose to overcome the salt-induced loss of activity also raises the haemolysis, so the usable window is set by the ratio of the two effects rather than by the absolute activity. Why the others are wrong: Potency can be engineered, convenience of measurement is irrelevant, and proteolytic stability is a distinct problem. Trap: Optimizing activity against the pathogen without regard to the host.

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Social reproduction describes how advantage is transmitted across generations through schooling, networks, and credentials. Tracking, differential parental involvement, and unequal school resources are proposed channels, and interventions that change one channel may leave others intact.
Investigators followed 3,000 students from entry to graduation across schools with different practices (Table 1).

qs.q: Which practice combination worked best?
qs.x: Correct: Opening access and adding support produced both the highest advanced-course participation and the highest graduation rate. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining practice produced lower figures on both measures. Trap: Treating access alone as sufficient.

qs.q: What does the last row add?
qs.x: Correct: Open enrollment without added staffing produced smaller gains, showing that changing a rule without resources limits the effect. Why the others are wrong: Open enrollment still beat tracking, and staffing clearly mattered. Trap: Reading a weaker result as a failed policy.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects these conclusions?
qs.x: Correct: Because schools selected their own practices, school characteristics may explain the differences rather than the practices themselves. Why the others are wrong: The remaining features are appropriate. Trap: Reading a multi-school comparison as a randomized trial.

qs.q: Which channel does tracking represent?
qs.x: Correct: Tracking is a school practice that sorts students into different curricula, which is an institutional channel. Why the others are wrong: Involvement, networks, and credentials were not measured here. Trap: Naming a channel the study did not examine.

qs.q: Which added measure would test durability?
qs.x: Correct: Following students after graduation shows whether the gains persist into later education or work. Why the others are wrong: Grades, course counts, and teacher ratings are measured during school. Trap: Confusing more detail with longer follow-up.

h: Share of low-income students in advanced courses

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: A gene on the X chromosome is inherited differently in the two sexes because males carry one copy and females two. A recessive allele on the X is expressed in any male who carries it and only in a female who carries two, which is why recessive X-linked conditions are far commoner in males.

The transmission pattern follows from the same asymmetry. An affected male passes his X to all his daughters and none of his sons, so the condition appears to skip a generation and reappear in his grandsons through his daughters.

Female carriers are not always unaffected. One X in each cell is inactivated at random early in development, so a carrier is a mosaic of cells expressing one allele or the other, and the proportion varies between tissues and between individuals.
Enzyme activity was measured in family members (Table 1).

The affected male had 3 percent activity with little variation between tissues, while the two carrier females averaged 52 and 19 percent with ranges spanning 18 to 86 and 9 to 31 percent. The mean activity of a carrier is near half the normal value, but the spread between tissues is what distinguishes a mosaic from a uniform half.
The second carrier's low mean reflects a skewed pattern of inactivation rather than a different genotype, which is why two women with identical genotypes can differ in whether they have symptoms.

Two qualifications apply. Mean activity is calculated across sampled tissues, and the tissues that matter clinically may not be among those sampled, so a woman with a normal mean in blood can have a low value in the organ that produces her symptoms. And inactivation is random at the time it occurs but is then inherited by all descendants of each cell, so a tissue derived from few founder cells shows more extreme values than one derived from many, which contributes to the spread.

qs.q: Why does an affected male have little variation between tissues?
o: His tissues are all derived from one founder cell
qs.x: Correct: With only one X there is nothing to inactivate, so every cell expresses the same allele and all tissues are alike. Why the others are wrong: His tissues have many founder cells, his activity is low, and he is not mosaic for this gene. Trap: Expecting variation wherever a gene is X-linked.

qs.q: Why can two carriers with the same genotype differ clinically?
o: One of them carries a second mutation elsewhere
qs.x: Correct: Which X is inactivated is decided at random in each cell early in development, so the fraction of cells expressing the mutant allele differs between individuals and determines whether symptoms appear. Why the others are wrong: The genotypes are stated to be identical, genotype is not sufficient here, and the two carriers plainly differ. Trap: Treating genotype as a complete predictor of phenotype.

qs.q: Why does a tissue from few founder cells show extreme values?
o: All tissues have the same number
Founder cells inactivate both X chromosomes
qs.x: Correct: The inactivation choice is made once per founder cell and inherited by its descendants, so a tissue built from a handful of founders samples that choice few times and can end up strongly skewed. Why the others are wrong: Only one X is inactivated per cell, founder numbers differ between tissues, and few founders give more extreme values. Trap: Expecting a random process to average out regardless of how many times it was sampled.

qs.q: What is the width of the skewed carrier's tissue range?
o: That is the other carrier's width.
qs.x: Correct: A range from 9 to 31 percent is 22 percentage points wide. Why the others are wrong: The others are the upper value, the mean, and the other carrier's range width. Trap: Reading a bound where a width was asked for.

qs.q: Why can a normal blood value coexist with symptoms?
o: The relevant tissue was not sampled
Blood is not affected by X inactivation
Symptoms are unrelated to enzyme activity
qs.x: Correct: The inactivation pattern differs between tissues, so an accessible tissue can have a favourable proportion while the organ responsible for the symptoms does not. Why the others are wrong: Blood cells are subject to inactivation, the symptoms follow the activity in the affected tissue, and the discordance is well described. Trap: Reading an accessible tissue as representative of the body.

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: Migration is analyzed in terms of push factors at the origin, which drive people to leave, and pull factors at the destination, which attract them. Push factors include conflict, crop failure and unemployment; pull factors include wages, safety and existing networks of earlier migrants. Intervening obstacles, such as distance, cost and legal barriers, determine which of those who want to move actually do.

Two refinements matter. Migration is selective: migrants are typically not a random sample of the origin population but are younger and, for longer moves, better educated, because the costs are paid up front and the returns accrue over a working life. And networks are self-reinforcing, since each earlier migrant lowers the cost of the next move by supplying information, housing and job contacts, which is why flows persist after the original push has eased.
Four origin-destination corridors were compared on the size of the flow and on three correlates measured in the same year (Table 1).

The wage ratio does not order the flows. Corridor Z has the highest ratio at 3.9 and the smallest flow at 2.1 per thousand, while Corridor Y has the lowest ratio at 1.8 and the second largest flow. What does track the flows is the combination of short distance and a high share of households with a prior migrant, which is the obstacles-and-networks account rather than a simple wage account.

Distance and network share are themselves closely related here, since corridors with short distances also have high prior-migrant shares, so the table cannot separate the two: a corridor that is near may send more people simply because moving is cheap, or because its long history of movement has built the networks. A corridor that was distant but had a high network share would distinguish them, and none of the four provides that combination.

The figures are also one year's snapshot of four corridors, so they describe a cross-section rather than a process, and the wage ratio is an average that says nothing about the wages available to the kind of worker who actually migrates.

qs.q: What does Corridor Z most clearly show?
o: A high wage gap need not produce a large flow
Wage ratios are measured with substantial error
Networks are unnecessary for migration to occur
Z has the smallest network share.
Distance has no relation to migration flows
Z is the most distant and smallest.
qs.x: Correct: Corridor Z combines the largest wage ratio in the table with the smallest flow, which is the clearest demonstration that a wage incentive alone does not determine how many people move. Why the others are wrong: Nothing suggests mismeasurement, Z is consistent with distance mattering rather than not, and its low network share supports the network account. Trap: Reading a counterexample to one factor as evidence against every factor.

qs.q: Why is migration described as selective?
o: Only those with networks are permitted to move
Migrants are younger and often better educated
Correct: costs are paid up front.
Every member of a household moves together
Destinations choose which applicants to admit
Legal selection is a separate matter.
qs.x: Correct: Because the costs of moving are borne immediately and the benefits accumulate over a working life, those with more years of work ahead and more transferable skills are overrepresented among migrants. Why the others are wrong: Admission policy is an obstacle rather than what selectivity means, networks reduce cost without granting permission, and partial household moves are common. Trap: Reading selectivity as selection by the destination.

qs.q: Why can this table not separate distance from networks?
o: Network share was reported by households
Only four corridors appear in the comparison
More corridors of the same kind would not help.
The two move together across all four corridors
Correct: near corridors have dense networks.
Distance is reported in kilometres rather than hours
qs.x: Correct: Every corridor that is close also has a high share of households with a prior migrant, so no contrast exists in which one varies while the other is held constant, and a distant corridor with dense networks is what the table lacks. Why the others are wrong: Units and self-report are minor issues, and adding corridors would not help unless they broke the pairing. Trap: Treating collinearity as a shortage of observations.

qs.q: Why do migration flows often persist after the original push factor eases?
o: Push factors never actually ease at the origin
Conflicts and crop failures do end.
Each earlier migrant lowers the next move's cost
Legal barriers fall as flows become established
Wage gaps widen automatically once a flow begins
Wages are not driven by the flow.
qs.x: Correct: Earlier migrants supply information, housing and job contacts, so the cost and risk of moving fall for those who follow, and the flow sustains itself once a network exists. Why the others are wrong: Flows do not raise wage gaps, push factors do ease, and legal barriers frequently tighten as flows grow. Trap: Looking for a continuing push when the explanation is a falling cost.

qs.q: Which corridor has the largest annual flow per 1,000 at the origin?
o: Correct: the largest in the column.
qs.x: Correct: Corridor W sends 18.4 migrants per thousand, the largest flow, and it combines the shortest practical distance with the highest prior-migrant share at 62%. Why the others are wrong: Corridor Y is second at 11.9, X third at 7.2 and Z smallest at 2.1. Trap: Choosing the corridor with the highest wage ratio.

h: Share with a prior migrant in the household

passages.title: Social interactions · passage
text: Erving Goffman described social life in dramaturgical terms. In the front stage, people manage the impression others form of them, following the expectations of the role they are performing. In the back stage, they step out of the performance. Impression management is this ongoing regulation of information about oneself. It includes ingratiation, trying to be liked; self-promotion, trying to be seen as competent; and self-handicapping, creating an obstacle in advance so that failure can be attributed to it rather than to ability.

Researchers studied these behaviors in job interviews. Trained observers coded 160 videotaped interviews for ingratiation, such as complimenting the organization and expressing agreement, and self-promotion, such as describing accomplishments. Interviewers rated each candidate's likability and competence, and reported whether they would recommend a hire (Table 1).

Goffman also described teams, in which several people cooperate to sustain a single performance, and the care taken to keep the back stage out of the audience's view. A restaurant kitchen and its dining room are his standard example: the staff maintain one presentation at the table and another behind the door, and the boundary between the two is defended. Goffman argued that the audience usually cooperates in maintaining the performance, overlooking small slips rather than exposing them, because an exposed performance is awkward for everyone present, a courtesy he called protective practice, or tact.

In a second study, 90 students were told they would take a difficult test of intellectual ability. Before the test, they chose between two drugs described to them, one said to improve performance and one said to impair it. Students who had succeeded on an earlier test through clear effort chose the impairing drug 14% of the time, while students who had succeeded on a test whose scoring they could not understand chose it 56% of the time.

qs.q: Which behavior best illustrates self-handicapping?
o: Studying extra hours before the test
Choosing a drug said to impair performance
Correct: it supplies an excuse in advance.
qs.x: Correct: Self-handicapping means arranging an obstacle before a performance so that failure can be blamed on the obstacle rather than on ability. Taking something expected to impair performance does exactly that. Why the others are wrong: Compliments are ingratiation, accomplishments are self-promotion, and extra study is the opposite of a handicap. Trap: Confusing an excuse made afterward with an obstacle arranged beforehand.

qs.q: Why did uncertain success raise self-handicapping so sharply?
o: Correct: the threat is to an image they cannot secure.
The aim is to protect the image, not to fail.
qs.x: Correct: Students who succeeded through effort they understood could expect to do so again. Those whose success came by means they could not identify faced a reputation they might not live up to, and arranging an excuse protects it. Why the others are wrong: Both groups had succeeded; the goal is to protect the self-image rather than to do badly; the descriptions were explicit. Trap: Reading self-handicapping as an intention to fail.

qs.q: What do the interview results suggest about the two tactics?
o: Self-promotion alone led to more hires.
Correct: likability and competence rise separately.
qs.x: Correct: Ingratiation raised likability (3.8 to 5.6) with little change in competence, while self-promotion raised competence (3.9 to 5.8) with little change in likability. Candidates using both were recommended most often (71%). Why the others are wrong: The two tactics affect different ratings; self-promotion alone outperformed ingratiation alone in hiring; all three outcomes varied. Trap: Assuming any favorable tactic improves every impression.

qs.q: What is the main limitation of the interview study?
o: Correct: candidates differ in other ways.
Both likability and competence were rated
qs.x: Correct: Candidates chose how to behave, so those who used more tactics may also have been more experienced or more qualified, which could explain the higher ratings. Only assigning behavior could separate the two. Why the others are wrong: Taping, trained coders and multiple ratings all strengthen the study. Trap: Choosing a methodological strength when asked for a limitation.

qs.q: Which behavior would Goffman describe as back stage?
o: That is still part of it.
qs.x: Correct: The back stage is where the person steps out of the role and drops the managed impression, such as speaking frankly with a friend once the audience is gone. Why the others are wrong: Dressing, rehearsing and parting courtesies are all part of presenting the performance. Trap: Treating preparation as back stage because it happens in private.

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: Fertility is measured in two ways that answer different questions. The crude birth rate counts births per thousand people in a year, and therefore depends on the age structure of the population: a population with many young adults has a higher crude rate even at the same childbearing behavior. The total fertility rate is the number of children a woman would have if she experienced the current age-specific rates throughout her reproductive years, which removes age structure and so permits comparison across populations.

Replacement-level fertility is about 2.1 in a low-mortality population, slightly above two because some girls do not survive to reproductive age and because slightly more boys than girls are born. Below replacement, a population shrinks in the long run unless immigration offsets it, though the decline is delayed for decades by momentum from an existing young age structure.

Fertility typically falls as female schooling and labor force participation rise, and several mechanisms are proposed: later age at first birth, greater opportunity cost of time out of work, lower desired family size, and improved access to contraception.
Four regions were compared on fertility and two correlates, each measured in the same year from national surveys (Table 1).

The gradient is clean and that is the problem. Schooling and labor force participation rise together across the four regions, from 3.1 years and 19% to 13.9 years and 71%, so the two correlates are nearly collinear and no comparison among these four regions can say which of them is doing the work, or whether a third factor driving both is responsible.

Two further cautions apply. These are four aggregate observations, so any pattern is a relationship among regions rather than among women, and inferring individual behavior from aggregate rates is unreliable. The total fertility rate is also a synthetic measure built from one year's age-specific rates, so it describes a hypothetical woman and can move sharply when births are merely postponed, which is why it can fall below the number of children women eventually have.

qs.q: Which region is nearest replacement-level fertility?
o: Its rate of 5.2 is far above replacement.
Its rate of 3.4 is well above replacement.
Correct: 2.2 against a replacement level near 2.1.
Its rate of 1.5 is well below replacement.
qs.x: Correct: Replacement is about 2.1 in a low-mortality setting, and Region 3 at 2.2 is within a tenth of it, while the others sit well above or well below. Why the others are wrong: Regions 1 and 2 are substantially above replacement, and Region 4 is substantially below it. Trap: Choosing the lowest rate on the assumption that lower is closer to replacement.

qs.q: Why can this comparison not separate the effects of schooling and paid work?
o: Four regions is too small a number to analyze at all
Even many regions would not help here.
The two correlates rise together across all four regions
The total fertility rate is measured with too much error
qs.x: Correct: Schooling and labor force participation increase in lockstep from Region 1 to Region 4, so every region with high schooling also has high participation and no contrast exists in which one varies while the other is held constant. Why the others are wrong: Measurement error and small variation in replacement level are not what blocks the inference, and adding regions would not help if the two variables continued to move together. Trap: Treating collinearity as a problem of sample size.

qs.q: What does the total fertility rate measure?
o: Infant deaths per thousand live births in a year
Births per thousand people in a population each year
That is the crude birth rate.
The share of women who have at least one child
Children per woman under current age-specific rates
qs.x: Correct: The total fertility rate sums current age-specific fertility rates to give the children a woman would bear if she lived through those rates, which makes it independent of the population's age structure. Why the others are wrong: Births per thousand people is the crude birth rate, the share of women with children is a parity measure, and infant deaths per thousand births is a mortality rate. Trap: Reading any fertility measure as a count of births in the population.

qs.q: What would sustained below-replacement fertility imply in the long run?
o: An immediate decline in the total population size
An age structure that remains unchanged
Population decline in the absence of immigration
A rising share of dependent children
qs.x: Correct: If each cohort of women bears fewer than about 2.1 children, each generation is smaller than the one before, so the population shrinks eventually, though net immigration can offset that entirely. Why the others are wrong: A young existing age structure sustains growth for decades, the child share falls rather than rises, and the age structure shifts markedly toward older ages. Trap: Converting a long-run implication into an immediate one.

qs.q: Why is it risky to infer how individual women behave from Table 1?
o: Female schooling cannot be measured in survey data
Only four of the world's regions were included here
That limits coverage, not the logic.
Regional averages need not describe individuals within them
Total fertility rates cannot be compared across the four regions
That is precisely what they are built for.
qs.x: Correct: A relationship that holds among regional aggregates can differ in size or even in direction among individuals within those regions, so the table supports claims about regions and not about the women in them. Why the others are wrong: The total fertility rate is designed for cross-population comparison, schooling is measured in surveys, and limited coverage is a separate concern from the aggregation problem. Trap: Treating a pattern across groups as if it described people.

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Enthalpy is a state function, so the enthalpy change of a reaction depends only on the initial and final states and not on the route between them. This is Hess's law, and it allows the enthalpy change of a reaction that is hard to measure to be computed from reactions that are easy to measure.

The method is to combine known reactions so that unwanted species cancel. A reaction may be reversed, which changes the sign of its enthalpy change, or multiplied by a coefficient, which multiplies the enthalpy change by the same factor. Adding the adjusted reactions gives the target reaction and the sum of the adjusted enthalpies gives its enthalpy change.

A common special case uses enthalpies of formation, the enthalpy change for making one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states. The reaction enthalpy is then the sum for the products minus the sum for the reactants, with elements in their standard states assigned zero by definition.
Three combustion reactions were measured calorimetrically in order to obtain the enthalpy change for the conversion of graphite to diamond, which cannot be measured directly (Table 1).

The derivation needs only the first two rows. Reversing the diamond combustion gives +395.4, and adding the graphite combustion of -393.5 cancels the oxygen and the carbon dioxide, leaving graphite converting to diamond with an enthalpy change of +1.9 kJ per mol.

The small positive value is informative. Diamond is slightly higher in enthalpy than graphite, which is why graphite is the standard state of carbon, and the difference is small enough that the conversion is thermodynamically unfavourable by a very narrow margin while being kinetically impossible at ordinary temperatures.

Two points about the method deserve note. The third row is not needed for this target, and including an unnecessary reaction does not change the answer but offers no information either, which is a useful check on whether a chosen route is minimal. And a derived value inherits the uncertainties of every measurement used, so a difference of 1.9 computed from two values near 395 is far less precise than either of them.

qs.q: Why is the derived value far less precise than the measurements?
o: It is not needed for this target.
A small difference of two large numbers
Only the first two reactions were used in it
qs.x: Correct: Each combustion enthalpy carries its own uncertainty, and subtracting two values of about 395 to obtain 1.9 leaves those uncertainties intact while the quantity itself is tiny, so the relative error is enormous. Why the others are wrong: Using fewer reactions reduces rather than increases accumulated error, the third reaction is genuinely unnecessary, and calorimetry measured all three. Trap: Assuming a derived quantity is as precise as the data it comes from.

qs.q: Why does reversing a reaction change the sign of its enthalpy?
o: Enthalpy depends on initial and final states
Direction does not change the species.
Enthalpy is always positive for products
Its sign depends on the reaction.
Reversed reactions always proceed more slowly
Rate is not a thermodynamic quantity.
qs.x: Correct: Because the enthalpy change is the difference between the final and initial states, exchanging which is which reverses the sign of that difference exactly. Why the others are wrong: Rate is unrelated, the species are unchanged by reversal, and enthalpy changes can be of either sign. Trap: Bringing kinetics into an argument about a state function.

qs.q: Why are elements in their standard states assigned zero?
o: Elements contain no enthalpy at all
They contain enthalpy that is not zero.
Their own enthalpies are far too small to measure
It fixes a reference for formation enthalpies
qs.x: Correct: Absolute enthalpies cannot be determined, so a reference point is chosen, and setting the elements in their standard states to zero makes every formation enthalpy a difference from a common baseline that cancels in any reaction. Why the others are wrong: Elements do possess enthalpy, they react exothermically, and the choice is a convention rather than a measurement limit. Trap: Reading a conventional reference as a physical claim about the substance.

qs.q: What enthalpy change results from reversing the diamond combustion?
o: That is the derived target value.
qs.x: Correct: The diamond combustion releases 395.4 kJ per mol, so the reverse reaction absorbs the same amount and its enthalpy change is +395.4. Why the others are wrong: -395.4 is the forward value, -393.5 is the graphite combustion, and +1.9 is the final result. Trap: Reporting the result of the whole derivation rather than the step asked for.

qs.q: What does including the third reaction achieve?
o: It improves the precision of the final result
It would add its own uncertainty.
Nothing, since it is not needed here
Correct: the route is already complete.
Only the derived reaction does that.
qs.x: Correct: The target is obtained from the first two rows alone, and the carbon monoxide reaction involves a species absent from the target, so adding it contributes no information while importing extra uncertainty. Why the others are wrong: It would worsen rather than improve precision, carbon monoxide is not an intermediate here, and it does not accomplish the conversion. Trap: Assuming every measurement provided must be part of the solution.

r: Graphite plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide
Diamond plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide
Carbon monoxide plus half oxygen gives carbon dioxide

passages.title: Attitude and behavior change · passage
text: Cognitive dissonance theory proposes that acting against one's own attitude produces an unpleasant state of tension. People can reduce the tension by changing the attitude so that it fits the behavior. A competing view, self-perception theory, holds that people simply infer their attitudes from their behavior, as an outside observer would, without any tension being involved. One way to separate the two accounts is to give people a different explanation for any tension they feel. If tension drives attitude change, people who can blame their tension on something else should have less need to change their attitude.

Researchers recruited 150 undergraduates who opposed a proposed $400 increase in the student activity fee. Each wrote a persuasive essay in favor of the increase. In the high-choice conditions, the experimenter said that writing the essay was voluntary, although all participants agreed. In the low-choice condition, participants were told the essay was required. Before writing, high-choice participants swallowed an inert capsule described as a memory supplement. One group was told it had no side effects. A second group was told it often makes people feel tense, and a third group was told it often makes people feel relaxed. A control group wrote no essay. Afterward, participants rated their own tension and their attitude toward the fee increase (Table 1).

Self-perception theory makes a different prediction for the capsule conditions. If people simply read their attitudes from their behavior, a story about the capsule should not matter, because the behavior, a freely written essay, was identical across the three high-choice groups. Dissonance theory predicts that the capsule story should matter a great deal, because it changes how people explain the tension they feel. The researchers chose the fee increase because a pilot survey showed that 88% of students opposed it, so writing in favor would be inconsistent with the views of most participants.
Participants were assigned to conditions at random, and the person who scored the attitude scales did not know each participant's condition.

qs.q: Why did the high-choice, no-side-effects group shift its attitude more than the low-choice group?
o: Choosing the act freely creates more dissonance
Correct: choice removes the outside excuse.
High-choice participants were paid for agreeing
Required essays are more persuasive to the writer
The required essay produced little change.
Low-choice participants did not write an essay
qs.x: Correct: When the essay is required, the instruction itself explains the behavior, so there is little tension to resolve. When people believe they chose to argue against their own view, the inconsistency is theirs to explain, tension rises (6.2 versus 3.1), and attitudes move toward the essay (7.9 versus 3.6). Why the others are wrong: The required essay produced almost no change; no reward was offered; both groups wrote essays. Trap: Assuming that saying something always changes attitudes, regardless of choice.

qs.q: Which interpretation best fits the group told the capsule causes tension?
o: They chose not to write the essay after hearing the warning
The capsule reduced their tension, so dissonance disappeared
The warning made the essay feel required
Choice was still described as voluntary.
They blamed their tension on the capsule
Correct: misattribution removed the need to change.
qs.x: Correct: This group felt as tense as the other high-choice groups (6.0) but changed its attitude very little (4.0). Having a ready external cause for the tension meant the essay no longer seemed responsible for it, so there was no pressure to change the attitude. Why the others are wrong: Tension was still high, so the capsule did not remove it; every participant wrote an essay; the choice instructions were the same as in the other high-choice groups. Trap: Equating a lack of attitude change with a lack of arousal.

qs.q: Why did the group told the capsule would relax them show the largest attitude change?
o: The capsule raised their liking for the experimenter
The relaxing suggestion made them agree more readily
Agreement was the same in all groups.
They felt less tension than the other high-choice groups
They blamed even more of their tension on the essay
Correct: more tension attributed to the act.
qs.x: Correct: These participants expected to feel calm, yet they felt tense (6.4). The only remaining explanation was the essay, so they attributed even more of the tension to their own counter-attitudinal act and shifted their attitude the most (9.6). Why the others are wrong: All high-choice participants agreed to write; liking was not measured; their tension was the highest of any group. Trap: Expecting a relaxant to reduce attitude change because it should reduce arousal.

qs.q: Which result would most weaken the claim that tension drives the attitude change in this study?
o: Low-choice participants report only a little tension
High-choice participants report the most tension
Attitudes shift equally in every high-choice group
The control group reports the lowest tension
That is expected under both theories.
qs.x: Correct: Self-perception theory predicts that attitudes follow behavior whatever people believe about their arousal. If the misattribution groups had changed just as much as the no-side-effects group, tension would not be doing the work. The actual drop to 4.0 in the tension-capsule group is what favors dissonance theory. Why the others are wrong: Low tension in the control and low-choice groups and high tension in the high-choice groups are all consistent with, or support, the dissonance account. Trap: Choosing a result that agrees with the claim when the question asks what would weaken it.

qs.q: A patient who chose a painful and costly rehabilitation program later rates it as more helpful than a patient assigned to the same program. Which process does this most directly illustrate?
o: Correct: a costly, chosen effort is valued more.
That concerns compliance after a small request.
That concerns explaining other people's behavior.
That concerns credit for success and failure.
qs.x: Correct: Effort justification is a form of dissonance reduction. Freely choosing something painful and expensive conflicts with the thought that it might not be worth it, so people resolve the tension by valuing it more. The assigned patient has an outside explanation and less need to justify the effort. Why the others are wrong: Self-serving bias concerns taking credit for success and blaming failure on circumstances; the foot-in-the-door effect involves agreeing to a large request after a small one; the fundamental attribution error concerns judging others. Trap: Choosing a familiar social-psychology term that sounds related but describes a different process.

h: Attitude toward fee increase (1 = strongly oppose, 15 = strongly favor)
r: Low choice, no side effects mentioned
High choice, no side effects mentioned
High choice, capsule said to cause tension
High choice, capsule said to relax

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: A neuron receives thousands of synaptic inputs and fires only if their combined effect at the site of initiation is sufficient. The individual potentials are graded and decay as they spread, so an input's influence depends on where on the cell it arrives as well as on its size.

Two kinds of summation combine them. Spatial summation adds inputs arriving at different places at the same time; temporal summation adds inputs arriving at the same place in quick succession, and it works only if the second arrives before the first has decayed, which makes it depend on the membrane time constant.

Inhibition does not simply subtract. An inhibitory input that opens chloride channels near the resting potential produces little voltage change on its own but greatly reduces the effect of excitatory inputs arriving nearby, because it holds the membrane close to rest.
Responses were recorded at the site of initiation (Table 1).

Two excitatory inputs together gave 7.4 millivolts against the 8.0 predicted by adding them, a small shortfall. Three proximal inputs with a nearby inhibitory input gave 4.1 against a predicted 18.6, a shortfall of more than fourteen millivolts, although the inhibitory input alone produced almost no voltage change.
The inhibition therefore acts by changing how the excitatory currents are handled rather than by adding a negative voltage, which is why its effect is far larger than its own signal.

Two qualifications apply.
