The recordings are from the site of initiation, which is where the decision to fire is made, but the same inputs recorded at the soma would give different amplitudes, so the numbers describe one location. And the predicted values assume the inputs are independent, which is not true even for two excitatory inputs because each reduces the driving force for the other, and that is the source of the small shortfall in the third row.

qs.q: Why does an input's location matter?
o: Distal synapses release less transmitter per vesicle
Correct Correct: distal inputs arrive smaller.
qs.x: Correct: A graded potential loses amplitude as it travels along the dendrite, so an input far from the initiation site contributes less than an identical input close to it. Why the others are wrong: Transmitter release is comparable, the location effect is large, and the proximal inputs were excitatory. Trap: Treating synaptic inputs as equivalent regardless of position.

qs.q: Why does the inhibitory input have such a large effect?
o: It holds the membrane near rest
Correct: it shunts the excitatory current.
It adds a large negative voltage of its own
qs.x: Correct: Opening chloride channels near the resting potential creates a low-resistance path that drains the excitatory current, so the voltage change at the initiation site is far smaller without the inhibition contributing a negative signal itself. Why the others are wrong: Its own voltage change is negligible, the synapses are intact, and the shortfall exceeds fourteen millivolts. Trap: Expecting inhibition to work by arithmetic subtraction.

qs.q: Why do two excitatory inputs fall slightly short of their sum?
o: One of the two inputs is actually inhibitory
Each reduces the other's driving force
qs.x: Correct: Depolarising the membrane reduces the electrochemical driving force for the current carried by the other synapse, so the two currents are slightly smaller together than separately. Why the others are wrong: Both inputs are excitatory, the measurement is precise, and the measured value is below the predicted one. Trap: Assuming simultaneous inputs add linearly.

qs.q: By how many millivolts did the third row fall short of its prediction?
o: That is the fourth row's shortfall.
qs.x: Correct: The measured 7.4 millivolts fell 0.6 short of the predicted 8.0. Why the others are wrong: The others are the measured value, another row's shortfall, and the prediction. Trap: Taking the shortfall from the wrong row.

qs.q: Why do these numbers describe one location?
o: Recordings cannot be made at the initiation site
All sites give the same amplitude
Correct: the soma would read differently.
qs.x: Correct: A graded potential has a different amplitude at every point along the cell, so the values recorded at the initiation site are specific to it even though that is the relevant site for firing. Why the others are wrong: Such recordings are made, amplitudes differ between sites, and location is central to the whole passage. Trap: Generalising amplitudes measured at one point to the whole cell.

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: Neurons at rest hold a negative membrane potential because the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains ion gradients and because the membrane at rest is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺. An action potential begins when depolarization opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, letting Na⁺ rush in. Those channels then inactivate, and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, letting K⁺ leave and returning the membrane toward rest. During the absolute refractory period, enough Na⁺ channels are inactivated that no stimulus can trigger another action potential; inactivation is removed only after the membrane repolarizes.

The action potential is all-or-none: once threshold is reached, its size does not depend on how strong the stimulus was. A stronger stimulus is encoded by a higher firing frequency, not by larger spikes.

Researchers recorded from squid giant axons in solutions of different composition and with channel-blocking drugs. Tetrodotoxin (TTX), from pufferfish, blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels (Table 1).

The researchers also noted why the squid giant axon was chosen. It is up to a millimeter across, wide enough for an electrode to be threaded down its length, and its contents can be squeezed out and replaced with a solution of known composition. This let the original investigators set the concentrations on both sides of the membrane and test directly whether the action potential depends on the ion gradients rather than on some property of the cytoplasm. Axons that large exist because the squid has no myelin and relies on diameter alone for rapid conduction.

In a further experiment, the axon was stimulated twice in quick succession. With a 0.5 ms interval the second stimulus produced no response at any strength; with a 3 ms interval it produced a full-sized action potential when the stimulus was stronger than usual; with a 10 ms interval a normal stimulus sufficed.

qs.q: Why does lowering external Na⁺ reduce the peak of the action potential?
o: A smaller gradient drives less Na⁺ inward
Correct: the peak approaches the Na⁺ equilibrium potential.
The resting potential becomes more negative
Fewer Na⁺ channels are present in the membrane
Na⁺ leaves the cell during the upstroke
qs.x: Correct: At the peak, the membrane is most permeable to Na⁺, so the potential moves toward the Na⁺ equilibrium potential, which depends on the ratio of external to internal Na⁺. Halving external Na⁺ lowers that equilibrium potential and the peak falls from +40 to +22 mV. Why the others are wrong: The solution change does not alter channel numbers; the resting potential was unchanged; Na⁺ flows inward during depolarization. Trap: Confusing the number of channels with the driving force through them.

qs.q: Why does raising external K⁺ depolarize the resting membrane?
o: K⁺ channels close when external K⁺ rises
Channel state is not the cause here.
The pump stops working in high K⁺
Correct: rest follows K⁺ most closely.
qs.x: Correct: The resting membrane is most permeable to K⁺, so the resting potential sits near the K⁺ equilibrium potential. Raising external K⁺ reduces the gradient, making that equilibrium potential less negative, and rest moves from −70 to −58 mV. Why the others are wrong: Rest is set by the gradient rather than by channel closure; external Na⁺ was unchanged; the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase needs external K⁺ to work. Trap: Looking for an explanation in Na⁺ when K⁺ sets the resting potential.

qs.q: What does the TEA result show about repolarization?
o: Na⁺ channels alone repolarize the membrane
K⁺ channels set the peak of the spike
The peak was unchanged at +41 mV.
K⁺ channels end the action potential
Correct: blocking them stretches it to 7.5 ms.
qs.x: Correct: With K⁺ channels blocked, the upstroke and peak were normal but repolarization took 7.5 ms instead of 1.0. The outward K⁺ current is therefore the main route back to rest, helped by Na⁺ channel inactivation. Why the others are wrong: The peak did not change; inactivation alone leaves the membrane depolarized for much longer; the normal upstroke shows Na⁺ entry was intact. Trap: Assuming a drug that lengthens the spike must affect its rising phase.

qs.q: Why does the second stimulus fail completely at 0.5 ms?
o: The membrane has not returned to rest
Being depolarized alone would lower threshold.
K⁺ channels have not yet opened
qs.x: Correct: In the absolute refractory period, so many Na⁺ channels are in the inactivated state that no stimulus, however strong, can open enough of them. Inactivation is only removed once the membrane repolarizes, which is why a response returns at 3 ms. Why the others are wrong: Depolarization on its own would make firing easier; the failure held at every stimulus strength; K⁺ channels open during repolarization. Trap: Explaining a refractory period by the membrane voltage instead of by channel state.

qs.q: How does the nervous system signal a stronger stimulus?
o: Duration is set by the channels.
Correct: the spike size is fixed.
Rest is maintained near a fixed value.
qs.x: Correct: Because each action potential is all-or-none, intensity cannot be carried by spike size. A stronger stimulus holds the membrane above threshold more of the time, so the neuron fires more frequently, and often more neurons are recruited as well. Why the others are wrong: Spike height and duration are properties of the channels, and the resting potential is maintained rather than used to encode intensity. Trap: Assuming a bigger stimulus produces a bigger signal at every stage.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: A thin converging lens obeys 1/f = 1/do + 1/di, where f is the focal length, do the object distance and di the image distance. Magnification is m = −di/do. A positive di means a real image on the far side of the lens, which can be projected onto a screen; a negative di means a virtual image on the same side as the object, which cannot be projected but can be viewed through the lens. The sign of m tells the orientation: negative is inverted, positive is upright.

A compound microscope uses two lenses. The objective, close to the specimen, forms a real inverted image inside the tube; the eyepiece then acts as a magnifier of that image. Total magnification is the product of the two.

Students measured image positions for a single converging lens of focal length 10.0 cm by moving an illuminated object along an optical bench and finding where a sharp image formed on a screen (Table 1).

The students also noted a practical point about measurement. Finding the sharp image by eye has some uncertainty, and that uncertainty grows when the image is far from the lens, because the image stays acceptably sharp over a longer range of screen positions. They therefore repeated each measurement three times and reported the mean, and they treated the 50.0 cm row, where the image is small and close to the focal point, as the most precise. They also checked the lens by using a distant window as the object: the image then formed 10.1 cm from the lens, confirming the stated focal length within their uncertainty.
In a second part, students replaced the lens with one of focal length 5.0 cm and placed the object 6.0 cm away, then viewed the image formed by that lens through a second lens used as an eyepiece.

qs.q: Where does the image form when the object is 12.0 cm from the 10.0 cm lens?
o: The object is outside the focal length.
qs.x: Correct: 1/di = 1/f − 1/do = 1/10 − 1/12 = (6 − 5)/60 = 1/60, so di = 60 cm, a real image beyond the lens. Why the others are wrong: The equation uses reciprocals, so the distances are neither averaged nor added, and a negative image distance arises only when the object is inside the focal length. Trap: Adding or subtracting the distances directly instead of their reciprocals.

qs.q: Why can the image at do = 5.0 cm not be projected onto a screen?
o: The image does not form on the far side.
It is virtual, on the object's side
The image is too small to see
It is twice the object's height.
The lens is too weak at that distance
qs.x: Correct: With the object inside the focal length, di is negative, meaning the rays leaving the lens diverge and only appear to come from a point on the object's side. No light actually converges there, so nothing can be captured on a screen; the image is seen by looking through the lens. Why the others are wrong: The image is magnified, not tiny; the focal length is a property of the lens; the geometry, not an obstruction, is what matters. Trap: Treating a virtual image as a faint real one.

qs.q: What does the row at do = 20.0 cm illustrate?
o: The lens produces no image at that distance
A sharp image formed on the screen.
The image is upright at that distance
Real images from a single lens are inverted.
At do = 2f the image matches the object
qs.x: Correct: When do = 2f, the equation gives di = 2f as well, so the image forms at the same distance on the other side and is the same size, with m = −1. This is the dividing line between enlarged and reduced real images. Why the others are wrong: An image did form; a real image from a single converging lens is inverted; the focal length is 10.0 cm. Trap: Reading the equality of the distances as a special property of the lens rather than of this object position.

qs.q: Why must the eyepiece be positioned so the objective's image falls just inside its focal length?
o: So the eyepiece forms an enlarged virtual image
Correct: that is how a magnifier works.
So the two images cancel their inversions
So the eyepiece forms a real image on the retina
The eye's own lens does that.
So the image distance becomes zero
qs.x: Correct: A lens used as a simple magnifier takes an object inside its focal length and produces an enlarged, upright virtual image that the relaxed eye can view, as the do = 5.0 cm row shows. The eyepiece treats the objective's real image as its object. Why the others are wrong: The eye's lens forms the retinal image; a compound microscope's final image is inverted relative to the specimen; a zero image distance is meaningless. Trap: Expecting the second lens to undo the first lens's inversion.

qs.q: How would a shorter objective focal length change the microscope?
o: No change, since magnification depends only on the eyepiece
Lower magnification with a brighter image
Higher magnification at a shorter working distance
Correct: the specimen must be closer.
Higher magnification at a longer working distance
Shorter f requires a closer object.
qs.x: Correct: For a fixed tube length, a shorter objective focal length gives a larger image distance relative to the object distance, so magnification rises, but the specimen must sit just outside the shorter focal length, leaving very little room between lens and slide. Why the others are wrong: The working distance shrinks rather than grows; magnification rises; total magnification is the product of both lenses. Trap: Assuming a higher-power objective is simply better with no trade-off.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: The bacteria of the large intestine ferment carbohydrate that the host has not digested, and the principal products are short-chain fatty acids: acetate, propionate and butyrate. These are weak acids, so their accumulation lowers the luminal pH, and they are also absorbed and used by the host, with butyrate serving as the main fuel of the colonic epithelium.

The pH matters for the composition of the community. Many of the organisms associated with putrefaction and with some pathogens grow poorly below pH 6, while the acid-producing organisms themselves tolerate it, so a well-fermented lumen is partly self-protecting.

Not all fermentable carbohydrate is equivalent. Substrates that reach the colon intact and are fermented slowly produce acid along the length of the colon, whereas rapidly fermented ones are consumed in the first part of it, and the distal colon, where most disease occurs, is left unaffected.
A controlled feeding trial compared three supplements against a control (Table 1).

Resistant starch produced the lowest pH and the highest total acid, and it doubled the butyrate share relative to the control. Inulin raised the bifidobacterial count most, by 1.5 logs, but produced less butyrate than resistant starch did.
Glucose changed almost nothing, which is expected since it is absorbed in the small intestine and little of it reaches the colon to be fermented at all.

Two qualifications apply. Faecal measurements describe the distal colon and the material leaving it, and they can miss a change confined to the proximal colon, so a supplement that acts early may appear inert. And a lower faecal pH is associated with outcomes thought favourable but is a marker rather than a mechanism, so the trial supports the fermentation pathway without establishing that the pH itself is what matters to the host, which would need a design that moved the pH on its own.

qs.q: Why does glucose change almost nothing?
o: It is absorbed before the colon
Colonic bacteria lack the enzymes needed to take up free glucose
qs.x: Correct: Glucose is absorbed in the small intestine, so very little arrives in the colon and there is almost nothing extra for the bacteria to ferment. Why the others are wrong: Glucose is among the most fermentable substrates, the pH was essentially unchanged rather than raised, and colonic bacteria use glucose efficiently. Trap: Concluding a substrate is not fermentable when it simply does not reach the fermenters.

qs.q: Why is a lower luminal pH partly self-protecting?
o: The host secretes bicarbonate in response to a lower luminal pH
Secretion is not the stated mechanism.
qs.x: Correct: The acid conditions produced by fermentation are tolerated by the acid-producing community but suppress several putrefactive and pathogenic organisms. Why the others are wrong: The producers themselves tolerate the acid, fermentation continues at these pH values, and host bicarbonate secretion is not what was described. Trap: Reading a selective effect as a general antibacterial one.

qs.q: Why might a supplement appear inert?
o: Faecal sampling misses the proximal colon
Bacteria in the proximal colon do not ferment any carbohydrate at all
Faecal pH cannot be measured accurately
Supplements are given at too low a dose
qs.x: Correct: What is measured in faeces reflects the distal colon, so a substrate fermented entirely in the first part of the colon produces no detectable change in the sample taken. Why the others are wrong: The doses were controlled, faecal pH measurement is reliable, and the proximal colon is where fermentation is most active. Trap: Treating a faecal measurement as a report on the whole colon.

qs.q: By how much did inulin raise the bifidobacterial count?
o: That is the resistant starch increase.
qs.x: Correct: Subtracting the control's 8.1 from inulin's 9.6 gives an increase of 1.5 logs. Why the others are wrong: The other values are the two individual counts and a different supplement's increase. Trap: Reading a count where the change between two was requested.

qs.q: Why does the trial not show that pH is what matters?
o: Faecal pH is unrelated to the colon
The trial had no control group to compare the supplements against
The pH change was too small
The pH is a marker here
Correct: it moved with everything else.
qs.x: Correct: The pH fell alongside the acid concentration and the community composition, so the design cannot separate the effect of the pH itself from that of the other changes. Why the others are wrong: The change was substantial, faecal pH does reflect the distal lumen, and a control diet was included. Trap: Picking one correlated variable out of several and treating it as the cause.

passages.title: Attitude and behavior change · passage
text: The elaboration likelihood model describes two routes to persuasion. In the central route, people think carefully about the content of a message, so strong arguments persuade and weak ones do not, and the resulting attitude tends to last and to predict behavior. In the peripheral route, people rely on cues such as the source's expertise, attractiveness or the sheer number of arguments, producing attitudes that are easier to change later. Which route operates depends on motivation and ability: personal relevance, a need for cognition and freedom from distraction all push people toward the central route.

Researchers asked 320 undergraduates to evaluate a proposal that their university require a comprehensive examination for graduation. Relevance was manipulated by saying the policy would start next year, affecting the participants themselves, or in ten years. Argument quality was manipulated by using either strong arguments supported by data or weak ones based on anecdote. Source expertise was manipulated by attributing the proposal to a national commission on education or to a local high school class. Attitudes were rated from 1 to 9, with higher numbers meaning more favor (Table 1).

Distraction was examined in a follow-up with 120 further participants. While reading the proposal, half heard a recording of numbers they had to monitor. Under distraction, the difference between strong and weak arguments shrank by about two-thirds even in the high-relevance condition, while the effect of source expertise grew. The researchers concluded that motivation alone is not enough: a person must also have the capacity to process the message.

Two weeks later, participants rated the proposal again. In the high-relevance group, attitudes had shifted by an average of 0.4 points; in the low-relevance group, by 1.9 points. Participants also completed a need-for-cognition scale; among low-relevance participants who scored in the top quarter, argument quality mattered about as much as it did in the high-relevance group.

qs.q: What does the high-relevance row show?
qs.x: Correct: When the policy would affect them next year, participants moved more than four points depending on argument quality (7.6 against 3.4 with an expert source) but barely at all depending on who made the proposal. That is the central route. Why the others are wrong: The source's effect is small in this row; the quality effect is large; the two effects are very different in size. Trap: Assuming expertise always matters.

qs.q: What does the low-relevance row show?
o: The two rows show the same pattern
Argument quality mattered more than the source
qs.x: Correct: With the policy a decade away, ratings depended mainly on whether a national commission or a high school class proposed it (6.2 against 4.1 with strong arguments), while argument quality changed little. That is the peripheral route. Why the others are wrong: Ratings did vary; the quality effect is small here; the two rows show opposite patterns. Trap: Expecting the same variable to dominate in every condition.

qs.q: Why did low-relevance attitudes shift more over two weeks?
o: Correct: they rest on cues, not on reasons.
Both were retested at two weeks.
They were told the policy had changed
qs.x: Correct: Attitudes formed by thinking about the content are supported by reasons the person can recall and defend, so they persist. Attitudes based on a cue such as the source have little behind them and drift, which is why the low-relevance group moved 1.9 points against 0.4. Why the others are wrong: Both groups were retested at the same interval with no new information. Trap: Explaining a change in attitude strength by forgetting the topic.

qs.q: What does the need-for-cognition result add?
o: Need for cognition replaces argument quality
Quality is what those participants responded to.
Motivation can come from the person, not the message
Only personal relevance can produce central processing
These participants showed it without relevance.
Need for cognition made participants more persuadable
qs.x: Correct: Participants who enjoy thinking responded to argument quality even when the policy would not affect them, which shows that the route depends on whether a person actually elaborates, however that motivation arises. Why the others are wrong: These participants responded to quality rather than to a trait substitute; relevance is one source of motivation among several; responding to strong arguments is not general persuadability. Trap: Treating personal relevance as the only path to careful processing.

qs.q: An advertiser wants an attitude that will still influence a purchase months later. What does the study suggest?
o: List as many arguments as possible, regardless of quality
Repeat the brand name as often as possible
Give strong arguments to an interested audience
Use an attractive celebrity in a brief advertisement
qs.x: Correct: Durable, behavior-predicting attitudes come from the central route, which requires both an audience motivated to think and arguments that reward thinking. Peripheral tactics can shift attitudes quickly but those attitudes fade, as the two-week results show. Why the others are wrong: Celebrity appeal, repetition and sheer number of arguments are all peripheral cues. Trap: Judging a persuasion tactic by its immediate effect alone.

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: A synapse must remove its transmitter quickly, or the signal would persist long after the presynaptic cell stopped firing. Three mechanisms do this: enzymatic breakdown in the cleft, reuptake into the presynaptic terminal or into glia, and simple diffusion away from the cleft.

Which mechanism dominates differs between synapses. Acetylcholine is destroyed in the cleft by an enzyme fast enough to clear it within a millisecond; the monoamines and glutamate are mostly taken back up by transporters; and at some synapses diffusion alone is enough because the cleft is narrow and short.

The choice has consequences for pharmacology. Blocking the clearance mechanism prolongs the transmitter's action, and the size of that effect depends on how much of the clearance that mechanism was doing.
Clearance was measured at four synapses (Table 1).

The neuromuscular junction cleared its transmitter with a half-life of 0.2 milliseconds, almost entirely by enzyme, while the noradrenergic synapse took 96 milliseconds and relied on uptake for 76 percent. The peptidergic synapse was slowest of all at 2400 milliseconds and depended mainly on diffusion.

The range of nearly four orders of magnitude in half-life matches the range of signalling functions: a synapse that must transmit each impulse separately needs clearance faster than the interval between impulses, and one that modulates over seconds does not.

Two qualifications apply. The half-lives are measured with electrodes or sensors placed near but not inside the cleft, so they report the concentration in the surrounding space and slightly overstate how long transmitter persists at the receptors themselves. And the shares were determined by blocking each mechanism in turn and attributing the change, which assumes the mechanisms are independent, whereas blocking the enzyme raises the concentration available to the transporters and so inflates the apparent uptake share. For that reason the three shares are best read as an ordering of importance at each synapse rather than as a partition that should add to a hundred, and the enzyme and uptake figures in particular are not independent of one another.

qs.q: Why does clearance speed differ so much between synapses?
o: Correct: fast synapses need fast clearance.
The transmitters differ in molecular weight substantially
All synapses clear at the same rate
qs.x: Correct: A synapse that must resolve individual impulses needs the transmitter gone before the next one arrives, while a modulatory synapse acting over seconds does not. Why the others are wrong: Molecular weight is not the determining factor, the rates differ enormously, and the pattern matches function. Trap: Explaining a functional range by a physical property of the molecules.

qs.q: Why does blocking the enzyme inflate the apparent uptake share?
o: The blocker also activates the transporters directly
It does not act on them.
qs.x: Correct: Transporter activity depends on the concentration presented to it, so removing the enzyme raises that concentration and makes uptake look like a larger share than it carried normally. Why the others are wrong: The blocker is enzyme specific, transport is concentration dependent, and the bias is upward. Trap: Assuming that blocking one route reveals the unaltered contribution of another.

qs.q: Why do the measured half-lives overstate persistence at the receptors?
o: The sensor is outside the cleft
Correct: it reads the surrounding space.
Sensors cannot detect these transmitters at all
qs.x: Correct: The measurement is made in the space around the synapse rather than within the cleft, and transmitter lingers longer there than at the receptors it has already left. Why the others are wrong: The sensors detect these transmitters, the direction of the error is upward, and the cleft is narrow. Trap: Reading a nearby measurement as an in-cleft one.

qs.q: How many fold do the neuromuscular and peptidergic half-lives differ?
qs.x: Correct: 2400 against 0.2 milliseconds is a difference of twelve thousand fold. Why the others are wrong: The others are the three half-lives themselves. Trap: Quoting a half-life where a ratio was asked for.

qs.q: Why does blocking clearance prolong action unevenly across synapses?
o: Correct: blocking a minor route does little.
The blockers differ in potency between synapses
qs.x: Correct: The effect of removing a mechanism is proportional to how much of the clearance it was performing, so blocking uptake transforms a noradrenergic synapse and barely touches the neuromuscular junction. Why the others are wrong: Potency was matched, the responses differ greatly, and blocking has substantial effects where the route matters. Trap: Expecting a drug's effect to be the same wherever its target exists.

passages.title: Responding to the world · passage
text: In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus (US) comes to elicit a conditioned response. Pairing alone is not sufficient: the conditioned stimulus (CS) must predict the US. If a second cue is added to one that already predicts the US reliably, the new cue gains little control, an effect called blocking, because the US is already fully predicted and nothing new is learned.

Several phenomena follow the same logic. In extinction, the CS is presented without the US and the response declines, but the original learning is not erased: after a rest the response partly returns as spontaneous recovery, and a single pairing can restore it quickly. In latent inhibition, a stimulus presented many times on its own before conditioning is harder to turn into a CS afterward.

Researchers conditioned rabbits to blink in response to a tone paired with a brief puff of air to the eye. The percentage of trials with a conditioned blink is shown for several groups after training (Table 1).

The researchers chose eyeblink conditioning because the circuit is well mapped. The conditioned response depends on the cerebellum, and lesions of one small region there abolish the learned blink while leaving the unconditioned blink to the air puff intact. That separation lets researchers distinguish a failure to learn from a failure to respond, which behavioral measures alone cannot do. The timing of the pairing also matters: a tone that begins about half a second before the puff produces strong learning, while a tone that begins after the puff produces almost none.

A fifth group was trained with the tone alone for 30 trials and then given 40 trials of the tone with no puff. Blinking fell from 84% to 11%. After 24 hours in the home cage with no training, the first ten test trials produced blinking on 38% of trials.

qs.q: Why does the light gain so little control in the blocking group?
o: Two stimuli cannot be conditioned at once
The light and puff were never paired
The light is too dim to be noticed
The standard group responded to it.
The tone already predicts the puff
Correct: the light adds no information.
qs.x: Correct: In phase 1 the tone became a complete predictor of the puff. When the light is added in phase 2, the puff is already expected, so there is nothing left to learn about the light and it controls responding on only 9% of trials. Why the others are wrong: The same light produced 58% responding in the standard group; the light was paired with the puff in phase 2; the standard group shows two cues can be learned together. Trap: Assuming that pairing a stimulus with a US always produces learning.

qs.q: What does the unpaired control group show?
o: The tone is too quiet to be heard
Rabbits cannot blink in response to a tone
qs.x: Correct: This group received the same tone, light and puff, but never in a predictive relationship. Responding stayed near zero, which shows that the learning in the other groups comes from the relationship between the cues and the US rather than from exposure to them. Why the others are wrong: Other groups blinked to the tone; the puff elicits an unconditioned blink; the tone supported 88% responding in the blocking group. Trap: Treating a control group as a weaker version of the experimental one.

qs.q: Why does the latent inhibition group respond less to the light?
o: The group received fewer phase 2 trials
The light was never paired with the puff
Correct: it is harder to condition later.
The tone blocked the light in that group
The tone was new in phase 2 for them.
qs.x: Correct: Presenting the light alone many times establishes it as a stimulus without consequences. That history interferes with later learning, so after the same 30 pairings the group responds to the light on only 14% of trials, against 58% in the standard group. Why the others are wrong: The light was paired in phase 2; trial numbers were equal; the tone had no prior history for this group, so blocking does not apply. Trap: Confusing latent inhibition with blocking, which requires a previously trained predictor.

qs.q: What does the return of blinking after 24 hours demonstrate?
o: No pairings occurred during the rest.
Correct: the response returns after a rest.
qs.x: Correct: Extinction reduced blinking from 84% to 11%, but after a day with no training the response returned at 38%. This shows that extinction suppresses the response rather than erasing the original learning. Why the others are wrong: Recovery shows the memory survived; the stimulus was unchanged, so this is not generalization; no training occurred in between. Trap: Treating extinction as unlearning.

qs.q: A therapist uses exposure therapy for a phobia and warns the patient that fear may return later. Which finding supports that warning?
o: The blocking group responded strongly to the tone
Blinking returned after a day of rest
Correct: extinction can be followed by recovery.
That shows the need for pairing.
The latent inhibition group responded less to the light
qs.x: Correct: Exposure therapy is extinction: the feared cue is presented without the feared outcome. Because the original association survives, fear can return after time or in a new setting, so therapists plan booster sessions. Why the others are wrong: Blocking, the unpaired control and latent inhibition describe how associations are acquired rather than how an extinguished response returns. Trap: Choosing a result about learning when the question is about relapse.

r: Tone, light and puff at random times

passages.title: Attitude and behavior change · passage
text: Two sequential-request techniques raise compliance with a large request, and they work by different routes. The foot-in-the-door technique begins with a small request that is almost always granted, and the act of granting it shifts the person's view of themselves toward being someone who supports the cause, so the later large request is consistent with that self-image. The door-in-the-face technique begins with an extreme request that is refused, and the subsequent smaller request succeeds through reciprocal concession, because the requester has visibly come down and the target feels obliged to meet them.

The two accounts make different predictions about the requester. A self-image shift travels with the person being asked, so it should survive a change of canvasser. A reciprocal concession is owed to a particular person who made the concession, so it should not transfer.

Canvassers approached 600 households about placing a large yard sign supporting a road-safety campaign. Households were assigned by street block to one of four conditions, and the share agreeing was recorded, along with how long the sign remained in place (Table 1).

Both techniques beat the direct request, and the final row is the informative one. Moving to a different canvasser cuts agreement from 53% to 28%, which a pure self-image account did not predict, while retention remains high at 18 days, close to the 21 days of the same-canvasser petition group and well above the 11 days of the door-in-the-face group.

Retention is the more revealing measure. Agreement can be produced by social pressure in the moment, but a sign that stays up for three weeks suggests a changed view of the issue, and that pattern follows the petition conditions rather than the extreme-request condition. The study has a real weakness: assignment was by street block rather than by household, so blocks could differ in traffic, in prior exposure to the campaign, or in how neighbors influence one another, and canvassers were not blind to condition, which leaves room for differences in enthusiasm to affect the results.

qs.q: Which result in Table 1 best distinguishes the two mechanisms?
o: The extreme-request group agreed more often than the direct group
That is the door-in-the-face effect itself.
Agreement fell when a different canvasser made the large request
Agreement in the direct-request group was the lowest among all four of the conditions
That shows only that both techniques work.
Retention is long in both petition conditions but short after the extreme request
qs.x: Correct: A changed self-image should keep the sign up, while a concession repaid in the moment should not, and retention of 21 and 18 days in the petition conditions against 11 days after the extreme request matches that contrast. Why the others are wrong: The direct and extreme-request comparisons show the techniques work without separating them, and the canvasser-change result bears on the self-image account rather than distinguishing the two cleanly. Trap: Using the compliance column when the mechanisms differ in what happens afterwards.

qs.q: What does the different-canvasser condition suggest?
o: The petition itself had no influence at all on household compliance
It still beat the direct request.
Part of the petition effect depends on the particular requester
Reciprocal concession requires the same person to concede
Sign retention is unrelated to whether the household agreed
qs.x: Correct: Agreement dropped from 53% to 28% when the canvasser changed, which is still above the 17% direct rate, so the petition produces a genuine effect but a substantial part of it is tied to the relationship with the individual who made the first request. Why the others are wrong: The petition retained an effect, retention was unchanged, and the point about reciprocity applies to the extreme-request condition. Trap: Reading a partial reduction as a complete failure of the technique.

qs.q: Which sequence defines the door-in-the-face technique?
o: Two requests of equal size are made in sequence
A single large request is made with no preliminary
An extreme request is refused, then a smaller one is made
A small request is granted first, and then a larger one is made
qs.x: Correct: The technique opens with a request extreme enough to be refused, and the requester's retreat to a smaller request creates an obligation to reciprocate the concession. Why the others are wrong: Granting a small request first is the other technique, equal requests involve no concession, and a lone request is the control condition. Trap: Confusing the two sequences because both involve two requests.

qs.q: Which design feature most threatens the causal interpretation?
o: Sign removal dates were recorded by the canvassers themselves
The message on the yard sign was the same throughout
Holding it constant is a strength.
Only one city's households were approached
Households were assigned by street block, not individually
qs.x: Correct: Assigning whole blocks means the conditions differ not only in the request sequence but in whatever else distinguishes those blocks, including neighbors talking to one another, so differences between blocks can masquerade as effects of the technique. Why the others are wrong: Unblinded recording of removals is a measurement worry, single-city sampling restricts generalization, and a constant message removes a rival explanation. Trap: Naming the most visible imperfection rather than the one that undermines the comparison.

qs.q: Which additional measure would most directly test the self-perception account?
o: The number of yard signs already visible on nearby lawns
Rated agreement that one is the kind of person who supports road safety
Correct: it measures the proposed mediator.
Reported household income in each of the four conditions that were assigned
Total minutes each canvasser spent at the door
qs.x: Correct: The account claims the first request changes how people see themselves, so measuring that self-view after the petition and before the large request tests the mediating step rather than inferring it from the behavior it is supposed to explain. Why the others are wrong: Income and neighborhood sign density are background characteristics, and time at the door measures the canvasser's effort. Trap: Adding a plausible covariate instead of measuring the mechanism.

r: Extreme request first, then the sign

passages.title: Responding to the world · passage
text: Operant conditioning strengthens a response that is followed by reinforcement, and the schedule on which reinforcement arrives shapes both how fast the response is emitted and how long it persists once reinforcement stops. Continuous reinforcement follows every response. Ratio schedules reinforce after a number of responses, interval schedules after a period of time, and each can be fixed or variable.

The characteristic patterns follow from what the schedule makes predictable. A fixed-ratio schedule produces rapid bursts with a brief pause after each reinforcement, because the next payoff is a known number of responses away. A variable-ratio schedule produces a high, steady rate with no pause, because any response might be the one reinforced. A fixed-interval schedule produces a scalloped pattern, with responding low early in the interval and accelerating as the time approaches, since early responses cannot be reinforced.

Resistance to extinction follows the same logic. Extinction requires the animal to detect that reinforcement has stopped, and that detection is easy under continuous reinforcement, where a single unrewarded response is already unusual, and hard under a variable schedule, where long unrewarded runs were a normal part of training.

Pigeons were trained to peck a key on one of four schedules until responding was stable, then reinforcement was discontinued and responses were counted until the rate fell below one peck per minute (Table 1).

The two columns dissociate. Fixed ratio 10 and variable ratio 10 deliver reinforcement at the same average cost and produce similar rates in training, 68 and 75, yet differ more than threefold in persistence, 340 against 1,120. Rate of responding during training is therefore not what determines resistance to extinction; predictability is.

Several things the table cannot settle remain. All four groups were run to stable responding rather than for a fixed number of sessions, so the ratio groups received more reinforcements in total, and total reinforcement is itself a candidate explanation for persistence. The extinction criterion is also arbitrary, and a different cutoff would compress or stretch the differences. Pigeons pecking a key for grain also differ from a person persisting at a slot machine in ways the paradigm does not capture, although the schedule logic transfers.

qs.q: Which comparison in Table 1 shows that training response rate does not drive persistence?
o: Both rate and persistence differ there.
Variable ratio 10 against fixed interval 1 min
Rates differ by more than twofold.
Correct: similar rates, very different persistence.
qs.x: Correct: The two ratio schedules produce 68 and 75 responses per minute, rates close enough that persistence of 340 against 1,120 cannot be attributed to how fast the birds were responding, leaving predictability as the difference between them. Why the others are wrong: In each of the other pairs the training rates differ substantially, so the two columns move together and neither can be ruled out. Trap: Choosing the pair with the largest gap in persistence rather than the pair that holds rate constant.

qs.q: Why does responding on a fixed-interval schedule stay low early in each interval?
o: Correct: time, not count, gates the payoff.
Interval schedules deliver no reinforcement at all
Pigeons are unable to discriminate elapsed time
Fixed intervals demand more responses per payoff
They demand only one, after the interval.
qs.x: Correct: On a fixed interval only the first response after the interval elapses is reinforced, so pecking in the early part of the interval never pays, and the animals come to withhold responding until the interval is nearly up, producing the scallop. Why the others are wrong: Interval schedules do reinforce, the scalloped pattern is itself evidence of timing, and a single response suffices once the interval has passed. Trap: Confusing an interval requirement with a ratio requirement.

qs.q: A parent occasionally gives in to a child's tantrum. Why does this make tantrums especially persistent?
o: Giving in functions as a punishment of the tantrum
It delivers what the child wanted.
Extinction is impossible once a behavior is learned
Extinction does occur, as the table shows.
qs.x: Correct: Giving in only sometimes puts the tantrum on a variable schedule, so a long run with no success is something the child has experienced many times before and does not signal that tantrums have stopped working. Why the others are wrong: Occasional compliance is not continuous reinforcement, giving in reinforces rather than punishes, and the continuous group in Table 1 extinguished in 60 responses. Trap: Reading occasional reinforcement as weak reinforcement rather than as a schedule.

qs.q: Which feature of the procedure leaves total reinforcement as an alternative explanation?
o: Twelve pigeons were assigned to each of the four schedules
Equal groups help rather than hurt.
Groups were trained to stable responding rather than for equal reinforcements
Correct: the ratio groups earned more.
Reinforcement was grain delivered after a key peck
The reinforcer was constant across groups.
Extinction was defined as a response rate falling below one peck in any minute
That is an arbitrary cutoff, not a confound.
qs.x: Correct: Training to a behavioral criterion means the groups differ in how many reinforcements they received, and a history of more reinforcements could itself produce more persistence, so schedule and total reinforcement are not separated. Why the others are wrong: The cutoff affects the scale of the numbers rather than introducing a group difference, and equal group sizes and a common reinforcer are features that strengthen the comparison. Trap: Treating an arbitrary measurement threshold as a confound.

qs.q: Which schedule best describes a slot machine?
o: Fixed ratio, paying after a set number of plays
Continuous, paying on every single play
Variable ratio: an unpredictable play count
Correct: that is what sustains play.
Fixed interval, paying after a set waiting time
Payoff does not depend on elapsed time.
qs.x: Correct: A slot machine pays after an unpredictable number of plays, which is a variable-ratio schedule, and that is why it sustains high steady rates of play and great resistance to the long unrewarded runs that ordinary play contains. Why the others are wrong: A fixed ratio would be countable, an interval schedule would make waiting rather than playing the effective strategy, and continuous reinforcement would mean no losses at all. Trap: Matching the schedule to how often one wins rather than to what determines the win.

passages.title: Responding to the world · passage
text: Observational learning is the acquisition of behavior by watching a model, without the observer being reinforced. Bandura's analysis separates acquisition from performance: an observer can learn what to do without doing it, and whether the behavior appears depends on the incentives in force at the time. Four processes are required for learning itself, namely attention to the model, retention of what was seen, the motor capacity to reproduce it, and motivation.

The consequences the model receives matter, and they matter through the observer's expectations rather than through any reinforcement the observer has had. Seeing a model rewarded raises the observer's expectation that the behavior pays; seeing a model punished lowers it. Because the learning is already in place, offering the observer an incentive afterwards should reveal behavior that the punished condition suppressed.

Children watched a short film of an adult performing a sequence of four novel actions with a toy. The model was then rewarded, punished, or neither, in randomly assigned conditions. Each child was observed alone with the toy for five minutes, and then, in a second session, was offered a sticker for showing everything the adult had done (Table 1).

The incentive session is the crux. Without it the three groups differ sharply, from 3.1 down to 0.7 actions, but with an incentive they are nearly identical at about 3.4, which means the punished group had learned the sequence all along and was not performing it.

The design has limits. Children were observed once per session by observers who knew the condition, so scoring was not blind, and the second session always followed the first, so the rise could partly reflect practice or a second opportunity rather than the incentive alone. A group offered the incentive in the first session would settle that. The novel actions also have no meaning outside the study, which is deliberate, since it ensures the children could not have learned them earlier, but it leaves open whether consequences to a model work the same way for behavior a child already knows.

qs.q: What does the incentive session establish?
o: Stickers are a stronger reward than praise
The reward condition produced the most learning
Punishment prevented all of the children from learning
They showed 3.3 actions with an incentive.
The punished group had learned without performing
qs.x: Correct: A group that showed 0.7 actions without an incentive and 3.3 with one must have retained the sequence throughout, so the consequence to the model affected whether the behavior appeared rather than whether it was acquired. Why the others are wrong: The punished group clearly had learned, the three groups converge rather than ranking, and no comparison with praise was made. Trap: Reading low performance as an absence of learning.

qs.q: Which process is required for observational learning but not for performance?
o: Attending to what the model was doing
That is also needed in both phases.
Observers were not reinforced during learning.
Retention of what the model actually did
Correct: it must be stored to be used later.
Having the physical ability to perform it
That is needed for performance too.
qs.x: Correct: Retention is what carries the observed sequence from the film to a later opportunity, which is why the punished children could produce it in the second session despite not having produced it in the first. Why the others are wrong: Observers received no reinforcement, and motor capacity and attention bear on performance as well as on learning. Trap: Choosing reinforcement because it appears in most accounts of learning.

qs.q: Which feature of the procedure most weakens the conclusion about the incentive?
o: The actions shown in the film were novel ones
The incentive session always came second
Correct: order and incentive are confounded.
Each session lasted five minutes for every child
Children were assigned to conditions at random
qs.x: Correct: Because every child met the incentive only in the second session, a rise could reflect a second opportunity with the toy rather than the incentive, and a group offered the incentive first would distinguish them. Why the others are wrong: Random assignment, novel actions and a fixed session length all strengthen the design. Trap: Naming a control as though it were a flaw.

qs.q: Why does seeing a model punished reduce performance?
o: The observer has been punished directly
The observer cannot attend to a punished model
Punishment erases the memory of the actions
The second session shows it did not.
It lowers the observer's expectation of reward
Correct: expectancy, not the observer's own history.
qs.x: Correct: The observer forms an expectation about what the behavior will bring, and a punished model supplies evidence that it brings something unwelcome, which suppresses performance while leaving the learning in place. Why the others are wrong: The observer received nothing, the memory survived, and attention was clearly adequate for later reproduction. Trap: Treating vicarious punishment as if the observer had been punished.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?
o: Consequences to a model affect performance more than learning
Correct: the groups converge with an incentive.
Rewarding a model has no effect on behavior
Observational learning requires some kind of direct reinforcement
None was given, yet learning occurred.
Children imitate a punished model as readily
Without an incentive they showed 0.7 actions.
qs.x: Correct: The three groups differ by 2.4 actions without an incentive and by 0.2 with one, which places the effect of the model's consequences on whether the behavior is shown rather than on whether it was acquired. Why the others are wrong: Learning occurred without reinforcement, spontaneous imitation of the punished model was low, and the reward condition clearly raised performance. Trap: Drawing a conclusion from one column when the two columns tell the story.

passages.title: Social interactions · passage
text: Nonverbal communication includes facial expression, gaze, posture, gesture and paralanguage, the vocal qualities that accompany speech such as pitch, loudness and rate. Two claims about it are often confused. The first is that certain facial configurations associated with basic emotions are recognized above chance across cultures. The second is that the circumstances in which an expression may be shown are learned and vary widely; these are display rules.

The two claims are compatible, and separating them requires comparing kinds of nonverbal signal within the same experiment. A signal whose form is learned within a community, such as an emblematic hand gesture, should be recognized well at home and poorly elsewhere. A signal with a strong biological component should show a smaller drop.

Participants from four widely separated regions viewed the same set of stimuli, which included photographed facial expressions of basic emotions, culture-specific gestures drawn from each of the four regions, silent posture-only video clips, and speech filtered to remove words while preserving tone of voice. Each participant chose from a fixed list of emotion or meaning labels, so chance accuracy was the same throughout (Table 1).

The drop column is the comparison of interest. Gestures fall 57 points, while the other three signal types fall between 9 and 13 points, so the design separates a signal whose meaning is conventional from signals that carry a substantial amount of information across cultural boundaries.

The facial expression result supports partial rather than complete universality. Accuracy drops only 9 points but it does drop, and 79% is well above chance yet below the within-region figure, so the data are consistent with a recognizable core shaped by local conventions in labeling. What the design cannot address is the production side: these participants judged expressions, and whether people in the four regions produce the same expressions in the same situations is a separate question, which display rules would be expected to affect strongly. The fixed label list also constrains responses, and a free-response procedure typically yields lower cross-cultural agreement.

qs.q: Which stimulus type shows the strongest cultural specificity?
o: Tone of voice with the words filtered out
qs.x: Correct: Gestures are recognized at 91% within their own region and 34% elsewhere, a 57-point drop that dwarfs the 9 to 13 points seen for the other signals, which is what a learned, conventional meaning predicts. Why the others are wrong: Faces, tone of voice and posture all fall by about a tenth, retaining most of their accuracy across regions. Trap: Comparing the own-region column, where gestures actually score highest.

qs.q: What does the facial expression row support?
o: Partial universality, with recognition above chance everywhere but reduced
Complete universality, with no cross-cultural difference of any kind at all
No cross-cultural recognition of facial expressions
Faces and gestures behave in the same way
Gestures drop six times as much.
qs.x: Correct: Accuracy falls from 88% to 79%, which is a real reduction but leaves cross-region recognition far above chance, so the result supports a recognizable core together with some local influence rather than either extreme. Why the others are wrong: A 9-point drop is not zero, 79% is not failure, and gestures show a far larger drop. Trap: Forcing a graded result into one of two absolute positions.

qs.q: Which concept explains why a felt expression is suppressed in some settings?
o: That concerns the use of space.
qs.x: Correct: Display rules are the culturally learned conventions about which emotions may be shown, to whom and in what setting, and they account for suppression without requiring that the underlying emotion or its expression differ. Why the others are wrong: Paralanguage refers to vocal features, basic emotion theory addresses the expressions themselves, and proxemics concerns interpersonal distance. Trap: Choosing the theory that names the expressions rather than the rule governing their display.

qs.q: What does this experiment not address?
o: Whether tone of voice carries information across regions
Whether gestures are recognized better within their own region
Whether people in the four regions produce expressions alike
Whether posture alone can convey an emotional state
qs.x: Correct: Every participant was a judge of stimuli, so the study measures recognition, and it is silent on whether the same situations elicit the same expressions in the four regions, which is where display rules would be expected to act most strongly. Why the others are wrong: Within-region gesture recognition, cross-region tone of voice and posture-only accuracy are each reported in the table. Trap: Assuming a study of one side of a communicative act covers both.

qs.q: Which feature of the procedure most strengthens the comparison across stimulus types?
o: Accuracy was the dependent measure in every one of the conditions
A common outcome is necessary but not sufficient.
All participants saw the same stimuli with the same label list
Correct: chance level is held constant.
Participants were drawn from four widely separated regions
That is the sampling, not the control.
All of the participants tested were adults
Age was constant but is not the key.
qs.x: Correct: Because every region saw an identical stimulus set and chose from a fixed list, the chance level and the response demands are the same for all four signal types, so differences in the drop column reflect the signals rather than differences in procedure. Why the others are wrong: Sampling four regions makes the comparison possible without controlling it, a common outcome measure is a prerequisite, and adult samples do not address the comparison across stimulus types. Trap: Naming a sampling decision when the question asks about experimental control.

passages.title: Social interactions · passage
text: Attraction is shaped by several well-documented factors. Proximity raises the chance of interaction and of repeated exposure; similarity in attitudes and values supports liking; reciprocity, the perception that liking is returned, strengthens it; and physical attractiveness influences first impressions more than later ones. The mere exposure effect is the finding that repeated encounters with a stimulus increase liking for it, even when the encounters are brief and the stimulus is not consciously noted.

Proximity ordinarily cannot be studied cleanly, because people choose where to live and the choice correlates with everything that also predicts friendship. A setting in which location is assigned by chance removes that problem, which is why housing lotteries are so useful.

Residents of a newly opened apartment building, whose units were assigned by lottery among applicants, were surveyed after one year. For each pair of residents the survey recorded whether each named the other as a friend, and residents also estimated how often they encountered each other in a typical week (Table 1).

The gradient follows the number of encounters closely, from 41% and 12 encounters for adjacent units down to 6% and 1 encounter for units with no shared route, which is what a mechanism based on repeated exposure and opportunity for interaction predicts.

The lottery is what makes this informative, since residents did not choose their neighbors or their position in the building, so the gradient cannot be explained by people who were already similar having selected adjacent units.

Two limits remain. Encounters were estimated by the residents themselves after the friendships had formed, so people may recall more encounters with those they came to like, which would produce the correspondence between the two columns without encounters having caused anything. The design also cannot separate repeated exposure from opportunity for extended conversation, since both rise together with proximity; a condition in which people passed each other often but could not easily talk, as in a busy corridor, would begin to separate them.

qs.q: Why does the lottery strengthen this study?
o: The survey was administered after a full year
Timing is not what the lottery fixes.
Neither neighbors nor location was chosen
Four relationships between units were compared
That is the design, not the lottery.
Encounters were reported by the residents
That is a weakness rather than a strength.
qs.x: Correct: Because units were assigned by chance, residents who ended up adjacent are no more similar to one another than residents on different floors, so the friendship gradient cannot be attributed to like people having chosen to live near one another. Why the others are wrong: The one-year interval and the four-way comparison are separate features, and self-reported encounters are a limitation. Trap: Crediting randomization with fixing a measurement problem.

qs.q: Which mechanism do the encounter data most directly support?
qs.x: Correct: The only variable measured alongside friendship is the frequency of encounters, which rises from 1 to 12 per week in step with the friendship rate, so exposure is the mechanism these data speak to. Why the others are wrong: Similarity, reciprocity and attractiveness are all plausible influences that this study did not measure at all. Trap: Choosing a known cause of attraction that the study did not assess.

qs.q: Which finding would most complicate the proximity account?
o: Few friendships formed across different stairwells
Residents sharing a stairwell formed some friendships
That is consistent with the account.
Encounter frequency failed to predict friendship
Correct: the proposed route would be broken.
Adjacent residents reported the most friendships
qs.x: Correct: Proximity is supposed to work by producing encounters, so if encounters bore no relation to friendship the gradient would have to be explained some other way, and the mechanism would be in doubt. Why the others are wrong: Stairwell friendships, the adjacency result and the scarcity of cross-stairwell friendships are all predicted by the account. Trap: Picking a result that supports the account because it is the most prominent one.

qs.q: Which comparison in Table 1 isolates the effect of floor separation?
o: Adjacent doors against the units that are four doors apart
That varies distance on one floor.
Same floor four doors apart against the same stairwell
Correct: route length is similar, floor differs.
qs.x: Correct: Units four doors apart on one floor and units on different floors sharing a stairwell involve comparable walking distance, so the contrast between 22% and 19% isolates what crossing a floor adds, which turns out to be very little. Why the others are wrong: The other three comparisons vary horizontal distance, shared route or both together. Trap: Choosing the comparison with the largest difference rather than the one holding distance constant.

qs.q: What is the mere exposure effect?
o: Liking that follows from shared attitudes
Liking that follows from being liked in return
Liking that grows from repeated encounters
qs.x: Correct: Mere exposure is the increase in liking produced by repeated encounters alone, independent of what is learned about the stimulus, which is why it operates even for brief and unremarked encounters. Why the others are wrong: Shared attitudes, returned liking and appearance are separate and well-documented influences on attraction. Trap: Attaching the term to whichever cause of liking se

h: Share naming the other a friend
r: Adjacent doors on the same floor

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Health insurance affects access through coverage breadth, cost sharing, and network adequacy. Underinsurance describes having coverage that still leaves high out-of-pocket costs, and coverage alone does not guarantee timely care.
A survey of 5,000 adults recorded coverage type and care experiences (Table 1).

qs.q: Which group best illustrates underinsurance?
qs.x: Correct: Adults with high-deductible plans had coverage but still faced substantial out-of-pocket burden and frequent cost-related delay, which is the definition of underinsurance. Why the others are wrong: The uninsured are not insured at all, and the remaining groups show lower cost burden. Trap: Equating any access problem with underinsurance.

qs.q: Which barrier does the narrow network row highlight?
qs.x: Correct: With low cost burden but elevated delay, the limiting factor is the availability of participating providers. Why the others are wrong: Cost burden was low, coverage was present, and literacy was not measured. Trap: Attributing every access problem to cost.

qs.q: Which inference is unwarranted?
qs.x: Correct: People select or are sorted into coverage types by income, employment, and health, so a causal claim is not supported. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining statement is descriptive. Trap: Treating coverage categories as an assigned treatment.

qs.q: Which group least often had a usual source of care?
qs.x: Correct: Uninsured adults least often reported a usual source of care. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining group was higher. Trap: Reading the delay column.

qs.q: Which policy would the table most support?
qs.x: Correct: Because covered adults with high deductibles still delayed care, reducing cost sharing addresses the gap the table documents. Why the others are wrong: Coverage counts alone miss underinsurance, narrower networks worsen access, and data publication does not change costs. Trap: Measuring success by coverage rates alone.

h: Share delaying care due to cost
Mean out-of-pocket spending as a share of income
Share with a usual source of care

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: In aqueous solution, glucose exists almost entirely as a six-membered ring. The C5 hydroxyl attacks the C1 aldehyde, forming a cyclic hemiacetal whose C1 becomes a new stereocenter called the anomeric carbon. The two forms produced, α and β, differ only at that carbon: in α-D-glucopyranose the C1 hydroxyl is on the opposite side of the ring from the C6 group, and in β it is on the same side. The ring opens and closes continuously through the straight-chain aldehyde, so the two anomers interconvert, a process called mutarotation.

Because the anomers differ in shape, they rotate plane-polarized light differently. Freshly dissolved α-D-glucose has a specific rotation of +112°, pure β is +19°, and an equilibrium mixture settles at +52.7°.

A reducing sugar is one whose anomeric carbon is free to open to the aldehyde or ketone form, which can then be oxidized. Benedict's reagent, containing Cu²⁺, is reduced by such sugars and forms a brick-red precipitate. When the anomeric carbon is locked in a glycosidic bond, the sugar cannot open and gives no precipitate.
Students dissolved several sugars and measured optical rotation over time and the result of a Benedict's test (Table 1).

The hemiacetal carbon explains why glucose is a reducing sugar but is also only weakly reactive in the aldehyde form: at equilibrium, less than 0.01% of dissolved glucose is open-chain at any moment. That small fraction is enough for oxidation to proceed, because each molecule that reacts is replaced as the equilibrium re-establishes itself. The same slow exposure of the aldehyde lets glucose react with protein amino groups over time, forming the glycated hemoglobin measured as HbA1c in diabetes care.
Students also hydrolyzed sucrose with dilute acid. The rotation changed from +66.5° to −20° over 30 minutes, and the hydrolyzed solution gave a positive Benedict's test.

qs.q: Why do both pure anomers of glucose reach +52.7°?
o: The solvent rotates light by that amount
Light changes the structure of the sugar
The polarimeter does not alter the sugar.
Both anomers decompose to the same product
The ring opens and closes repeatedly
qs.x: Correct: Each anomer opens to the straight-chain aldehyde and closes again, producing the other anomer. Given time, both samples reach the same equilibrium mixture, about two-thirds β and one-third α, with a rotation of +52.7°. Why the others are wrong: Measuring rotation does not change the molecule; glucose is not decomposing; the water itself does not rotate light. Trap: Treating a change in rotation as a chemical reaction rather than a shift between forms.

qs.q: Why is sucrose not a reducing sugar while maltose is?
o: Sucrose is too large for the reagent
Both anomeric carbons are in its glycosidic bond
Sucrose contains fructose, which cannot be oxidized
Free fructose gives a positive test.
qs.x: Correct: In sucrose, C1 of glucose is joined to C2 of fructose, so the anomeric carbon of each sugar is tied up. Neither ring can open to an aldehyde or ketone, and no oxidation occurs. In maltose only one anomeric carbon is in the bond, leaving the other free. Why the others are wrong: Free fructose does reduce Benedict's reagent after isomerizing; size is not the obstacle; sucrose has many hydroxyls. Trap: Assuming a disaccharide cannot be a reducing sugar.

qs.q: Why does maltose's rotation change only slightly over six hours?
o: Only one anomeric carbon is free
Acid is needed for any mutarotation
Both of its rings open freely
One anomeric carbon is in the bond.
Maltose does not mutarotate at all
qs.x: Correct: Maltose has one free anomeric carbon, which equilibrates between α and β, and one locked in the α1→4 bond. Only part of the molecule can change, so the rotation shifts by a small amount rather than the 60° seen with glucose. Why the others are wrong: It does mutarotate; one ring is locked; glucose mutarotated in plain water. Trap: Expecting a yes-or-no answer where the structure allows a partial change.

qs.q: Why does the rotation of hydrolyzed sucrose become negative?
o: D-glucose is not converted to L-glucose.
Fructose rotates light to the left
Correct: it outweighs glucose's positive value.
Dilute acid is not optically active.
qs.x: Correct: Hydrolysis gives equal amounts of D-glucose (+52.7°) and D-fructose (−92°). Their sum is negative, so the solution's rotation passes through zero and ends near −20°. This is the origin of the name "invert sugar." Why the others are wrong: The products are still chiral; hydrolysis does not change configuration at every center; dilute acid does not rotate light. Trap: Assuming that mixing two sugars must give a positive rotation because glucose is positive.

qs.q: Why does methyl α-D-glucoside give a constant rotation and a negative test?
o: Methanol prevents oxidation of any sugar
The methyl group is bonded, not free.
Its anomeric carbon is an acetal
qs.x: Correct: Replacing the anomeric hydroxyl with a methoxy group converts the hemiacetal to an acetal, which is stable in neutral water. The ring cannot open, so the compound neither mutarotates nor reduces Benedict's reagent. Why the others are wrong: It is a glucose derivative with several stereocenters, and the methyl group is attached rather than present as free methanol. Trap: Overlooking that hemiacetals open while acetals do not.

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: An ester can be split into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol by hydrolysis, and the mechanism and outcome differ according to the catalyst. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is a reversible equilibrium that gives the carboxylic acid and the alcohol. Base-promoted hydrolysis, or saponification, gives the carboxylate salt and is effectively irreversible.

The difference in reversibility has a thermodynamic explanation. Under base, the carboxylic acid formed is immediately deprotonated to its carboxylate, which is not electrophilic and cannot be attacked by the alcohol, so the reaction cannot run backwards. Under acid, both products remain capable of recombining, and the position of equilibrium depends on the concentrations present.

A practical consequence is that acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is driven by using a large excess of water, while saponification needs only a stoichiometric amount of hydroxide, since nothing pulls the reaction back. The base is consumed rather than catalytic, which is why the term catalysis is inaccurate for it.
Methyl benzoate was hydrolyzed under both conditions, with the extent of reaction measured after four hours (Table 1).

The two conditions respond to stoichiometry quite differently. Under acid, reducing the water from a large excess to five equivalents lowers conversion from 87% to 52% because the equilibrium shifts back, while under base the conversion tracks the hydroxide supplied almost exactly, 96% with one equivalent and 49% with half.

The base result is the signature of an irreversible reaction consuming its reagent. Half an equivalent of hydroxide hydrolyzes about half the ester and then stops, which is what a reaction that cannot reverse and cannot regenerate its reagent must do.

Two further points apply. Recovering the free acid from a saponification requires acidifying the carboxylate afterwards, so the base route involves an extra step even though its conversion is higher. And the rates here are for a methyl ester; a bulkier alkoxy group slows attack at the carbonyl considerably, so these extents of reaction at four hours do not transfer to a tertiary ester.

qs.q: Why does half an equivalent of hydroxide stop at about half conversion?
o: The ester decomposes after four hours
Correct: it is a reagent here.
Hydroxide becomes less reactive over time
qs.x: Correct: Each ester molecule hydrolyzed consumes one hydroxide, and the carboxylate product cannot give it back, so the reaction stops when the hydroxide runs out rather than at an equilibrium position. Why the others are wrong: The reaction is effectively irreversible, hydroxide's reactivity is unchanged, and nothing indicates decomposition. Trap: Reading a stoichiometric limit as an equilibrium.

qs.q: Why is saponification effectively irreversible?
o: The carboxylate cannot be attacked by the alcohol
Hydroxide is a much stronger nucleophile than water
The alcohol evaporates from the mixture
The products are insoluble in the solvent
qs.x: Correct: Deprotonation of the acid gives a carboxylate whose negative charge removes the electrophilic character needed for the alcohol to attack, so the reverse reaction has no pathway. Why the others are wrong: Evaporation is not involved, nucleophile strength affects the forward rate, and the carboxylate salt is soluble. Trap: Explaining irreversibility by the removal of a product rather than by its unreactivity.

qs.q: Why does acid-catalyzed hydrolysis need excess water?
o: Water acts as the real catalyst in that route
The acid is diluted by the extra water
It shifts a reversible equilibrium forward
Water removes the alcohol as it forms
qs.x: Correct: Because the reaction is a genuine equilibrium, a large excess of one reactant pushes the position of equilibrium toward the products, which is why conversion falls from 87% to 52% when the water is limited. Why the others are wrong: The acid is the catalyst, dilution does not drive the equilibrium, and the alcohol is not removed. Trap: Assigning the role of catalyst to the reactant used in excess.

qs.q: How much does limiting the water cost in conversion under acid?
o: That compares the two hydroxide rows.
qs.x: Correct: Conversion falls from 87% with excess water to 52% with five equivalents, a loss of 35 points. Why the others are wrong: 47 points is the difference between the two hydroxide rows and the other values match no stated comparison. Trap: Comparing rows across the two different conditions.

qs.q: Why does the base route involve an extra step?
o: The hydroxide must be removed by distillation
The ester must be purified beforehand
Both routes start from the same ester.
The product precipitates and needs filtering
Filtering is not an extra chemical step.
The carboxylate must be acidified afterwards
Correct: to obtain the free acid.
qs.x: Correct: Saponification yields the carboxylate salt, so recovering the carboxylic acid itself requires a subsequent acidification that the acid-catalyzed route does not need. Why the others are wrong: Hydroxide is neutralized rather than distilled, the starting material is the same for both, and filtration is a workup detail rather than the chemical step at issue. Trap: Comparing two routes on conversion alone without counting the steps each requires.

r: 1 M sulfuric acid, water as solvent

passages.title: Translational motion, forces, work, energy, and equilibrium in living systems · passage
text: When a body segment rotates about a joint, the relevant quantity is torque: τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the axis to the point where the force acts and θ is the angle between r and the force. A muscle that inserts close to a joint has a small r, so it must generate a large force to produce a given torque, but a small shortening of the muscle produces a large movement at the end of the limb. Rotational equilibrium requires the sum of torques about any axis to be zero.

Researchers studied elbow flexion in 12 adults. The forearm was held horizontal while the participant supported a weight in the hand. The biceps tendon inserts about 4.0 cm from the elbow joint and pulls nearly vertically on the forearm in this position. The forearm plus hand has a mass of 1.6 kg with its center of mass 15 cm from the elbow, and the hand holds the weight 32 cm from the elbow.
