Urea does not dissolve membranes at this concentration.
Urea pumps Na⁺ into the cells actively
qs.x: Correct: Urea crosses the membrane until its concentration is equal on both sides. Inside, it adds to the cell's own impermeant solutes, so water enters and the cells swell and burst. The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic. Why the others are wrong: Urea is not a detergent; shrinking cells crenate; urea does not pump ions. Trap: Equating isosmotic with isotonic.

qs.q: Which solution caused the cells to shrink the most?
qs.x: Correct: 2.0% NaCl is hypertonic, so water leaves the cells and volume falls to 0.62. Why the others are wrong: 0.45% NaCl is hypotonic; sucrose and 0.9% NaCl are near isotonic. Trap: Confusing hypotonic and hypertonic.

qs.q: Why did only 45% of cells lyse in 0.45% NaCl?
o: Cells differ in how much swelling they withstand
Half the cells were already isotonic to the solution
All cells began at about 290 mOsm/L.
NaCl at this concentration repairs membranes
Half the cells lack aquaporins and cannot swell
qs.x: Correct: Older and more spherical RBCs have less spare membrane and burst sooner, so lysis in a moderately hypotonic solution is partial. Why the others are wrong: Average volume rose; salt has no repair effect; cells started with the same osmolarity. Trap: Expecting an all-or-none response from a population.

qs.q: Which term describes 300 mM sucrose relative to RBCs?
o: Sucrose does not cross the RBC membrane.
qs.x: Correct: Sucrose cannot cross the membrane and has nearly the same osmolarity as cytoplasm, so volume barely changes. Why the others are wrong: Large volume changes would occur in strongly hypo- or hypertonic solutions; sucrose is impermeant. Trap: Treating every solute as permeant like urea.

qs.q: A patient receives a large volume of 5% dextrose in water (about 280 mOsm/L) intravenously. What happens to RBC volume after the glucose is taken up and metabolized?
o: It decreases, because water moves into the kidney tubules
This does not determine RBC volume.
It decreases, because glucose raises plasma osmolarity
It stays the same, because the solution was isosmotic
Isosmotic is not isotonic once glucose is used.
It increases, because free water is left
Correct: the solution becomes effectively hypotonic.
qs.x: Correct: Glucose is transported into cells and metabolized, leaving water that dilutes plasma and causes cells to swell. Why the others are wrong: Glucose does not stay in plasma; isosmotic does not mean isotonic; renal handling does not set RBC volume directly. Trap: Judging tonicity by initial osmolarity alone.

passages.title: Self-identity · passage
text: Self-efficacy is the belief that one can carry out a specific action in a specific situation. It is not global self-worth; a person can hold high self-efficacy for public speaking and low self-efficacy for swimming. The distinction matters because self-efficacy predicts behavior in the domain it refers to, while global self-esteem predicts it weakly.

Four sources are proposed, and they are not interchangeable. Mastery experience, the direct experience of succeeding at a graded version of the task, is held to be the strongest, because it supplies evidence that is hard to discount. Vicarious experience works through observing a model, and depends on the observer judging the model to be similar to themselves. Verbal persuasion works through what a credible other says. The fourth source is the interpretation of physiological arousal: a racing heart read as fear lowers efficacy, while the same arousal read as readiness does not.

Eighty adults enrolled in a beginners' swimming course were randomly assigned to one of four confidence-building sessions held before their first attempt in deep water. Self-efficacy was rated on a ten-point scale immediately after the session, and completion of the deep-water swim was recorded (Table 1).

The ordering matches the theory's ranking, with mastery first and verbal persuasion last, and the two columns move together, which is what the construct predicts: efficacy ratings should track behavior in the same domain.

Three limits deserve note. The relaxation condition manipulated the level of arousal rather than its interpretation, so it does not test the fourth source as the theory states it; a condition reframing arousal as readiness would. Self-efficacy was also rated after the session but before the swim, so the ratings may partly reflect how encouraging each session felt rather than a stable belief. Finally, randomization was to session type, not to the outcome measure, and the instructor who recorded completions knew which session each participant had received.

qs.q: Which result in Table 1 fits the theory's ranking of the four sources?
o: Verbal encouragement outperformed watching a similar peer succeed
Relaxation training outperformed every one of the other approaches tested here
Graded mastery produced the highest rating and the highest completion rate
Correct: mastery is held to be strongest.
The four approaches produced essentially identical results
qs.x: Correct: The theory ranks mastery experience first, and the mastery condition leads on both the efficacy rating of 7.9 and the completion rate of 78%, with verbal persuasion last on both as the theory also predicts. Why the others are wrong: Relaxation ranked third, encouragement ranked below modeling, and the conditions differ substantially rather than being equivalent. Trap: Checking only one of the two columns before deciding the ranking holds.

qs.q: Why does the modeling condition use a peer judged to be similar?
o: Similarity makes the model's success feel relevant to the observer
Observing a similar peer eliminates physiological arousal
Similar peers are generally able to give much more accurate instruction
Peers who are similar swim faster than expert models do
qs.x: Correct: Vicarious experience works by inference, and the inference that a success is achievable for oneself is only warranted if the model is comparable, so similarity is what converts an observation into evidence about one's own capability. Why the others are wrong: Modeling involves watching rather than being taught, arousal is a distinct source, and swimming speed is irrelevant to the mechanism. Trap: Explaining a vicarious effect by the quality of the advice given.

qs.q: Why does the relaxation condition fail to test the fourth source as the theory states it?
o: The theory concerns how arousal is interpreted, not its level
Correct: the manipulation misses the construct.
Physiological arousal is unrelated to self-efficacy
Arousal cannot be manipulated in a swimming course
Relaxation training requires more than one practice session to work
qs.x: Correct: The source is the interpretation of arousal, so the appropriate manipulation reframes a racing heart as readiness rather than fear, whereas lowering arousal tests a different claim and leaves the interpretive step untouched. Why the others are wrong: The number of sessions is not what the theory specifies, arousal was manipulated successfully, and the theory treats arousal as one of its four sources. Trap: Accepting a condition as a test of a construct because it mentions the same physiological variable.

qs.q: How does self-efficacy differ from self-esteem?
o: It is a global evaluation of one's own worth
It refers to a specific task rather than to the self overall
It is unrelated to what a person actually does
It is a stable personality trait that is fixed quite early in life
qs.x: Correct: Self-efficacy is a judgment about performing a particular action in a particular setting, which is why it predicts behavior in that domain, while self-esteem is a global appraisal of worth that predicts specific behaviors only weakly. Why the others are wrong: Self-efficacy is changed by experience rather than fixed, it tracked completion in this trial, and the global appraisal described is self-esteem. Trap: Treating the two as interchangeable because both are beliefs about the self.

qs.q: Which feature of this trial most limits the conclusion drawn from the completion column?
o: Participants were randomly assigned to the four sessions
Self-efficacy was rated on a ten-point scale
The instructor recording completions knew the assigned condition
Twenty of the adults were assigned to each of the four conditions
qs.x: Correct: Completion of a deep-water swim involves judgment at the margin, and an instructor who knows which session a participant attended may encourage or evaluate differently, which can produce the group differences without any effect on belief. Why the others are wrong: Random assignment, a standard rating scale and equal group sizes all strengthen rather than weaken the design. Trap: Naming a design feature that protects the study instead of the one that leaves it open.

passages.title: Self-identity · passage
text: Erikson described development as a sequence of eight psychosocial stages, each posing a conflict whose resolution shapes what follows. The adolescent stage is identity versus role confusion, and it is followed in young adulthood by intimacy versus isolation, then generativity versus stagnation in midlife and integrity versus despair in late life. The sequencing claim is substantive: a person who has not formed a workable sense of who they are is held to be at a disadvantage in forming close relationships, because intimacy requires something to share.

Marcia operationalized the adolescent stage with two dimensions, exploration of alternatives and commitment to a choice, which cross to give four statuses. Achievement combines exploration with commitment. Moratorium is active exploration without commitment. Foreclosure is commitment without exploration, typically to a path adopted from family. Diffusion is neither.

Clinicians conducted semistructured interviews with 60 young adults aged 20 to 24 about career plans and values, and two raters classified each participant by status with disagreements resolved by discussion (Table 1).
The distribution is unremarkable for this age range, with moratorium and achievement most common, which is what a model placing identity work in the late teens and early twenties would expect.

What the design cannot do is test Erikson's sequencing claim, and that is its central limit. Status was measured once, in one age band, with no measure of the subsequent stage, so there is no way to ask whether identity achievement predicts later intimacy. Adding a measure of intimacy and following the same people forward would test it directly. Classification by interview also depends on the raters, and although two raters were used with disagreements resolved, agreement before discussion was not reported, so the reliability of the classification is unknown. The sample is small for estimating four proportions, and nothing here establishes that the four statuses are stable categories rather than positions a person moves through.

qs.q: Which status describes commitment without exploration?
o: Correct: a path is adopted without examining alternatives.
qs.x: Correct: Foreclosure is commitment reached without having explored alternatives, typically to a career or set of values taken over from family, and Table 1 records it as the only status with commitment but no exploration. Why the others are wrong: Moratorium is the reverse pattern, achievement has both, and diffusion has neither. Trap: Matching the status to how settled the person sounds rather than to the two dimensions.

qs.q: Which Eriksonian conflict follows identity versus role confusion?
o: Correct: it is the young-adult stage.
qs.x: Correct: Identity work in adolescence is followed in young adulthood by intimacy versus isolation, which is why the sequencing claim is that identity formation supports the capacity for close relationships. Why the others are wrong: Industry comes earlier in childhood, and generativity and integrity come later in midlife and old age. Trap: Choosing a later stage because it sounds more mature.

qs.q: Why can this study not test the sequencing claim?
o: No measure of the following stage was taken
Participants were young adults aged 20 to 24
That is the relevant age band.
Only four identity statuses were used
The interviews were semistructured in format
qs.x: Correct: The claim is that identity resolution affects the stage that follows, which requires measuring that later stage in the same people, and this study measured identity status alone at a single point in time. Why the others are wrong: The four-status scheme is standard, semistructured interviews are appropriate, and the age band is the one where identity work is expected. Trap: Naming a limitation of the method when the gap is a missing variable.

qs.q: Which status is the most common in this sample?
qs.x: Correct: Moratorium accounts for 31% of the sample, slightly ahead of achievement at 28%, which fits an age range in which many people are actively exploring without having settled. Why the others are wrong: Achievement is second at 28%, foreclosure third at 24%, and diffusion smallest at 17%. Trap: Choosing achievement because it is the status the model treats as the endpoint.

qs.q: What would most improve confidence in the classifications themselves?
o: Using three clinicians instead of two raters
More raters without a reliability figure.
Increasing the sample from 60 to 200 adults
That is what was already done.
qs.x: Correct: Agreement reached by discussion tells you nothing about how reproducible the coding is, so the informative statistic is how often the two raters agreed independently, before they conferred. Why the others are wrong: Discussion is the existing procedure, a larger sample sharpens the proportions rather than the coding, and adding raters without reporting their agreement leaves the same gap. Trap: Adding effort to a procedure instead of reporting the statistic that evaluates it.

passages.title: Atoms, nuclear decay, electronic structure, and atomic chemical behavior · passage
text: Radioactive decay is a random process at the level of a single nucleus but highly regular in bulk. The number of decays per second is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present, so the quantity falls exponentially and is characterized by a half-life: the interval over which half the nuclei remaining at any moment decay.

Positron emission tomography depends on this. A positron-emitting nucleus is incorporated into a molecule the body takes up, and the positron annihilates with a nearby electron to produce two photons travelling in opposite directions. Detecting both lets the scanner place the annihilation on a line, and many such lines reconstruct an image.

The half-life sets the logistics of the scan. Too short and the tracer decays before it can be delivered and taken up; too long and the patient carries an unnecessary dose after the images are acquired. The commonly used positron emitters span three orders of magnitude in half-life for this reason.
Four positron emitters were compared for the fraction remaining at fixed times after production (Table 1).

Fluorine-18 retains 88% of its activity after 20 minutes while oxygen-15 retains about one tenth of one percent, which is why fluorine-18 tracers can be produced centrally and shipped while oxygen-15 must be made beside the scanner.
The two shortest-lived nuclides are not tabulated at 110 minutes because the remaining fraction is far below anything detectable, not because the decay law has ceased to apply.

Two points qualify the comparison. The physical half-life is not the whole story, because the tracer is also cleared from the tissue biologically, and the effective half-life is shorter than the physical one. And the choice of nuclide is constrained by chemistry as well: a nuclide is only useful if it can be attached to a molecule the body handles in the way the study requires.

qs.q: Why must oxygen-15 be produced beside the scanner?
o: Almost none of it survives transport
Correct: its half-life is two minutes.
Its photons are too weak to detect
It cannot be attached to molecules
It is used in water tracers.
qs.x: Correct: With a 2.04 minute half-life, the activity falls by a factor of about 800 in 20 minutes, so any delivery time destroys the tracer. Why the others are wrong: Oxygen-15 is routinely used as labelled water, every positron annihilation gives the same 511 keV photons, and the constraint is physical rather than regulatory. Trap: Seeking a chemical or administrative reason for a limit set by the half-life.

qs.q: Why does detecting both photons locate the annihilation?
o: Their energies differ with the position
A photon carries no such record.
qs.x: Correct: The two photons are emitted back to back, so a pair detected at two points places the annihilation somewhere on the line joining them, and many lines intersect to give the distribution. Why the others are wrong: A photon carries no positional label, the energies are equal, and the arrival times differ only slightly. Trap: Imagining the information is in a single photon rather than in the geometry of the pair.

qs.q: Why is the effective half-life shorter than the physical one?
o: Decay rates are unaffected by it.
The dose is reduced before injection
The body also clears the tracer
qs.x: Correct: Activity in the tissue falls both because nuclei decay and because the molecule is excreted or metabolized, and the two processes combine to give a shorter effective half-life. Why the others are wrong: Nuclear decay is independent of the chemical environment, the scanner only detects photons, and the administered dose does not change any half-life. Trap: Assuming the physical half-life governs how long a tracer is actually present.

qs.q: By what factor does fluorine-18 exceed carbon-11 in fraction remaining at 110 minutes?
o: That is the ratio of the half-lives.
qs.x: Correct: Dividing 0.500 by 0.0237 gives about 21.1, so fluorine-18 retains twenty-one times as much activity at that point. Why the others are wrong: The other values are one of the fractions, the ratio of half-lives, and a half-life itself. Trap: Using the ratio of half-lives where the ratio of surviving fractions was asked.

qs.q: Why are the shortest-lived nuclides left blank at 110 minutes?
o: Decay stops after very many half-lives
The table has no room for them
qs.x: Correct: After 54 half-lives of oxygen-15 the surviving fraction is vanishingly small, so no number is reported, though the exponential law applies throughout. Why the others are wrong: Decay does not stop, those nuclides were measured at the earlier time, and the omission is not a formatting choice. Trap: Reading a blank entry as a failure of the decay law.

passages.title: Atoms, nuclear decay, electronic structure, and atomic chemical behavior · passage
text: The light emitted by a heated gas is not continuous but confined to particular wavelengths, and each element has its own pattern. This was known long before any explanation existed, and it was the hydrogen pattern, with its simple arithmetic regularity, that the first successful atomic model was built to reproduce.

That model assigns the electron to orbits of fixed energy, with the energy of the level inversely proportional to the square of an integer. Light is emitted when the electron moves from a higher level to a lower one, and the photon carries exactly the energy difference, so the wavelengths are determined by differences between two of these levels.

The arrangement explains why the lines crowd together toward short wavelengths: the levels themselves converge as the integer rises, so transitions from high levels differ little in energy. It also explains why the spectrum of each element differs, since the level pattern depends on the nuclear charge and on the other electrons present.
Hydrogen emission lines ending on the second level were measured and compared with the model (Table 1).

The agreement is exact to the precision quoted, which is why the model was accepted despite its arbitrary postulates. The spacing between successive lines shrinks from 170 nanometres between the first two to 24 nanometres between the last two, converging on the series limit.
The series limit corresponds to a transition from an unbound electron to the second level, and no line appears beyond it, only a continuum, because the initial energy is then no longer quantized.

Two limitations matter. The model reproduces hydrogen but fails for atoms with more than one electron, where the repulsion between electrons is not accounted for, and it offers no reason why the orbits should be stable at all. And it predicts single lines where careful measurement finds closely spaced components, which required a later treatment to explain.

qs.q: Why do the emission lines crowd together at short wavelengths?
o: Short wavelengths are harder to resolve
More transitions exist at high energy
The count is not the reason.
The energy levels converge further up
The electron moves faster at high levels
Speed does not set the spacing.
qs.x: Correct: Because the level energy goes as the inverse square of the integer, successive levels lie closer together, so transitions from high levels have nearly equal energies and nearly equal wavelengths. Why the others are wrong: The crowding is in the spectrum rather than in the instrument, orbital speed does not determine line spacing, and the number of transitions is not what compresses them. Trap: Blaming an instrumental limit for a pattern the energy levels require.

qs.q: Why does a continuum appear beyond the series limit?
o: The instrument is not at fault.
Levels above the limit are too close
They do not exist as levels.
The gas becomes opaque at that point
qs.x: Correct: Past the series limit the electron starts from an unbound state whose energy can take any value, so the emitted photon energies form a continuous range rather than discrete lines. Why the others are wrong: Opacity is not the mechanism, there are no bound levels beyond ionization, and the continuum is a property of the emission. Trap: Explaining a continuous spectrum by crowded lines rather than by unquantized initial states.

qs.q: Why does each element give a different line pattern?
o: Each element emits at its own temperature
Its level energies are different ones
Heavier atoms move more slowly in gas
qs.x: Correct: The spacing of the energy levels depends on the nuclear charge and on the shielding by other electrons, so each element has its own set of differences and therefore its own wavelengths. Why the others are wrong: Temperature affects how brightly lines appear, thermal motion broadens rather than positions them, and restating that the photons differ explains nothing. Trap: Accepting a restatement of the observation as its explanation.

qs.q: How much does the line spacing shrink across the series?
o: Those are the predicted and observed limit.
qs.x: Correct: The gap between the first two lines is about 170 nanometres and that between the last two is about 24 nanometres, so the spacing falls by roughly sevenfold. Why the others are wrong: The other pairs are wavelengths, energies, and the two values at the series limit. Trap: Quoting line positions where the question asks about the intervals between them.

qs.q: Why was the model nevertheless replaced?
o: Spectral lines were later found continuous
Computational cost was not an issue.
qs.x: Correct: The model reproduces hydrogen but cannot handle atoms where electrons repel one another, and it supplies no reason for the stability of its own orbits. Why the others are wrong: Its hydrogen predictions are excellent, the lines are still discrete, and the arithmetic is trivial. Trap: Assuming a superseded model must have been inaccurate in the case it was built for.

passages.title: Atoms, nuclear decay, electronic structure, and atomic chemical behavior · passage
text: Carbon-14 is produced continuously in the upper atmosphere when cosmic ray neutrons strike nitrogen. It mixes into atmospheric carbon dioxide and enters the food chain, so a living organism holds carbon with the same carbon-14 to carbon-12 ratio as its environment. At death the intake stops and the carbon-14 begins to decline with a 5,730 year half-life.

A date therefore follows from measuring the surviving ratio and comparing it with the living value. Because the decline is exponential, the measurable range is set by how small a ratio can be distinguished from background, which in practice limits the method to roughly fifty thousand years, or about nine half-lives.

The method rests on an assumption that the atmospheric production rate has been steady. It has not been exactly steady, and the record is corrected using tree rings and other independently dated material, which is why a raw radiocarbon age and a calibrated calendar age are reported separately.
Four samples were measured against a modern standard (Table 1).

The fraction remaining falls smoothly with age, and each sample's raw age follows from the number of half-lives its fraction represents. The calibrated ranges diverge increasingly from the raw ages for older samples, by about 2,000 years at the wooden post and 4,000 at the bone.
The divergence is systematic rather than random, since it reflects the known history of atmospheric carbon-14 rather than any error in the individual measurement.

Two cautions attach to the method. Contamination with modern carbon raises the apparent ratio and makes a sample look younger, and because the effect is proportionate it matters far more for old samples: one percent modern carbon has almost no effect on the linen but shifts the bone by thousands of years. And the date obtained is the date the organism stopped exchanging carbon, which for a wooden post is when the tree grew rather than when the post was set.

qs.q: Why does the method stop working past about fifty thousand years?
o: Too little carbon-14 remains to measure
The half-life itself changes over the time
Older samples contain no carbon at all
qs.x: Correct: After nine half-lives the surviving fraction is a few thousandths of a percent, which cannot be distinguished reliably from instrumental background. Why the others are wrong: Exponential decay never completes, the half-life is a constant, and old organic samples still contain abundant stable carbon. Trap: Treating a detection limit as the disappearance of the isotope.

qs.q: Why does contamination matter more for old samples?
o: The surviving signal is far smaller yet
Old samples absorb carbon more readily
The half-life is less reliable at age
It does not vary with age.
Contamination is heavier in old deposits
qs.x: Correct: One percent modern carbon added to a sample retaining 80% of the modern ratio is negligible, but added to one retaining 1.5% it roughly doubles the apparent ratio and shifts the age enormously. Why the others are wrong: Uptake is not the mechanism, the amount of contamination is not greater in older deposits, and the half-life does not change. Trap: Thinking an absolute amount of contamination has a fixed effect on the date.

qs.q: Why are raw and calibrated ages reported separately?
o: Raw ages are measured less precisely
Production has not been truly constant
qs.x: Correct: The raw age assumes a steady atmospheric carbon-14 ratio, and the calibrated age applies the measured history of that ratio from independently dated material. Why the others are wrong: Precision is comparable, calibration does not alter the half-life, and both refer to the same sample. Trap: Reading a calibration as a correction for measurement error.

qs.q: How many half-lives has the bone fragment undergone?
o: That is the raw age in years.
qs.x: Correct: A remaining fraction of 0.0154 corresponds to about 6.02 half-lives, since each halves the amount. Why the others are wrong: The other values are the fraction itself, another sample's figure, and the age in years. Trap: Confusing elapsed half-lives with the elapsed years they represent.

qs.q: Why is the post's date not the date the structure was built?
o: The post was contaminated after burial
It dates when the tree was growing
Wood cannot be dated by this method
qs.x: Correct: Carbon exchange ceases when the wood is laid down, so the measurement dates the growth of that part of the tree, which may precede the building by decades or centuries. Why the others are wrong: Wood is routinely dated, contamination is a different problem, and calibration corrects the atmospheric record rather than the use of the timber. Trap: Taking the date of a material as the date of the event it was used in.

passages.title: Nature of molecules and intermolecular interactions · passage
text: A molecule is chiral if it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, and the commonest cause is a carbon bearing four different groups. The two mirror-image forms, enantiomers, have identical melting points, boiling points, densities and solubilities in ordinary solvents, because every interaction they make with an achiral environment is identical.

They are distinguished only by something that is itself chiral. Plane-polarized light is rotated in opposite directions by the two forms, and a chiral reagent, a chiral solvent or a chiral surface interacts with them differently, which is what makes separation possible at all.

This is why biology discriminates between them. An enzyme's active site is chiral, so two enantiomers of a substrate bind with different affinities and react at different rates, and a drug's two enantiomers can differ in potency, in metabolism and in toxicity.
A racemic drug was analyzed by several methods (Table 1).

The two achiral methods give a single peak or fraction, as the identical physical properties require, while both chiral methods separate the enantiomers cleanly. The chiral acid works by converting the pair into two salts that are not mirror images of one another and therefore differ in solubility.

The salts formed in that last method are diastereomers rather than enantiomers, and diastereomers differ in every physical property, which is what makes the separation possible with ordinary crystallization.

Two qualifications apply. Chiral chromatography separates but does not by itself say which peak is which, so an independent assignment is needed, usually by comparison with a sample of known configuration. And the biological difference between enantiomers is not always large: some drugs are given as the racemate because the two forms are comparable in effect, and separating them would add manufacturing cost without any clinical benefit, so the decision is made case by case rather than as a rule.

qs.q: Why does ordinary chromatography give one peak?
o: Silica binds all organic compounds with equal strength
They have the same molecular mass
Mass is not what separates them.
qs.x: Correct: An achiral stationary phase offers the same interactions to both enantiomers, so they are retained identically and emerge together. Why the others are wrong: Their identical behavior follows from symmetry rather than coincidence, equal mass does not prevent chromatographic separation of other compounds, and silica does distinguish compounds by polarity. Trap: Reading a single peak as a coincidence rather than a consequence of symmetry.

qs.q: Why does a chiral acid allow crystallization to work?
o: It raises the melting points of both salts by the same amount
Equal changes would not separate them.
qs.x: Correct: Combining a racemate with a single enantiomer of an acid gives two salts that are not mirror images, and such diastereomers differ in solubility like any two distinct compounds. Why the others are wrong: Neither enantiomer is destroyed, the configuration is unchanged, and an equal change in both would separate nothing. Trap: Expecting a chiral reagent to alter the molecules rather than to pair them into distinguishable salts.

qs.q: Why can two enantiomers differ in toxicity?
o: Enantiomers are metabolized by completely different organs
Their reactivity matches in achiral media.
qs.x: Correct: Enzymes and receptors are built from chiral amino acids, so their binding sites accommodate the two forms differently and the biological consequences diverge. Why the others are wrong: Their physical properties in achiral media are identical, as is their reactivity there, and metabolism occurs in the same tissues. Trap: Looking for a physical difference between enantiomers where none exists.

qs.q: How many of the four methods separate the enantiomers?
o: That would include a chromatography on silica.
That counts the achiral methods too.
qs.x: Correct: The chiral chromatography and the crystallization with a chiral acid separate the pair; the two achiral methods do not. Why the others are wrong: The other counts include or exclude the achiral methods incorrectly. Trap: Counting any chromatographic method as a separation of enantiomers.

qs.q: Why is an independent assignment needed after chiral chromatography?
o: Retention order does not reveal configuration
Chiral columns give the two peaks in a random order each time
qs.x: Correct: A chiral column reliably separates the two forms but gives no information about which configuration is retained longer, so a known standard is required to assign the peaks. Why the others are wrong: The peaks are resolved, the sample survives, and the elution order is reproducible for a given column. Trap: Assuming a separation that distinguishes two species also identifies them.

passages.title: Nature of molecules and intermolecular interactions · passage
text: When more than one valid Lewis structure can be drawn for the same arrangement of atoms, the molecule is not any one of them and does not alternate between them. The real structure is a single one in which the electrons are spread over the atoms involved, and the drawn structures are a device for describing that distribution with lines and dots.

Delocalization lowers the energy, and the stabilization is largest when the contributing structures are equivalent. The carbonate ion, with three equivalent structures, has three identical carbon-oxygen bonds of a length between that of a double and a single bond, and no evidence of one being different from the others.

The consequences are measurable. Benzene's six carbon-carbon bonds are all the same length, intermediate between those of ethane and ethene, and its heat of hydrogenation is far less exothermic than three isolated double bonds would predict, the shortfall being the delocalization energy.
Bond lengths and hydrogenation enthalpies were compared (Table 1).

Benzene's hydrogenation releases 208 kilojoules per mole against the 360 predicted from three cyclohexene double bonds, a shortfall of 152 kilojoules that measures its delocalization energy. Its bonds are all 139 picometres, between the 133 of a double bond and the 154 of a single one.
The carbonate ion's three bonds are likewise identical, at 129 picometres, which is shorter than a carbon-oxygen single bond and longer than a double one.

Two qualifications apply. The equivalence of the drawn structures is a sufficient condition for strong delocalization but not a necessary one, and a molecule whose contributing structures differ in energy is still stabilized, only less so. And bond lengths intermediate between single and double are evidence of delocalization but are not proof of it on their own, since other effects such as hybridization also shift bond lengths.

qs.q: Why does benzene release less energy on hydrogenation than predicted?
o: Benzene has fewer than three double bonds to hydrogenate
qs.x: Correct: The delocalized starting material lies lower in energy than three isolated double bonds would, so less energy is given out on reaching the same product. Why the others are wrong: The product is ordinary cyclohexane, the reaction goes to completion, and three equivalents of hydrogen are consumed. Trap: Looking for the anomaly in the product when the starting material is the stabilized species.

qs.q: Why are all three carbonate bonds identical?
o: The ion rotates fast enough to average the bonds out
qs.x: Correct: The single real structure has the electrons spread over all three oxygens, so there is no sense in which one bond is a double bond and the others are not. Why the others are wrong: The molecule does not oscillate between structures, the charge distribution follows from the delocalization, and molecular rotation does not change bond lengths. Trap: Imagining resonance as rapid interconversion between the drawn forms.

qs.q: Why is equivalence not a necessary condition?
o: Delocalization occurs only in rings of alternating single and double bonds
qs.x: Correct: Any set of valid structures spreads the electrons and lowers the energy; equivalence maximizes the effect rather than being required for it. Why the others are wrong: Equivalence is common but not universal, unequal structures are legitimate contributors, and delocalization is not confined to aromatic rings. Trap: Converting a condition for maximum effect into a condition for any effect.

qs.q: What is benzene's delocalization energy from these data?
qs.x: Correct: The difference between the predicted 360 and the measured 208 kilojoules per mole is 152 kilojoules per mole. Why the others are wrong: The other values are the measured and predicted enthalpies and a reference compound's value. Trap: Quoting one enthalpy where the difference between two was requested.

qs.q: Why is an intermediate bond length not proof of delocalization?
o: Bond length depends only on the atoms joined, never on the electrons
qs.x: Correct: Hybridization and the electronegativity of neighbouring atoms also change bond lengths, so an intermediate value is consistent with delocalization without establishing it by itself. Why the others are wrong: Bond lengths are measured accurately, most bonds are not intermediate, and bond length depends on the electron distribution as well as on the atoms. Trap: Taking a single piece of consistent evidence as a demonstration.

passages.title: Nature of molecules and intermolecular interactions · passage
text: The shape of a molecule follows from the number of regions of electron density around its central atom, since those regions repel one another and adopt the arrangement that keeps them furthest apart. Two regions give a linear arrangement, three a trigonal plane, four a tetrahedron, five a trigonal bipyramid and six an octahedron.

A lone pair counts as a region but occupies more space than a bonding pair, because it is held by only one nucleus and spreads out. A lone pair therefore compresses the angles between the remaining bonds, which is why the bond angle in ammonia is less than the tetrahedral value and that in water is smaller still.

The arrangement of regions is not the same as the shape of the molecule, which describes only the positions of the atoms. Four regions with two lone pairs give a bent molecule even though the regions themselves are tetrahedrally arranged, and this distinction is what makes water polar.
Four molecules with four regions each were compared (Table 1).

The bond angle falls from 109.5 to 104.5 degrees as lone pairs are added, by about two and a half degrees per lone pair, which is what the greater spatial demand of a lone pair predicts. All four molecules have four regions of electron density around the central atom.
Hydrogen fluoride has only one bond, so no angle can be defined, although the electron arrangement around fluorine is still tetrahedral.

Two qualifications apply. The model predicts shapes well but says nothing about bond strength or reactivity, and two molecules with the same shape can behave entirely differently. And it treats a double bond as a single region, which is adequate for predicting approximate geometry but conceals the fact that the π system has its own spatial distribution, so the model should not be used to reason about where a reagent approaches.

qs.q: Why does a lone pair compress the bond angles?
o: It is closer to the nucleus
Lone pairs repel each other but not the bonding pairs nearby
Correct: held by one nucleus only.
qs.x: Correct: A lone pair is attracted by only one nucleus and therefore spreads out more than a bonding pair, pushing the bonding pairs closer together. Why the others are wrong: Both kinds of pair are negative, a lone pair extends further from the nucleus rather than closer, and it repels bonding pairs as well as other lone pairs. Trap: Explaining the compression by charge when both pair types are equally charged.

qs.q: Why is the electron arrangement not the molecular shape?
o: Lone pairs are not really present
Molecular shape is determined by the positions of all the electron regions
qs.x: Correct: The regions set the geometry of the electron distribution, but the shape named for the molecule refers only to where the atoms sit, so two lone pairs leave a bent molecule. Why the others are wrong: Lone pairs are real, the arrangement does not fluctuate, and shape by convention describes the atoms. Trap: Naming the shape from the electron arrangement rather than from the atoms.

qs.q: Why can no angle be defined for hydrogen fluoride?
o: Its electron arrangement is linear rather than tetrahedral
qs.x: Correct: A bond angle is defined between two bonds, and hydrogen fluoride has only one, so the quantity does not exist for it. Why the others are wrong: Fluorine carries three lone pairs, the molecule is polar, and the electron arrangement around fluorine is tetrahedral. Trap: Describing a diatomic molecule's geometry as if an angle were missing rather than undefined.

qs.q: By how much does the angle fall from methane to water?
qs.x: Correct: Subtracting 104.5 from 109.5 degrees gives a five degree reduction. Why the others are wrong: The other values are the per-lone-pair change and the two individual angles. Trap: Giving the change per lone pair where the total change was requested.

qs.q: Why should the model not be used to reason about reagent approach?
o: Electron regions move out of the way as a reagent approaches the molecule
That is not the limitation described.
A double bond counts as one region
Correct: its real shape is hidden.
The model gives the wrong shapes
qs.x: Correct: Treating a double bond as a single region gives the right approximate geometry but says nothing about the π system's distribution above and below the plane, which is what determines where a reagent can reach. Why the others are wrong: The predicted shapes are reliable, reagent approach is directional, and the stated limitation is about the model's simplification rather than about electron mobility. Trap: Extending a geometric model into a question about reactivity.
